knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Sign Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound sign abstraction for real scalar expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real scalar expression \(e\) with attainable-value set \(V(e)\subseteq\mathbb R\), scalar sign metadata is a sound tag drawn from \(\{\mathrm{zero},\mathrm{nonnegative},\mathrm{nonpositive},\mathrm{unknown}\}\). Soundness requires \[\mathrm{zero}:V(e)\subseteq\{0\},\qquad \mathrm{nonnegative}:V(e)\subseteq[0,\infty),\qquad \mathrm{nonpositive}:V(e)\subseteq(-\infty,0].\] The tag \(\mathrm{unknown}\) imposes no sign restriction. Because zero satisfies both weak inequalities, an implementation may retain the more precise zero tag or safely weaken it to either compatible tag. Metadata must overapproximate all admissible evaluations, never merely a sampled value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar sign metadata soundly overapproximates every attainable real value as zero, nonnegative, nonpositive, or unrestricted.
assumptions_latex: \(e\) is real and scalar valued.
\(V(e)\) contains all values allowed by the expression domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign tag is sound exactly when its associated set contains \(V(e)\).

notation.meaning: set of all attainable values of e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sound overapproximation formulation is coherent and fits scalar sign metadata, but the four-tag lattice and permitted weakening of zero are implementation-specific claims lacking an authoritative DCP metadata source.

children.title: Elementwise Sign Metadata
children.top_down_role: Entrywise sign classifications for vector or matrix expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Elementwise Sign Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound coordinatewise sign abstraction for real array expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e\) be a real array expression with index set \(I\) and attainable-value set \(V(e)\subseteq\mathbb R^I\). Elementwise sign metadata assigns each \(i\in I\) a tag \(\sigma_i\in\{\mathrm{zero},\mathrm{nonnegative},\mathrm{nonpositive},\mathrm{unknown}\}\). It is sound when every \(x\in V(e)\) satisfies the restriction associated with every coordinate tag: \(x_i=0\), \(x_i\geq0\), or \(x_i\leq0\), respectively, with no restriction for \(\mathrm{unknown}\). A uniform array tag is the special case \(\sigma_i=\sigma\) for all \(i\). Coordinatewise metadata asserts no relation between distinct entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elementwise sign metadata gives a sound sign restriction for each array entry but does not encode relationships among different entries.
assumptions_latex: \(e\) is real array valued.
\(V(e)\) includes every admissible evaluation of \(e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metadata is sound iff each tagged coordinate restriction holds for every \(x\in V(e)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise soundness definition fits the leaf and is internally consistent, but per-coordinate sign tags and the uniform-tag specialization are system-specific metadata choices with no cited source.

children.title: Cone-Order Metadata
children.top_down_role: Expression attributes relative to supported proper cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Order Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound order-sign abstraction for expressions valued in an ordered finite-dimensional vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space ordered by a closed, convex, pointed cone \(K\), with \(x\preceq_K y\) meaning \(y-x\in K\). For an expression \(e\) and its attainable-value set \(\mathcal V(e)\subseteq V\), cone-order metadata is a label in \(\{K,-K,0,?\}\). The labels are sound precisely when \(K\) implies \(\mathcal V(e)\subseteq K\), \(-K\) implies \(\mathcal V(e)\subseteq-K\), and \(0\) implies \(\mathcal V(e)\subseteq\{0\}\). The label \(?\) makes no order assertion; it may be returned whenever no preceding inclusion is certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone-order metadata soundly records whether every attainable expression value lies in a cone, its negative, or zero; unknown makes no order claim.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(K\subseteq V\) is closed, convex, and pointed.
\(\mathcal V(e)\) is the set of attainable values of \(e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(e)=K\Rightarrow\mathcal V(e)\subseteq K\), \(m(e)=-K\Rightarrow\mathcal V(e)\subseteq-K\), and \(m(e)=0\Rightarrow\mathcal V(e)\subseteq\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Partial order induced by the cone.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports general cone-order metadata semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Cone-Order Metadata leaf and its mathematical intent is plausible, but no inspectable source supports this particular metadata abstraction. In addition, the phrase “K implies” should formally read “m(e)=K implies”; sourcing is needed before settling the exact label semantics.

children.title: Matrix-Order Metadata
children.top_down_role: Positive-semidefinite, negative-semidefinite, plus unknown matrix-order classifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Order Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Löwner-order specialization of ordered-sign metadata for real symmetric matrix expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a symmetric matrix expression \(E\) of size \(n\), matrix-order metadata is a label in \(\{\mathrm{PSD},\mathrm{NSD},0,?\}\). Writing \(\mathcal V(E)\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) for its attainable matrices, soundness requires \(\mathrm{PSD}\) only if every \(X\in\mathcal V(E)\) satisfies \(X\succeq0\), \(\mathrm{NSD}\) only if every such \(X\) satisfies \(X\preceq0\), and \(0\) only if \(\mathcal V(E)\subseteq\{0\}\). The unknown label \(?\) asserts none of these inclusions. Thus the metadata uses the Löwner order, not entrywise comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-order metadata soundly classifies every attainable symmetric value as positive semidefinite, negative semidefinite, zero, or unresolved under the Löwner order.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a real symmetric matrix-valued expression of fixed size \(n\).
\(\mathcal V(E)\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) contains all attainable values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(E)=\mathrm{PSD}\Rightarrow\mathcal V(E)\subseteq\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(m(E)=\mathrm{NSD}\Rightarrow\mathcal V(E)\subseteq-\mathbb S_+^n\).

notation.meaning: Real symmetric matrices of size n.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.5 Monotonicity of the Löwner partial order p. 22

review_flags: Locator supports the Löwner order; modeling-metadata formulation requires review.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.5 Monotonicity of the Löwner partial order p. 22

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit Matrix-Order Metadata, and the Löwner-order formulas are standard. The cited locator supports the underlying partial order but does not establish the PSD/NSD/zero/unknown modeling-metadata convention, so a DCP or modeling-system source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Order-Information Loss
children.top_down_role: Operations or representations that weaken sign or generalized-order knowledge.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Information Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound but incomplete loss of order facts during compositional metadata propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nontrivial pointed cone and suppose metadata propagation uses only sound set inclusions for immediate subexpressions. For an expression \(u-u\), exact semantics gives the singleton value set \(\{0\}\). If the two occurrences are abstracted independently only by membership in \(K\), compositional subtraction yields the enclosure \(K-K\), which is generally contained in neither \(K\) nor \(-K\). The propagated label may therefore be \(?\), although the expression is identically zero. Such an unknown result records loss of relational information between repeated subexpressions, not failure of the underlying order property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent abstraction can forget relationships between repeated subexpressions, producing unknown order metadata even when the complete expression is identically zero.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nontrivial pointed convex cone.
Metadata propagation treats the two occurrences of \(u\) independently.
Only the enclosure \(u\in K\) is retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal V(u-u)=\{0\}\) while the compositional enclosure is \(K-K\), so a sound incomplete analyzer may return \(?\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski difference of the cone with itself.

review_flags: A source on incompleteness of compositional DCP metadata is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind correctly matches Order-Information Loss, and the repeated-subexpression example coherently illustrates a sound but incomplete abstraction. No cited source supports this compositional-analysis failure phenomenon or the assumed transfer behavior.

children.title: Curvature Metadata
children.top_down_role: Constant, affine, convex, concave, and unresolved classifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound curvature classification of scalar-valued expressions on a convex effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e:D\to\mathbb R\) be an expression on a convex set \(D\). Its curvature metadata is one label in \(\{\mathrm{constant},\mathrm{affine},\mathrm{convex},\mathrm{concave},?\}\). The convex label requires \(e(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\leq\theta e(x)+(1-\theta)e(y)\); the concave label reverses this inequality; and the affine label requires equality, for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\). Constant means \(e(x)=e(y)\) throughout \(D\). The label \(?\) means that the analyzer has certified none of these classes and does not imply nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature metadata soundly labels an expression as constant, affine, convex, concave, or unresolved on its convex effective domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is convex.
\(e:D\to\mathbb R\) is finite-valued on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each nonunknown label entails its defining equality or inequality for every \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\).
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses DCP curvature metadata.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Curvature Metadata and correctly distinguishes unknown from nonconvexity. The five-label DCP metadata convention and its treatment of constant and affine classes require an authoritative modeling-system source with a specific locator.

children.title: Argumentwise Monotonicity Metadata
children.top_down_role: Coordinate-sensitive and sign-dependent monotonicity classifications.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for sign- or domain-conditioned argument labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(t)=t^2\), \(f\) is nondecreasing on \([0,\infty)\) and nonincreasing on \(( -\infty,0]\), but it is neither nondecreasing nor nonincreasing on \(\mathbb R\). A monotonicity label inferred from sign metadata may therefore be used only while the argument is certified to remain in the associated sign region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The square function has opposite monotonicity on the two sign regions, so neither regional label applies when sign is unknown.
assumptions_latex: The usual order on \(\mathbb R\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\uparrow\text{ on }[0,\infty),\quad f\downarrow\text{ on }(-\infty,0],\quad f\text{ is not monotone on }\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.title: Regional Monotonicity Does Not Globalize
Argumentwise Monotonicity Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-argument monotonicity labels, optionally conditional on certified sign or domain regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\subseteq X_1\times\cdots\times X_p\to Y\), where each argument space and \(Y\) carry specified partial orders. For argument \(i\) and a certified region \(S\subseteq D\), monotonicity metadata is one of \(\{\uparrow,\downarrow,\mathrm{constant},?\}\). The label \(\uparrow\) requires \(f(x_{-i},u)\preceq f(x_{-i},v)\) whenever both tuples lie in \(S\) and \(u\preceq_i v\); \(\downarrow\) requires the reversed output inequality. Constant requires equality. A sign-dependent label is valid only while the argument tuple remains in its recorded region \(S\); \(?\) makes no monotonicity assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each argument receives a sound increasing, decreasing, constant, or unresolved label, possibly valid only on a certified sign or domain region.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_i\) and \(Y\) has a specified partial order.
\(S\subseteq D\) is the region certified for the label.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed \(x_{-i}\), the recorded nonunknown label governs all comparable \(u,v\) whose corresponding tuples belong to \(S\).

notation.meaning: Region on which the label is certified.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.5 Monotonicity of the Löwner partial order p. 22

review_flags: Locator is matrix-order-specific; general argumentwise metadata needs corroboration.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.5 Monotonicity of the Löwner partial order p. 22

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Argumentwise Monotonicity Metadata and explicitly handles partial orders and region-dependent labels. The cited matrix-analysis locator concerns Löwner-order monotonicity, not general per-argument or sign-dependent DCP metadata, so it does not support the stated abstraction.

children.title: Domain-Range Metadata
children.top_down_role: Explicit and atom-implied restrictions associated with expressions.

children.title: Explicit Domain Metadata
children.top_down_role: User-declared restrictions associated with variables, parameters, constraints, or expression contexts.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Domain Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain information introduced directly by declarations and user-written constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an expression \(e\) depending on model variables \(z\in Z\), explicit domain metadata is a represented set \(D_{\mathrm{exp}}(e)\subseteq Z\) obtained solely from variable declarations, structural attributes, and constraints explicitly present in the model syntax. It is sound when every assignment admitted by those declarations and explicit constraints belongs to \(D_{\mathrm{exp}}(e)\). It excludes restrictions contributed only by the domains of atomic functions occurring inside \(e\). If no informative explicit restriction is certified, the metadata may be the ambient set \(Z\), rather than an assertion that all assignments make \(e\) well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit domain metadata records restrictions written in model declarations or constraints, excluding restrictions contributed solely by atomic-function semantics.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) ranges over an ambient assignment space \(Z\).
Declarations and explicit constraints have well-defined feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{explicit\ feasible}}\subseteq D_{\mathrm{exp}}(e)\subseteq Z\), with atom-only restrictions omitted from its construction.

notation.meaning: Explicit domain metadata for the expression.

review_flags: The explicit-versus-implied domain convention requires a modeling-system source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Explicit Domain Metadata, but the separation between declarations, explicit constraints, and atom-only restrictions is system-specific. No source establishes this convention or whether the represented set is exact or an outer approximation.

children.title: Atom-Implied Domain Metadata
children.top_down_role: Input restrictions carried by atomic functions or structured operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Atom-Implied Domain Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive representation of restrictions contributed by atomic-function domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose an expression node has the form \(e=f(e_1,\ldots,e_p)\), where the atomic function \(f\) has domain \(D_f\subseteq Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_p\). Its atom-implied domain is represented recursively by
\[
D_{\mathrm{atom}}(e)=\bigcap_{i=1}^p D_{\mathrm{atom}}(e_i)\cap\{z:(e_1(z),\ldots,e_p(z))\in D_f\}.
\]
For a leaf carrying no atom restriction, take \(D_{\mathrm{atom}}(e_i)=Z\). Any computable metadata approximation \(\widehat D_{\mathrm{atom}}(e)\) is sound only if \(D_{\mathrm{atom}}(e)\subseteq\widehat D_{\mathrm{atom}}(e)\); thus it may omit precision but may not exclude an assignment on which every atom is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Atom-implied domain metadata recursively intersects child restrictions with the preimage of each atomic function’s domain.
assumptions_latex: All expressions depend on assignments \(z\in Z\).
Each atom \(f\) has a specified domain \(D_f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{atom}}(e)=\bigcap_iD_{\mathrm{atom}}(e_i)\cap(e_1,\ldots,e_p)^{-1}(D_f)\).

notation.meaning: Exact atom-implied domain of expression e.

review_flags: No supplied source covers recursive atom-domain propagation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits Atom-Implied Domain Metadata, and the recursive preimage formula is coherent when every child-domain set is interpreted in the common assignment space Z. A source is still required for this recursion and for the stipulated outer-approximation direction.

children.title: Value-Range Metadata
children.top_down_role: Known output signs, intervals, cones, value spaces, plus structural ranges.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Range Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound enclosure of values attainable over an expression’s certified effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e:D_e\to Y\) be an expression with effective domain \(D_e\) in assignment space \(Z\). Value-range metadata is a represented set \(R(e)\subseteq Y\) satisfying
\[
\{e(z):z\in D_e\}\subseteq R(e).
\]
The representation may be a sign class, interval, cone, matrix-order class, or the entire codomain \(Y\). Smaller valid enclosures are more informative. The unknown range is represented by \(Y\) and makes no claim beyond codomain membership. Range metadata concerns output values only and does not enlarge the assignments on which \(e\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Value-range metadata is any sound enclosure of all expression values attained on the effective domain; the whole codomain represents unknown range.
assumptions_latex: \(e:D_e\to Y\) is well-defined.
\(D_e\subseteq Z\) is the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(D_e)\subseteq R(e)\subseteq Y\).
review_flags: A source for the modeling-system range abstraction is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Value-Range Metadata and consistently describes an outer enclosure of attainable values. No cited source supports the modeling abstraction, its permitted representations, or the convention that the whole codomain denotes unknown range.

children.title: Domain–Value Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between admissible inputs, inferred output ranges, plus enclosing expression contexts.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain–Value Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency condition coupling effective-domain and value-range metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widehat D(e)\subseteq Z\) be certified inner domain information on which evaluation is guaranteed, and let \(R(e)\subseteq Y\) be value-range metadata. Domain–value consistency requires
\[
\forall z\in\widehat D(e),\qquad e(z)\text{ is defined and }e(z)\in R(e).
\]
If an atom additionally certifies a semantic implication \(z\in D_e\Rightarrow e(z)\in Q\), then range refinement to \(R(e)\cap Q\) is consistent. Conversely, a claimed range must not be used to admit assignments outside the effective domain \(D_e\); domain validity precedes evaluation and range classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On every assignment certified as evaluable, the expression must be defined and its value must lie in the recorded range.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat D(e)\) contains only assignments certified as evaluable.
\(R(e)\) is a proposed output-range enclosure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(\widehat D(e))\subseteq R(e)\), and range information does not imply membership outside \(D_e\).

notation.meaning: Assignments certified to lie in the effective domain.

review_flags: The choice of inner versus outer domain approximation needs system-specific sourcing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Domain–Value Consistency, but the statement specifically chooses inner domain information while neighboring records use outer enclosures for domain metadata. That polarity may be coherent for guaranteed evaluation, but it is system-specific and needs a source before the precise consistency condition can be accepted.

children.title: Unknown Metadata Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where available declarations do not determine domain or value classifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown Metadata Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unknown denotes insufficient static information, not a negative mathematical classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha\) be a sound metadata abstraction ordered by informativeness, with top element \(\top\) denoting no certified restriction. If an expression’s attainable domain or range cannot be enclosed more precisely using the analyzer’s available transfer rules, the corresponding metadata is \(\top\). Soundness requires only that the concrete set be contained in the concretization \(\gamma(\top)\), which is the relevant ambient domain or codomain. Consequently, unknown domain, range, sign, monotonicity, or curvature metadata does not imply undefinedness, unrestricted values, nonmonotonicity, or nonconvexity; it records failure to certify a stronger abstract fact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown metadata is the least informative sound result and records failure to certify a property, not failure of the property itself.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha\) is a sound abstraction with concretization map \(\gamma\).
\(\top\) is its least informative element.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C(e)\subseteq\gamma(\top)\), while no stricter classification follows from the unknown label.
review_flags: No supplied source establishes the abstract-interpretation convention for unknown DCP metadata.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits Unknown Metadata Regimes, and the distinction between failure to certify and falsity is appropriate. No source establishes the assumed abstraction order, concretization map, top-element convention, or its uniform application across domain, range, sign, monotonicity, and curvature metadata.

children.title: Extended-Value Domain Semantics
children.top_down_role: Treatment of restricted domains as part of function and set semantics.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Chapter 3, basic properties and operations preserving convexity

children.title: Atom-Implied Domains
children.top_down_role: Domain restrictions originating in atomic functions and sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Atom-Implied Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective-domain restrictions induced by extended-valued atomic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an atomic convex function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in X:f(x)<+\infty\}\); outside this set, its extended value is \(+\infty\). For an atomic concave function \(g:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\), define \(\operatorname{dom}g=\{x:g(x)>-\infty\}\), with value \(-\infty\) outside. When such an atom is composed with an argument expression \(h\), the atom-implied domain is the preimage \(h^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) or \(h^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}g)\). Nested expressions intersect these preimages over all atomic nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atom restricts its arguments to the preimage of its effective domain; nested expressions intersect the restrictions from every atom.
assumptions_latex: Convex atoms use the positive-infinity extended-value convention.
Concave atoms use the negative-infinity extended-value convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{f\circ h}=h^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), with intersections taken over nested atoms.

notation.meaning: Effective domain of an extended-valued atom.
Preimage of a set under the argument expression.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports extended-value DCP atom-domain semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Atom-Implied Domains and the extended-value conventions are standard, but no source is supplied. Moreover, the displayed equality for the domain of f composed with h requires h to be defined on the relevant assignments; otherwise the composition domain must also intersect the effective domain of h. A source is needed to settle the intended recursive formulation.

children.title: Implicit Domain Constraints
children.top_down_role: Model constraints induced by expression semantics rather than explicit syntax.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Domain Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility restrictions generated semantically by expression domains rather than written constraint syntax.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a model with explicit feasible set \(F_{\mathrm{exp}}\subseteq Z\) and expression trees whose atomic nodes are \(f_j(h_j(z))\). The implicit domain constraint generated by node \(j\) is \(h_j(z)\in\operatorname{dom}f_j\). Hence the semantic feasible set is
\[
F=F_{\mathrm{exp}}\cap\bigcap_j\{z\in Z:h_j(z)\in\operatorname{dom}f_j\}.
\]
These constraints apply even when absent from the user-written constraint list. A canonicalization may encode them explicitly, but it must preserve the displayed feasible set and the extended-value convention governing boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model feasibility equals the explicit feasible set intersected with every atomic expression’s domain preimage, even when those restrictions are unwritten.
assumptions_latex: All model expressions depend on assignments \(z\in Z\).
Each atomic node \(f_j\) has a specified effective domain.
\(F_{\mathrm{exp}}\) is the set defined by explicit constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=F_{\mathrm{exp}}\cap\bigcap_jh_j^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f_j)\).

notation.meaning: Argument tuple supplied to atom j.

review_flags: A disciplined-modeling source for implicit domain constraints is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits Implicit Domain Constraints, and the intersection formula is plausible when the indexed nodes include every atom in every semantically evaluated model expression. No disciplined-modeling source supports the formula, the treatment of unwritten constraints, or the canonicalization and boundary-semantics requirements.

children.title: Domain Boundary Semantics
children.top_down_role: Semantic treatment of open domains, limiting values, and singular boundaries.

children.title: Open-Domain Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Excluded boundary points associated with strict positivity, strict definiteness, or other open restrictions.

assumptions_latex: The ambient space is \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
The set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
The function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundary is excluded by assigning \(+\infty\) outside \(D\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex extended-value semantics for a function whose effective domain is open.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the extended-value function \(\bar f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) by
\[
\bar f(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\operatorname{dom}\bar f=D\). In particular, every point of \(\partial D\) is outside the effective domain even when \(f(x_k)\) has a finite limit along some sequence \(x_k\in D\) converging to that point. Thus feasibility requiring a finite value of \(\bar f\) enforces the strict domain condition \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open-domain convex atom takes its ordinary value inside the domain and positive infinity on the boundary and outside, thereby encoding strict domain feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Open-Domain Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the open-domain boundary container, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports the extended-value convention.

children.title: Finite Boundary Extensions
children.top_down_role: Finite limiting values assigned through lower-semicontinuous or upper-semicontinuous extension conventions.

assumptions_latex: The set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
The function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
For the boundary point \(x\in\partial D\), the interior limit exists and is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Assigning the finite interior limit at \(x\) gives the canonical lower-semicontinuous boundary value there.

notation.meaning: relative interior limit from the domain

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite extension at a boundary point where the full interior limit is well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
L_x=\lim_{y\to x,\,y\in D}f(y)\in\mathbb{R},
\]
define \(f_{\mathrm{ext}}(x)=L_x\) and retain \(f_{\mathrm{ext}}(y)=f(y)\) for \(y\in D\). Equivalently, the lower-semicontinuous boundary assignment is
\[
f_{\mathrm{ext}}(x)=\liminf_{y\to x,\,y\in D}f(y)=L_x.
\]
This assignment includes \(x\) in the effective domain. Extending simultaneously to boundary points with finite interior limits yields the finite-valued portion of the closed convex extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every interior approach to a boundary point has the same finite limit, that limit supplies the canonical closed boundary value.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Boundary Extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-limit construction fits the container, but the claims of canonical lower-semicontinuous extension and preservation under simultaneous boundary extension require a cited source.

children.title: Infinite Boundary Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extended-real boundary values used to encode inadmissible or limiting arguments.

assumptions_latex: The set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and convex.
The function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
A point \(x\in\overline D\setminus D\) satisfies \(\liminf_{y\to x,\,y\in D}f(y)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed extended-value assignment at \(x\) is \(+\infty\), so \(x\) remains outside the effective domain.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary divergence for a proper convex function represented with extended values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At such a boundary point, the lower-semicontinuous extension satisfies
\[
(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\liminf_{y\to x,\,y\in D}f(y)=+\infty.
\]
Consequently, \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{cl}f)\). Any sequence \((x_k)\subset D\) with \(x_k\to x\) has objective values unbounded above in the liminf sense. In extended-value modeling, assigning \(+\infty\) therefore records both the singular limiting behavior and exclusion of the boundary point from finite-valued feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a convex function diverges to positive infinity at a boundary, its closed extension is infinite there and the boundary remains outside its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Boundary Extensions

children.title: Closure Conventions
children.top_down_role: Library choices governing closed extensions of functions, sets, epigraphs, or hypographs.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional ambient-space lower-semicontinuous closure convention for proper convex extended-value functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), define its lower-semicontinuous closure in the Euclidean topology by
\[
\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y).
\]
In finite dimensions, the Fenchel--Moreau theorem gives
\[
\operatorname{cl}f=f^{**}.
\]
Thus boundary values are fixed by ambient lower-semicontinuous closure rather than by arbitrary pointwise assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure convention closes the epigraph in the ambient Euclidean space, equivalently taking ambient lower-limit values. For a proper finite-dimensional convex function, this closure equals its Fenchel biconjugate.
assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex.
Closures and limits use the Euclidean topology of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lower-semicontinuous closure satisfies \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}\) and \(\operatorname{cl}f=f^{**}\).

children.title: Singular Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Rank-deficient, zero-denominator, logarithmic, spectral, plus matrix-singularity boundary cases.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical restricted-domain scalar atoms illustrating singular boundaries in convex models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the restricted-domain atoms \(\phi:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\psi_p:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(\phi(t)=-\log t\) and \(\psi_p(t)=t^{-p}\), where \(p>0\). Both are convex on \((0,\infty)\), and
\[
\lim_{t\downarrow0}\phi(t)=+\infty,
\qquad
\lim_{t\downarrow0}\psi_p(t)=+\infty.
\]
Their closed extended-value representations on \(\mathbb{R}\) assign \(+\infty\) whenever \(t\leq0\). Thus an argument reaching a nonpositive value crosses the declared singular boundary and has no finite value under these atom conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As convex atoms declared on the positive half-line, the negative logarithm and positive inverse powers diverge at zero and take positive infinity at nonpositive arguments in their closed extended-value representations.
assumptions_latex: The scalar argument satisfies \(t>0\).
The exponent satisfies \(p>0\).
The formulas are treated as atoms whose declared domain is \((0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restricted-domain atoms \(-\log t\) and \(t^{-p}\) are convex on \((0,\infty)\) and diverge to \(+\infty\) as \(t\downarrow0\).

children.title: Leaf Expression Classes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes affinity in optimization variables from joint dependence on variables and parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameter \(\theta\) is constant with respect to the optimization variables during a solve. Consequently, for fixed \(\theta\), the expression \(x\mapsto\theta x\) is affine in \(x\). This does not make \((x,\theta)\mapsto\theta x\) jointly affine: the joint expression is generally bilinear. Parameter leaves are therefore affine terminals relative to the solve variables, not jointly affine variables of an enlarged problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter is constant relative to one solve: theta times x is affine in x for fixed theta but generally bilinear jointly in x and theta.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is an optimization variable.
\(\theta\) is assigned before the solve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\mapsto\theta x\text{ is affine for fixed }\theta,\quad (x,\theta)\mapsto\theta x\text{ is generally bilinear.}
knowledge_statements.title: Solve-Time Parameter Affinity Boundary

assumptions_latex: Expressions take values in a specified finite-dimensional scalar, vector, or matrix space.
Each parameter value is fixed before optimization begins.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficiency but Not Completeness of Composition Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convex expression not certified by the standard curvature-monotonicity composition rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard DCP composition rule is sufficient but not necessary for mathematical convexity or concavity. For the scalar atoms \(h(t)=\sqrt{t}\) on \(t\ge 0\) and \(g(x)=x^2\), \[h(g(x))=\sqrt{x^2}=|x|,\] which is convex. Nevertheless, the ordinary concave, nondecreasing signature of \(h\) does not certify composition with the convex nonaffine argument \(g\). Acceptance requires simplification or an additional registered rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DCP composition rules are sufficient, not complete: square root of a square is convex but is not certified by the ordinary concave-increasing composition rule.
assumptions_latex: The square and square-root atoms have their standard real domains and curvature metadata.
No special simplification or additional composition rule is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sqrt{x^2}=|x|\text{ is convex but is not certified by the ordinary composition rule for }\sqrt{\cdot}.

notation.meaning: Concave nondecreasing square-root atom on the nonnegative reals

knowledge_statements.title: Sufficiency but Not Completeness of Composition Rules
Atomic Function Applications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard argument-wise DCP composition conditions for registered atomic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h\) be a registered atom with domain, curvature, and argument-wise monotonicity metadata, and let \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) be dimension-compatible expressions. If \(h\) is convex, the standard composition rule certifies \(h(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\) as convex when, for every argument \(i\), at least one of the following holds: \(g_i\) is affine; \(h\) is nondecreasing in argument \(i\) and \(g_i\) is convex; or \(h\) is nonincreasing in argument \(i\) and \(g_i\) is concave. If \(h\) is concave, the corresponding rule uses affine arguments, nondecreasing arguments that are concave, or nonincreasing arguments that are convex. In every case the values must satisfy
\[
(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\in\operatorname{dom}h.
\]
An application is classified as affine when the applicable affine or structural rule certifies that classification; registered special rules may provide additional certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A registered atom application receives a standard DCP certificate when each argument satisfies the curvature and monotonicity rule for the atom and the argument tuple lies in its domain. Affine classification requires an applicable affine or structural rule, while registered special rules may add further certificates.
assumptions_latex: The atom \(h\) has registered domain, curvature, and argument-wise monotonicity metadata.
Each expression \(g_i\), for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), has certified curvature and dimensions compatible with argument \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard DCP composition rule certifies \(h(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\) when every argument satisfies the appropriate curvature-monotonicity condition and \((g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\in\operatorname{dom}h\).

children.title: Addition Operators

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature propagation for dimension-compatible pointwise addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For expressions \(e_1,e_2\) with identical dimensions and values in a common real vector space, addition is the affine map \((u,v)\mapsto u+v\). Hence \(e_1+e_2\) is affine when both operands are affine, convex when both are convex, and concave when both are concave. Adding an affine expression preserves the other operand's convexity or concavity. No generic DCP curvature certificate follows solely from one operand being nonaffine convex and the other nonaffine concave. For example, \(x^2+(-\tfrac12x^2)=\tfrac12x^2\) is convex, whereas \(x^2+(-2x^2)=-x^2\) is concave, although the operand curvature tags have the same convex-plus-concave pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible expressions add pointwise. Like curvatures and affine perturbations are preserved, but a generic convex-plus-concave mixture has no determined curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) have identical dimensions.
Their values lie in a common real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{curv}(e_1+e_2)\text{ follows the stated affine, convex, and concave closure rules; a convex-plus-concave tag pair alone is inconclusive.}
knowledge_statements.title: Addition Curvature Rules

assumptions_latex: The expressions \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) have identical dimensions.

Subtraction is represented as
\[
e_1-e_2=e_1+(-e_2).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient representation of a two-sided matrix multiplication operator with fixed outer factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times m}\) and \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\) be constant. The map \(L:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}\), \(L(X)=AXB\), is linear, and column-wise vectorization gives \[\operatorname{vec}(AXB)=(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X).\] Thus two-sided multiplication by fixed, dimension-compatible matrices preserves affine dependence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjoint operation on complex matrix expressions viewed through the underlying real affine calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For compatible complex matrices, \[(\alpha X+\beta Y)^*=\overline{\alpha}X^*+\overline{\beta}Y^*.\] Hence \(X\mapsto X^*\) is conjugate-linear over \(\mathbb{C}\), linear over the underlying real vector spaces, and involutive: \((X^*)^*=X\). Consequently, conjugate transpose preserves affine dependence when complex expressions are represented by real and imaginary coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature preservation when the complete inner mapping is affine.

No monotonicity assumption on \(h\) is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave-Outer Composition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard argumentwise DCP composition rule for a concave scalar outer function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(g_i:C\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(h:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) be concave with \(g(x)=(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\in D\). Then \(h\circ g\) is concave if, for every coordinate \(i\), one of the following holds on the relevant domain: \(h\) is nondecreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i\) is concave; \(h\) is nonincreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i\) is convex; or \(g_i\) is affine. Monotonicity may be restricted to the range implied by the known domain and sign of \(g_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave outer function yields a concave composition when each inner curvature agrees with the outer function’s coordinatewise monotonicity.

\(h\) is concave and \(g(C)\subseteq D\).

children.title: Sign-Dependent Composition Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when the certified range crosses regions on which the outer function has opposite monotonicities.

The range of \(g\) intersects both sign regimes, and \((h\circ g)(x)=(x^2-1)^2\) is not convex because \((h\circ g)''(0)=-4\).

Sign-Dependent Composition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition rule when an outer atom’s monotonicity changes across sign-defined regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:C\to I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) and let \(h:I\to\mathbb{R}\) have known curvature but monotonicity that varies across \(I\). Thus, if \(h\) is convex and nondecreasing on \(I_+\), then convex \(g\) with \(g(C)\subseteq I_+\) makes \(h\circ g\) convex; if \(h\) is convex and nonincreasing on \(I_-\), then concave \(g\) with \(g(C)\subseteq I_-\) does so. If the range crosses regimes and \(g\) is nonaffine, this rule alone gives no curvature certificate.

children.title: Coordinatewise Vector Composition

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Vector Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature propagation for a vector map whose components are composed coordinate by coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(g_i:C\to I_i\), and define \(F:C\to\mathbb{R}^m\) by \(F_i(x)=h_i(g_i(x))\). Each component is classified independently: \(F_i\) is convex when \(h_i\) is convex and either nondecreasing with convex \(g_i\), nonincreasing with concave \(g_i\), or composed with affine \(g_i\). Replacing convex by concave and reversing the compatible inner curvatures gives the concave case. Consequently, \(F\) is componentwise convex or componentwise concave exactly when every component receives the corresponding scalar certificate; no scalar curvature is assigned to the vector as a whole without an order convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinatewise vector composition applies the scalar composition rule separately to each output component and requires an order convention for vector curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
\(g_i(C)\subseteq I_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) has the claimed componentwise curvature precisely when each \(F_i=h_i\circ g_i\) has that scalar curvature.

notation.meaning: The ith coordinate of the composed vector map.

children.title: Product-Order Composition
children.top_down_role: Composition regimes governed by componentwise inequalities in product cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Order Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector composition under the coordinatewise partial order induced by the nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(\mathbb{R}^m\) with the product order \(u\preceq v\) when \(u_i\leq v_i\) for all \(i\). Let \(G:C\to\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfy \(G(tx+(1-t)y)\preceq tG(x)+(1-t)G(y)\), equivalently, let every component of \(G\) be convex. If \(h:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex, product-order nondecreasing, and \(G(C)\subseteq D\), then \(h\circ G\) is convex. The corresponding concave rule holds when \(G\) is componentwise concave and \(h\) is concave and product-order nondecreasing. Coordinate reversals may be represented by reversing the associated component order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product-order monotone convex outer function composed with a componentwise convex vector map is convex; the concave analogue is symmetric.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) are convex.
\(G(C)\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\circ G\) is convex under the convex hypotheses, and concave under their stated concave analogues.

notation.meaning: Coordinatewise product order on Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concavity counterpart of ordered convex composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a convex cone. If \(h:D\to\mathbb R\) is concave and \(K\)-nondecreasing and \(G:C\to D\) is \(K\)-concave, meaning \(tG(x)+(1-t)G(y)\preceq_K G(tx+(1-t)y)\), then \(h\circ G\) is concave. If \(h\) is \(K\)-nonincreasing, the same conclusion holds when \(G\) is \(K\)-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave cone-monotone outer function preserves concavity under the matching ordered curvature of the inner map.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(D\) are convex.
\(G(C)\subseteq D\).
\(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a convex cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Monotone Concave Composition
Cone-Monotone Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered convex composition for a vector map under an order induced by a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a convex cone and write \(u\preceq_K v\) when \(v-u\in K\). A map \(G:C\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is \(K\)-convex if \(G(tx+(1-t)y)\preceq_K tG(x)+(1-t)G(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). If \(h:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and \(K\)-nondecreasing, meaning \(u\preceq_K v\) implies \(h(u)\leq h(v)\), and if \(G(C)\subseteq D\), then \(h\circ G\) is convex. Replacing \(K\) by \(-K\) gives the order-reversing formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function monotone for a cone order remains convex after composition with a vector map convex in that order.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) are convex.
\(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a convex cone and \(G(C)\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is }K\text{-convex and }h\text{ is convex and }K\text{-nondecreasing}\implies h\circ G\text{ is convex}.\)

notation.meaning: Partial preorder induced by the cone K.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-monotone composition specialized to symmetric matrices and the Loewner order.

children.title: Incomparable-Order Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-order failure when the scalar outer function lacks compatible Loewner monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb S^2\), let \(h(X)=X_{11}-X_{22}\), which is affine but neither Loewner-nondecreasing nor Loewner-nonincreasing. The maps \(G_1(x)=\operatorname{diag}(x^2,0)\) and \(G_2(x)=\operatorname{diag}(0,x^2)\) are both matrix convex. Nevertheless, \((h\circ G_1)(x)=x^2\) is convex and \((h\circ G_2)(x)=-x^2\) is concave and nonaffine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two matrix-convex inner maps yield opposite scalar curvatures under the same outer function when it lacks Loewner monotonicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Loewner-Order Monotonicity Boundary
Incomparable-Order Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of ordered composition when the outer function does not respect the inner map’s order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Use the product order on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and define the affine convex outer function \(h(z_1,z_2)=z_1-z_2\), which is neither product-order nondecreasing nor product-order nonincreasing. Both maps \(G_1(x)=(x^2,0)\) and \(G_2(x)=(0,x^2)\) are product-order convex on \(\mathbb{R}\). Nevertheless, \((h\circ G_1)(x)=x^2\) is convex, whereas \((h\circ G_2)(x)=-x^2\) is concave and nonaffine. Hence product-order convexity of an inner map, without compatible outer monotonicity, cannot determine the curvature of the scalar composition.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Orientation Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DCP admissibility conditions for minimization and maximization objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the feasible set described by admissible DCP constraints, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) or \(g:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\) be scalar objective expressions. The problem \(\operatorname{minimize}_{x\in C} f(x)\) is DCP-admissible only when \(f\) is certified convex. The problem \(\operatorname{maximize}_{x\in C} g(x)\) is DCP-admissible only when \(g\) is certified concave. An affine objective satisfies both orientations. A concave nonaffine minimization objective or convex nonaffine maximization objective is outside the disciplined convex problem form, regardless of whether a particular instance has an easily found optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DCP permits convex minimization and concave maximization objectives; affine objectives may be used in either orientation.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is represented by DCP-admissible constraints.
The objective is scalar and has a certified curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in C}f(x)\text{ requires convex }f,\qquad \max_{x\in C}g(x)\text{ requires concave }g.\)

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the modeled problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave maximization as convex minimization by sign reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-orientation equivalence for convex and quasiconvex programs over an unchanged feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\max_{x\in X} f_0(x)\), where \(X\) is defined by convex inequalities \(f_i(x)\leq 0\) and affine equalities \(a_j^Tx=b_j\). If \(f_0\) is concave, this is equivalent to the convex minimization problem \(\min_{x\in X}-f_0(x)\). If \(f_0\) is quasiconcave, then \(-f_0\) is quasiconvex and the same sign reversal gives the corresponding quasiconvex minimization form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximizing a concave objective under convex inequalities and affine equalities is equivalent to minimizing its convex negative over the same feasible set. Likewise, quasiconcave maximization becomes quasiconvex minimization.
assumptions_latex: f_0\text{ is concave, respectively quasiconcave}
f_i\text{ is convex for }i=1,\ldots,m
a_j^Tx=b_j\text{ are affine equality constraints}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between ordinary DCP scalar inequalities and strict feasibility conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A strict scalar constraint \(f(x)<g(x)\) generally defines an open feasible set and cannot in general be replaced exactly by \(f(x)\leq g(x)-\varepsilon\) for a prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\); the latter imposes a stronger margin. The standard closed scalar DCP interface therefore uses non-strict inequalities. Strict feasibility is instead a qualification or a separately justified margin condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict inequalities are not generally equivalent to non-strict inequalities with an arbitrary positive margin and lie outside the standard closed DCP interface.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are real-valued on their common domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f<g\not\equiv f\leq g-\varepsilon\) in general for a prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Inequality Boundary
Scalar Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature-oriented admissibility rule for scalar inequalities in disciplined convex problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be scalar expressions on a convex domain \(C\). The inequality \(f(x)\leq g(x)\) is DCP-admissible when \(f\) is convex and \(g\) is concave; equivalently, the convex expression \(f-g\) is constrained by \(f(x)-g(x)\leq0\). The inequality \(f(x)\geq g(x)\) is admissible when \(f\) is concave and \(g\) is convex; equivalently, \(g(x)-f(x)\leq0\). Affine expressions satisfy either curvature role. Inequalities with the opposite nonaffine orientation are not certified by the scalar DCP inequality rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar DCP inequality places a convex expression below a concave one, or equivalently a concave expression above a convex one.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
\(f\) and \(g\) are scalar expressions with certified curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\leq g\text{ is admissible if }f\text{ is convex and }g\text{ is concave};\quad f\geq g\text{ uses the reversed roles}.\)

Then the equality constraint \(u(x)=v(x)\) is admitted by the DCP grammar. Defining \(h=u-v\), the same constraint can be written as \(h(x)=0\), and \(h\) is affine. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why general convex or concave residuals are not admitted as equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity of an equality residual does not generally make its zero-level set convex. For \(f(x)=x^2-1\), the function is convex on \(\mathbb R\), but \(\{x:f(x)=0\}=\{-1,1\}\) is not convex. Thus curvature metadata weaker than affinity cannot generally justify equality admissibility, although particular nonlinear equalities may have convex solution sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonlinear convex equality can have a nonconvex feasible set, so the disciplined equality rule requires affine sides.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Representation of Vector Affine Equalities

Hence a vector affine equality is exactly a finite conjunction of scalar affine equalities, and both descriptions define the same affine feasible set.

Convex-Set Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Membership interface for a fixed convex set in a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a fixed convex set represented by the modeling library, and let \(z:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be certified affine. The membership constraint \(z(x)\in C\) is admissible. Indeed, its feasible set is the affine preimage \(z^{-1}(C)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:z(x)\in C\}\), which is convex. Membership in a set depending nonaffinely on decision variables is not covered by this interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine expression may be constrained to a fixed library-represented convex set; its affine preimage is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is fixed and convex.
\(z\) is certified affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint \(z(x)\in C\) is convex-set-membership admissible.

source_refs.locator: 1. Basic Concepts of Convex Analysis p. 1

source_witnesses.locator: 1. Basic Concepts of Convex Analysis p. 1

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition and its finite-dimensional affine-preimage argument are mathematically precise and fit the leaf, but the cited general convex-analysis chapter does not specifically support the claimed modeling-library or DCP membership rule.

children.title: Cone Membership
children.top_down_role: Constraints represented directly as membership in supported cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic specialization of fixed convex-set membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a fixed convex cone known to the modeling system, and let \(z(x)=Ax+b\) be affine. The conic constraint \(z(x)\in K\) is admissible and has feasible set \(\{x:Ax+b\in K\}\). This set is convex because it is an affine preimage of \(K\). Closedness or pointedness of \(K\) is not required for convexity, although a solver interface may impose such additional representability conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership of an affine expression in a fixed convex cone is a convex conic constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a fixed convex cone.
\(z(x)=Ax+b\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set \(\{x:z(x)\in K\}\) is convex.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Semidefinite cone and semidefinite programs p. 139

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Semidefinite cone and semidefinite programs p. 139

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical claim is standard and the condition kind fits, but the cited locator is specifically a semidefinite-cone section and does not inspectably support the statement for an arbitrary fixed convex cone or its generic modeling-system admissibility.

children.title: Cone-Ordered Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Generalized inequalities interpreted through an associated cone order.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic structure induced by an ordering cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a convex cone and define \(a\preceq_K b\iff b-a\in K\). Then \(\preceq_K\) is reflexive and transitive. It is antisymmetric, hence a partial order, exactly when \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone induces a preorder and induces a partial order exactly when it is pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\preceq_K\text{ is a partial order}\iff K\cap(-K)=\{0\}.\)

notation.meaning: Relation induced by the cone K

knowledge_statements.title: Preorder and Partial-Order Conditions
Cone-Ordered Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between cone order and cone membership for affine expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), define \(a\preceq_K b\) by \(b-a\in K\). If \(u,v:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) are affine, then
\[u(x)\preceq_K v(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v(x)-u(x)\in K.\]
Thus a cone-ordered affine inequality is exactly a cone-membership constraint. Its feasible set is convex because \(v-u\) is affine and \(K\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone-ordered affine inequality is equivalent to requiring the affine difference of its right and left sides to lie in the cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone.
\(u\) and \(v\) are affine with codomain \(\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint \(u(x)\preceq_K v(x)\) is equivalent to \(v(x)-u(x)\in K\) and is convex.

notation.meaning: Partial preorder induced by the cone

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Semidefinite cone and semidefinite programs p. 139

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Semidefinite cone and semidefinite programs p. 139

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly converts a cone-ordered inequality into cone membership. However, the supplied locator concerns the semidefinite cone and is too narrow to support the arbitrary-convex-cone formulation. Also, without pointedness the induced relation is a preorder rather than a partial order, although the statement itself does not rely on antisymmetry.

children.title: Semidefinite Inequalities
children.top_down_role: Symmetric or Hermitian matrix inequalities under positive-semidefinite order.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix inequality interpreted through the positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F,G:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{S}^p\) be affine symmetric-matrix-valued expressions. The semidefinite inequality \(F(x)\preceq G(x)\) means
\[G(x)-F(x)\in\mathbb{S}_+^p,\]
where \(\mathbb{S}_+^p\) is the cone of positive-semidefinite matrices. Equivalently, \(y^{\mathsf T}(G(x)-F(x))y\geq0\) for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^p\). The constraint is convex because it is affine membership in a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine semidefinite inequality requires the matrix difference to be positive semidefinite, equivalently to have nonnegative quadratic forms in every direction.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(G\) are affine and symmetric-matrix-valued.
Both expressions take values in \(\mathbb{S}^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(F(x)\preceq G(x)\) is an admissible convex cone constraint.

notation.meaning: Real symmetric matrices of order p

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Semidefinite cone and semidefinite programs p. 139
2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Semidefinite cone and semidefinite programs p. 139
2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complex Hermitian analogue of the real symmetric semidefinite interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F,G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb H^p\) be affine Hermitian-matrix-valued expressions. Then \[F(x)\preceq G(x)\iff G(x)-F(x)\in\mathbb H_+^p\iff y^*(G(x)-F(x))y\geq0\quad\forall y\in\mathbb C^p.\] This constraint defines a convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hermitian variant uses the complex positive-semidefinite cone and nonnegative Hermitian quadratic forms.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(G\) are affine Hermitian-matrix-valued expressions of the same size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)\preceq G(x)\) is affine membership in \(\mathbb H_+^p\).
knowledge_statements.title: Hermitian Semidefinite-Inequality Variant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral equivalent of a real affine semidefinite inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric affine matrix expressions \(F,G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb S^p\), \[F(x)\preceq G(x)\iff \lambda_{\min}(G(x)-F(x))\geq0.\] Equivalently, every eigenvalue of the ordered difference is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite inequality holds exactly when the ordered difference has nonnegative minimum eigenvalue.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)\) and \(G(x)\) are symmetric matrices of the same size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)\preceq G(x)\iff\lambda_{\min}(G(x)-F(x))\geq0.\)

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Eigenvalue Formulation

children.title: Membership Admissibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Unsupported sets, incompatible dimensions, nonaffine cone arguments, plus missing structural attributes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when the fixed membership target is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{-1,1\}\) and \(z(x)=x\). The affine membership constraint \(z(x)\in C\) has feasible set \(\{-1,1\}\), which is not convex. Affine dependence is therefore insufficient when the target is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine member expression can produce a nonconvex feasible set when the target itself is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonconvex \(C\) can make \(z^{-1}(C)\) nonconvex even for affine \(z\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Target Counterexample

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the generic membership rule for a nonaffine member expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[1,\infty)\) and \(z(x)=x^2\). Although \(C\) is closed and convex, \[\{x:z(x)\in C\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty),\] which is not convex. Thus a convex target does not make an arbitrary nonaffine preimage convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed closed convex target can have a nonconvex preimage under a nonaffine expression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^{-1}(C)\) need not be convex when \(z\) is nonaffine.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonaffine Member Counterexample

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Difference between mathematical convexity and availability of a certified modeling representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed set \(C\) may be mathematically convex yet unavailable to the generic membership interface when the modeling system has neither a primitive target for \(C\) nor a trusted exact representation of it. Convexity of \(C\) establishes convexity of affine preimages but does not by itself furnish a finite canonicalization or an admissibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mathematical convexity alone does not make a target admissible when no primitive or trusted exact representation is available.
assumptions_latex: The interface accepts only registered primitives or trusted exact reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ convex}\not\Rightarrow C\text{ is supported by the membership grammar}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Convex Targets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-formedness boundary for set and cone membership expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A membership expression \(z(x)\in C\) is well formed only when the codomain of \(z\) matches the ambient space of \(C\). Structured targets impose additional requirements; for example, membership in \(\mathbb S_+^p\) requires a \(p\times p\) symmetric matrix expression unless an explicit symmetrization convention is provided. A dimension mismatch or missing required structural attribute makes the interface expression ill typed rather than merely infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership requires compatible dimensions and every structural attribute demanded by the target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{codom}(z)=\operatorname{amb}(C)\) and the target's structural type must be certified.
knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Space and Structural Typing Failures

assumptions_latex: The generic membership rule has no dedicated certificate for variable-dependent sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Variable-dependent convex-set membership is not generically DCP-admissible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating certified fixed-set membership from generally nonconvex variable-dependent membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity of every fiber \(C(x)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) does not imply convexity of \(\{x:z(x)\in C(x)\}\). For example, take \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \(z(x)=x\), and \(C(x)=\{x^2\}\). Every fiber is a singleton and hence convex, but membership becomes \(x=x^2\), whose feasible set is \(\{0,1\}\), which is not convex. Therefore the generic membership rule requires a fixed certified convex set and an affine member expression, unless a dedicated trusted rule supplies a stronger certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex fibers alone do not ensure convex membership: variable-dependent sets can yield nonconvex feasible sets, so the generic rule requires a fixed set and affine expression.
knowledge_statements.title: Membership Admissibility Boundaries

children.title: DCP Soundness Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Correctness of accepted expressions and problems together with dependence on the trusted atom library.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Convexity verification by construction

children.title: Expression-Curvature Soundness
children.top_down_role: Correctness of curvature classifications produced by the grammar.

knowledge_statements.title: Expression-Curvature Soundness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural soundness theorem for recursive DCP curvature inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an expression tree whose leaves have correct affine, convex, or concave classifications and whose internal nodes are trusted atoms with valid curvature, domain, and argument-monotonicity metadata. Suppose each composition is accepted only when the standard monotone-composition rule verifies every argument. Then the recursively assigned classification is sound: an expression labeled convex is convex on its recorded domain, one labeled concave is concave there, and one labeled affine is both convex and concave there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Correct atom metadata and valid composition checks guarantee that every curvature label inferred recursively is mathematically correct on the recorded domain.
assumptions_latex: Leaf classifications are correct.
Every atom's curvature, domain, and monotonicity metadata are correct.
Every composition passes the applicable DCP composition rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every inferred affine, convex, or concave classification is valid on the expression's recorded domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem has suitable hypotheses and matches expression-curvature soundness, but no citation supports the formal recursive soundness claim or the exact composition-rule assumptions.

children.title: Problem-Convexity Soundness
children.top_down_role: Correctness of accepted objective and constraint combinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem-Convexity Soundness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness of top-level DCP objective and constraint admissibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume all expression curvature and domain certificates are sound. A minimization problem with a certified convex objective, convex inequalities \(f_i(x)\leq0\), affine equalities \(h_j(x)=0\), and certified convex-set memberships \(z_k(x)\in C_k\) has a convex feasible set and convex objective. Dually, a maximization problem is convex-form admissible when its objective is concave and the same constraint rules hold. Hence every problem accepted by these top-level rules is a convex optimization problem on its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sound expression certificates plus correctly oriented objectives, convex inequalities, affine equalities, and convex memberships ensure that an accepted problem is convex.
assumptions_latex: All constituent expression and domain certificates are sound.
Each \(C_k\) is fixed and convex.
Every \(z_k\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted problem has a convex feasible set and the required convex minimization or concave maximization objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem correctly combines convex objectives, convex sublevel constraints, affine equalities, and affine preimages of fixed convex sets. Its exact DCP top-level soundness formulation nevertheless has no cited source.

children.title: Domain Preservation
children.top_down_role: Retention of atom-implied restrictions during certification.

assumptions_latex: Each trusted atom has a correct joint-domain specification.
Canonicalization preserves every specified atom-domain restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every certified feasible point belongs to the joint domain of every atom occurrence in the expression graph.

notation.meaning: Certified joint domain of atom occurrence q
Atom-induced effective domain of the expression graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation of atom domains through an accepted expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a finite expression graph depend on \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\mathcal{A}\) index its atom occurrences. For each \(q\in\mathcal{A}\), write the occurrence as \(a_q(e_{q1},\ldots,e_{q r_q})\), and let \(D_q\) be its certified joint argument domain. Recursive certification retains the atom-induced domain
\[D_{\mathrm{atom}}=\bigcap_{q\in\mathcal{A}}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:(e_{q1}(x),\ldots,e_{q r_q}(x))\in D_q\}.\]
Acceptance must preserve every such restriction, either explicitly or through an equivalent canonical constraint. Consequently, every point declared feasible lies in the domain of every evaluated atom; deleting a nonredundant atom-domain restriction invalidates this guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound checker intersects all atom-implied domains and preserves them explicitly or canonically, ensuring every feasible point makes every atom well-defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Preservation

children.title: Library-Relative Certification
children.top_down_role: Dependence of recognition scope on available trusted atoms and sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic incompleteness of certification relative to a fixed trusted library.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a trusted DCP registry \(\mathcal L\). Two expressions \(e_1,e_2\) may define the same function on the same effective domain while only one has a derivation using the atoms and composition rules of \(\mathcal L\). Thus \(\mathcal L\)-certifiability concerns an available representation and derivation, not solely the represented function; failure for one representation neither disproves convexity nor precludes certification after an equivalent rewrite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent formulas can receive different DCP outcomes because certification is representation- and library-relative.
assumptions_latex: \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) agree pointwise on the same effective domain.
The registry \(\mathcal L\) is fixed and sound but need not be complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Noncertification of \(e_1\) does not imply nonconvexity or noncertification of an equivalent \(e_2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Dependent Nonrecognition
Library-Relative Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition is relative to the trusted atom, set, and composition-rule registry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be a trusted registry of atoms, sets, domains, curvature labels, monotonicities, and composition rules. A model is \(\mathcal{L}\)-certifiable when it has an expression representation whose leaves and internal nodes are recognized by \(\mathcal{L}\) and whose recursive rule applications succeed. If \(\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathcal{L}'\) and every certificate in \(\mathcal{L}\) is retained unchanged, then every \(\mathcal{L}\)-certifiable model is \(\mathcal{L}'\)-certifiable. Failure of certification establishes only nonrecognition relative to the registry, not nonconvexity of the represented function or problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DCP recognition depends on the trusted library; extending a consistent library can certify more models, while rejection does not prove nonconvexity.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{L}'\) retains all certificates and rules of \(\mathcal{L}\).
Registry entries used by certification are sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Certification is monotone under sound registry extension, and noncertification is not a nonconvexity certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle is internally coherent, fits the library-relative leaf, and correctly distinguishes nonrecognition from nonconvexity. No source is provided for the defined certification model or its monotonicity under registry extension.

children.title: DCP Checker Architecture
children.top_down_role: Implementation families for metadata propagation and grammatical validation.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: DCP analysis and expression diagnostics

children.title: Bottom-Up Metadata Analysis
children.top_down_role: Recursive analysis over expression trees or DAGs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic recursive metadata analysis over a finite expression tree or DAG, excluding registry implementation, top-level problem rules, and caching policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite expression DAG with edges from children to parents. Initialize leaf metadata from declared constants, variables, and parameters. Process nonleaves in a child-before-parent topological order. At \(v=a(v_1,\ldots,v_r)\), apply the selected atom contract and DCP composition transfer to the current child metadata, producing either node metadata or a local failure. If all reached transfers succeed, the root metadata equals recursive evaluation of the same transfers. With transfer cost \(T_v\), total work is \(O(|V|+|E|+\sum_v T_v)\); termination follows from finiteness and acyclicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process a finite expression DAG from leaves to roots, applying each atom's metadata transfer after its children. The result equals recursive transfer evaluation, terminates, and costs graph traversal plus the transfer costs.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
Each local transfer is deterministic for its selected contract and child metadata.
Leaf declarations and selected atom contracts are trusted inputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_{\mathrm{root}}=\operatorname{Eval}_{\mathrm{transfer}}(G),\qquad \operatorname{work}=O\!\left(|V|+|E|+\sum_{v\in V}T_v\right).

notation.meaning: Metadata or local failure at node v
Cost of the local transfer at node v

knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic Bottom-Up Transfer Analysis
