children.title: Weighted-Sum Atoms
children.top_down_role: Affine combinations of scalar or array expressions using admissible numerical weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Sum Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-coefficient affine combination of equally shaped expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), and let \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\in\mathbb{R}\) be fixed coefficients. For \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_k)\in V^k\), define the weighted-sum atom by \[S(X_1,\ldots,X_k)=\sum_{i=1}^k a_iX_i.\] For all \(X,Y\in V^k\) and every \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\), where tuple operations are componentwise, \[S(\theta X+(1-\theta)Y)=\theta S(X)+(1-\theta)S(Y).\] Hence \(S\) is affine jointly in its arguments, independently of the coefficient signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted-sum atom multiplies equally shaped inputs by fixed real coefficients and adds them; the resulting map is affine regardless of coefficient signs.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(k\in\mathbb{N}\).
\(X_i\in V\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\).
\(a_i\in\mathbb{R}\) are fixed during optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(X_1,\ldots,X_k)=\sum_{i=1}^k a_iX_i\) is affine jointly in its arguments.

children.title: Scalar Offset Atoms
children.top_down_role: Addition of fixed or parameterized scalar offsets to compatible expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Offset Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Addition of a fixed scalar offset to a scalar expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scalar input \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) and a fixed scalar \(b\in\mathbb{R}\), the scalar-offset atom is \[T_b(x)=x+b.\] For all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\), \[T_b(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)=\theta T_b(x)+(1-\theta)T_b(y).\] Thus \(T_b\) is affine. In disciplined convex modeling, \(b\) must be numerical data or a parameter fixed for the optimization instance; an optimization variable is not an offset parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar-offset atom adds a fixed scalar to a scalar input and is an affine scalar map; the offset must remain fixed during optimization.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).
\(b\in\mathbb{R}\) is fixed during optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_b(x)=x+b\) is an affine scalar map.

children.title: Array Offset Atoms
children.top_down_role: Addition of fixed or parameterized vector or matrix offsets under supported shape rules.

knowledge_statements.title: Array Offset Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entrywise addition of a fixed array with compatible shape.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be fixed. The array-offset atom is \[T_B(X)=X+B,\] where addition is entrywise. For all compatible arrays \(X,Y\) and every \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\), \[T_B(\theta X+(1-\theta)Y)=\theta T_B(X)+(1-\theta)T_B(Y).\] Thus the atom is affine. Any broadcasting convention is admissible only when it deterministically expands fixed data to the input shape before applying this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An array-offset atom adds fixed, shape-compatible data entrywise. It is affine; broadcasting is valid only when its expansion rule is fixed and unambiguous.
assumptions_latex: \(X,B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\).
\(B\) is fixed during optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_B(X)=X+B\) is an affine map on \(\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\).

children.title: Coefficient Admissibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Variable-dependent coefficients, incompatible dimensions, unsupported broadcasting, plus uncertified parameter roles.

knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient Admissibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between fixed affine coefficients and variable-dependent bilinear products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an affine-combination atom \(S(X)=\sum_{i=1}^k a_iX_i+B\), each coefficient \(a_i\) and offset \(B\) must be fixed with respect to the optimization variables. Their signs are unrestricted when every \(X_i\) is affine. If a coefficient depends nontrivially on an optimization variable, the product is generally not affine and cannot be admitted as an affine atom. Concretely, \(g(x,y)=xy\) has Hessian \[\nabla^2g(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\] whose eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(-1\); hence \(g\) is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed coefficients may have any sign, but variable-dependent coefficients create products such as xy, which are generally neither affine nor convex or concave.
assumptions_latex: All affine-combination inputs have compatible shapes.
Parameters called fixed do not vary within the optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed coefficients preserve affinity; variable-dependent coefficients are inadmissible in general, as witnessed by \(g(x,y)=xy\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary affine-map criterion and bilinear Hessian counterexample
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-coefficient boundary and bilinear counterexample are correct and appropriately classified as a failure boundary, but the record lacks an inspectable citation.

children.title: Indexing Atoms

knowledge_statements.title: Indexing Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed coordinate selection, repetition, or slicing as a linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(I=(i_1,\ldots,i_p)\) be a fixed sequence with \(i_j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The indexing atom is \[E_I(x)=(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_p})=S_Ix,\] where row \(j\) of \(S_I\in\{0,1\}^{p\times n}\) is the coordinate row vector selecting \(i_j\). Because \(I\) is fixed, \(E_I\) is linear, including when indices are repeated or reordered. Multidimensional fixed slicing is the same construction after a fixed vectorization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed index or slice selects, repeats, or reorders coordinates through a selection matrix, so indexing is linear in its input.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
The index sequence \(I\) is fixed independently of optimization variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_I(x)=S_Ix\) is a linear map.

children.title: Reshaping Atoms
children.top_down_role: Rank or dimension changes that preserve expression entries under declared ordering conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reshaping Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shape change preserving a fixed ordering of all entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional real array spaces with \(\dim V=\dim W=N\), and fix linear vectorization isomorphisms \(v_V:V\to\mathbb{R}^N\) and \(v_W:W\to\mathbb{R}^N\). The reshaping atom is \[R=v_W^{-1}\circ v_V.\] It changes only the declared shape and preserves the fixed entry order. Consequently, for all \(X,Y\in V\) and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), \[R(\alpha X+\beta Y)=\alpha R(X)+\beta R(Y),\] so reshaping is a linear bijection. A reshape with unequal source and target entry counts is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reshaping changes dimensions while preserving a fixed entry order. Equal entry counts make it a linear bijection; unequal counts make the operation undefined.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and \(W\) are finite-dimensional real array spaces with \(\dim V=\dim W=N\).
\(v_V\) and \(v_W\) are fixed linear vectorization isomorphisms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=v_W^{-1}\circ v_V\) is a linear bijection from \(V\) to \(W\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reshape is a coordinate relabeling linear isomorphism

children.title: Stacking Atoms
children.top_down_role: Vertical, horizontal, block, plus axis-based concatenation of compatible expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Stacking Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered concatenation of finitely many vector or array inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and let \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\). The stacking atom forms the ordered concatenation \[S(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\ \vdots\\ x_k\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_1+\cdots+n_k}.\] For tuples \(x,y\in\prod_{i=1}^k\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) and scalars \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), with tuple operations defined componentwise, \[S(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha S(x)+\beta S(y).\] Thus, with the block order and stacking axis fixed, \(S\) is linear on the product space. Horizontal, vertical, and higher-dimensional stacking follow the same definition after fixing compatible non-stacking dimensions and a vectorization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stacking concatenates compatible inputs along a fixed axis and in a fixed order; as a map from their product space, it is linear.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\).
The stacking axis, block order, and non-stacking dimensions are fixed and compatible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is a linear map from \(\prod_{i=1}^k\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) to \(\mathbb{R}^{\sum_{i=1}^k n_i}\).

notation.meaning: number of scalar entries in the ith input

children.title: Permutation Atoms
children.top_down_role: Axis reordering, transposition, vectorization, plus layout-preserving affine transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed bijective reordering of coordinates or array axes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi\) be a fixed permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(P_\pi\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) be its permutation matrix. The permutation atom is \[T_\pi(x)=P_\pi x,\qquad (T_\pi(x))_j=x_{\pi(j)}.\] It is a linear bijection with inverse \(T_{\pi^{-1}}\), and \[P_\pi^{-1}=P_\pi^{\mathsf T}.\] Axis transposition and array permutation are the same operation after a fixed vectorization convention. The permutation must be structural data, not selected by an optimization variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation atom applies a fixed bijective coordinate reordering. Its matrix is linear and orthogonal, with the inverse given by the reverse permutation.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(\pi\) is fixed independently of optimization variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\pi(x)=P_\pi x\) is a linear bijection and \(T_\pi^{-1}=T_{\pi^{-1}}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of permutation matrices and their action as affine coordinate-reordering operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(n\times n\) permutation matrix \(A\) has exactly one entry equal to one in each row and exactly one entry equal to one in each column, with all other entries zero. Equivalently, both \(A\) and \(A^T\) are selector matrices. Thus there exists a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \((Ax)_i=x_{\pi_i}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A permutation matrix is a square zero-one matrix with exactly one one in each row and column. Multiplying by it reorders a vector's coordinates according to a permutation.

A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}

children.title: Shape-Transformation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Invalid indices, incompatible stack dimensions, ambiguous layouts, plus unsupported shape conversions.

knowledge_statements.title: Shape-Transformation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between fixed affine shape operations and variable-dependent structural transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a finite-dimensional real array space, and let \(T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb{R}^{m_1\times\cdots\times m_k}\) be constructed by fixed indexing, permutation, reshaping, or stacking of entries, possibly together with fixed constant entries. Then there exist a linear map \(L\) and a constant array \(B\) such that \(T(x)=L(x)+B\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\); hence \(T\) is affine. This classification requires every selected index, axis permutation, output dimension, and stacking pattern to be fixed modeling data. An operation whose indices, output shape, or branch selection depend on a decision variable is not a fixed affine map and lies outside this atom family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed indexing, reshaping, permutation, and stacking, with optional fixed constant entries, define affine maps. Variable-dependent indices, shapes, or structural choices lie outside the affine shape-transformation family.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a finite-dimensional real array space.
All indices, axis orders, target dimensions, and stacking patterns are fixed independently of the variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is affine; variable-dependent structural choices are outside this affine atom family.

children.title: Matrix Linear-Map Atoms
children.top_down_role: Matrix products with constant data, traces, diagonals, and related maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Linear-Map Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional matrix maps with fixed coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times m}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\), and \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}\), where \(A,B,C\) are fixed. The map \(X\mapsto AXB+C\) is affine because \(\operatorname{vec}(AXB+C)=(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X)+\operatorname{vec}(C)\). For fixed \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), the map \(X\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(D^{\mathsf T}X)\) is linear. Diagonal extraction \(X\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(X)\) for square \(X\), and diagonal formation \(x\mapsto\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) for \(x\in\mathbb{R}^r\), are linear. Any finite sum of compatible maps of these forms plus a fixed offset is affine. A product involving two variable expressions is outside this constant-coefficient family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix multiplication by fixed coefficients, trace inner products, diagonal extraction, and diagonal formation are affine maps; products of two variable expressions are outside this family.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is the matrix argument.
All coefficient matrices and offsets have the stated compatible dimensions and are fixed modeling data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each displayed map is affine in its variable argument.

notation.meaning: Fixed compatible coefficient matrices or offsets.
A variable vector used in diagonal formation.

children.title: Affine Aggregation Atoms
children.top_down_role: Summation and aggregation across expression dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Aggregation Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sums and weighted sums over fixed array dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_k}\), and fix a set of axes \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Define \(\Sigma_S X\) by summing the entries of \(X\) over the index tuple \(i\) associated with the axes in \(S\), while retaining the complementary index tuple \(j\). For conformable arrays \(X,Y\) and scalars \(a,b\), \(\Sigma_S(aX+bY)=a\Sigma_SX+b\Sigma_SY\), so \(\Sigma_S\) is linear. More generally, if every weight \(w_{i,j}\) and offset \(c_j\) is fixed, then the output defined by \(Z_j=\sum_i w_{i,j}X_{i,j}+c_j\) is affine in \(X\). The axes, weights, and offsets must be fixed rather than decision-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summing or taking fixed weighted sums across predetermined array axes is linear; adding a fixed offset yields an affine aggregation atom.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_k}\).
The aggregation axes, weights, and offsets are fixed modeling data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregation over fixed dimensions is linear, and adding a fixed offset makes it affine.

notation.meaning: A fixed set of aggregated axes.
Index tuples for aggregated and retained axes, respectively.

children.title: Maximum Atoms

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite pointwise maximum of scalar arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}x_i\), and define the active set \(I(x)=\{i:x_i=f(x)\}\). The function \(f\) is finite, convex, continuous, and nondecreasing in every coordinate. Its epigraph is \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):x_i\leq t\text{ for every }i\}\). Accordingly, if each scalar expression \(g_i\) is convex, then \(z\mapsto\max_i g_i(z)\) is convex under the standard coordinatewise composition rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of finitely many scalars is convex and nondecreasing in each argument; its epigraph is described by one upper-bound inequality per argument.
assumptions_latex: \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(n\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\max_i x_i\) is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar absolute value and its convex modeling representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The absolute-value atom is \(|x|=\max\{x,-x\}\). It is finite, convex, continuous, and even on \(\mathbb{R}\); it is nonincreasing on \(( -\infty,0]\) and nondecreasing on \([0,\infty)\), but is not monotone on all of \(\mathbb{R}\). Its epigraph satisfies \(t\geq|x|\) if and only if \(t\geq x\) and \(t\geq -x\). Its subdifferential is \(\partial|x|=\{1\}\) for \(x>0\), \(\partial|x|=\{-1\}\) for \(x<0\), and \(\partial|0|=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute value is the maximum of a scalar and its negative. It is convex, has a two-inequality epigraph, and is nondifferentiable at zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Value Atoms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar hinge at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the positive part by \(x_+=\max\{x,0\}\). The map \(x\mapsto x_+\) is finite, convex, continuous, nonnegative, and nondecreasing on \(\mathbb{R}\). Its epigraph satisfies \(t\geq x_+\) if and only if \(t\geq x\) and \(t\geq0\). Its subdifferential is \(\partial x_+=\{0\}\) for \(x<0\), \(\partial x_+=\{1\}\) for \(x>0\), and \(\partial x_+=[0,1]\) at \(x=0\). Therefore, composition with a convex scalar expression preserves convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive part is the maximum of a scalar and zero. It is convex, nondecreasing, and has a two-inequality epigraph.

children.title: Extremum Tie Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nondifferentiable points where multiple extremal branches share the selected value.

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) are differentiable at \(x\).
The active index set is nonempty and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a tie, the extremum's generalized first-order set is the convex hull of the active gradients.

notation.meaning: Indices attaining the extremum at the point.
The convex subdifferential or concave superdifferential.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order behavior when several smooth branches attain the same extremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is convex and differentiable at \(x\), and let \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=F(x)\}\). Then \(\partial F(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\). Thus a unique active gradient gives differentiability, whereas distinct active gradients generally produce a kink. Dually, if every \(f_i\) is concave and \(G(x)=\min_i f_i(x)\), then \(\partial^+G(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla f_i(x):i\in I(x)\}\), where \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=G(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When several smooth branches tie at a maximum or minimum, the relevant sub- or superdifferential is the convex hull of their active gradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Extremum Tie Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive powers strictly above one on the nonnegative domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(p>1\), define \(f_p:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) by \(f_p(x)=x^p\). The function is continuous on \([0,\infty)\), strictly increasing, and strictly convex. On \((0,\infty)\), its derivatives are \(f_p'(x)=p x^{p-1}>0\) and \(f_p''(x)=p(p-1)x^{p-2}>0\). Hence the disciplined convex composition \(f_p(g(z))\) is convex whenever \(g\) is convex and its values are constrained to \([0,\infty)\). The limiting case \(p=1\) is affine rather than strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed exponent above one, the nonnegative power function is increasing and strictly convex; composing it with a nonnegative convex expression preserves convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Power Atoms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative powers on the strictly positive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(p<0\), define \(f_p:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)\) by \(f_p(x)=x^p\). Its derivatives satisfy \(f_p'(x)=p x^{p-1}<0\) and \(f_p''(x)=p(p-1)x^{p-2}>0\), so \(f_p\) is strictly decreasing and strictly convex. Moreover, \(f_p(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\). Under disciplined convex composition, \(f_p(g(z))\) is convex when \(g\) is concave and constrained to be strictly positive, reflecting the atom's convexity and decreasing monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed negative power is strictly decreasing and strictly convex on positive scalars, diverging at zero; convex composition therefore requires a positive concave argument.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional positive powers on the nonnegative domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(q\in(0,1)\), define \(r_q:[0,\infty)\to[0,
\infty)\) by \(r_q(x)=x^q\). The function is continuous and strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\). On \((0,\infty)\), \(r_q'(x)=q x^{q-1}>0\) and \(r_q''(x)=q(q-1)x^{q-2}<0\), so \(r_q\) is strictly concave. Consequently, \(r_q(g(z))\) is concave whenever \(g\) is concave and constrained to be nonnegative. The ordinary \(k\)-th root corresponds to \(q=1/k\) for an integer \(k\geq2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional positive power is increasing and strictly concave on nonnegative scalars; this includes ordinary integer roots.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar reciprocal on its positive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(r:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)\) by \(r(x)=x^{-1}=1/x\). Since \(r'(x)=-x^{-2}<0\) and \(r''(x)=2x^{-3}>0\), the reciprocal is strictly decreasing and strictly convex. Its epigraph admits the equivalent description \(t\geq1/x\) if and only if \(x>0\), \(t\geq0\), and \(xt\geq1\); equivalently, \(\begin{pmatrix}x&1\\1&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\). Thus the reciprocal has a directly checkable conic representation, while its value diverges as \(x\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal is decreasing and strictly convex on positive scalars. Its epigraph is equivalently described by a product inequality or a two-by-two semidefinite constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Atoms

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Sum-Exp Atoms

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Atoms

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Family Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary conventions for exponential, logarithmic, entropy, and relative-entropy atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exponential atom is finite on all of \(\mathbb R\). The logarithm requires \(x>0\) and approaches \(-\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=(a^{\mathsf T}x+b)/(c^{\mathsf T}x+d)\) on the convex domain \(D=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:c^{\mathsf T}x+d>0\}\). Thus \(F\) is both quasiconvex and quasiconcave on \(D\), although generally neither convex nor concave.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm Parameter Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp exponent boundary for standard finite-dimensional vector norm atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\geq1\), the functional \(\|x\|_p=(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^p)^{1/p}\), with the maximum convention at \(p=\infty\), is a convex norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) containing \(0\), its gauge is \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\geq0:x\in tC\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] The gauge is convex, nonnegative, and positively homogeneous: \(\gamma_C(\alpha x)=\alpha\gamma_C(x)\) for \(\alpha\geq0\). knowledge_statements.title: Atomic-Set Specializations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic norms generated by compact, symmetric spanning sets in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact, centrally symmetric, and spanning, and set \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\). The associated atomic norm and its dual satisfy
\[
\|x\|_{\mathcal A}=\gamma_C(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k c_i:x=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i a_i,\ c_i\ge0,\ a_i\in\mathcal A\right\},
\qquad
\|y\|_{\mathcal A}^*=\sigma_C(y)=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle y,a\rangle.
\]
For \(\mathcal A=\{\pm e_i:1\le i\le n\}\), these specialize to \(\|x\|_1\) and \(\|y\|_\infty\). For unit-norm rank-one matrix atoms, they specialize to the nuclear and spectral norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atomic norm is the gauge of an atom hull; its dual is the atom-set support function, specializing to familiar norm pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\subset\mathbb R^n\) is compact, centrally symmetric, and spans \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x\|_{\mathcal A}=\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)}(x)\) and \(\|y\|_{\mathcal A}^*=\sigma_{\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)}(y)\).

notation.meaning: support function of the set C

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective-domain boundaries for gauges and support functions of closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) containing \(0\),
\[
\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\bigcup_{\lambda\ge0}\lambda C=\operatorname{cone}(C),
\qquad
\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=\left\{y:\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle<+\infty\right\}.
\]
Thus \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\) outside \(\operatorname{cone}(C)\). If \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(C)\) and \(\langle y,d\rangle>0\), then \(\sigma_C(y)=+\infty\). In particular, compactness of \(C\) makes \(\sigma_C\) finite everywhere, while absorption of \(\mathbb R^n\) by \(C\) makes \(\gamma_C\) finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge fails outside its set’s conic hull; a support function fails along dual directions that increase on recession rays.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\notin\operatorname{cone}(C)\Rightarrow\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\), and \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(C),\ \langle y,d\rangle>0\Rightarrow\sigma_C(y)=+\infty\).

notation.meaning: effective domain where f is finite

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order-Cone Atom Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical epigraph representations for norm and quadratic-over-linear atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\mathcal Q_{m+1}=\{(t,z):t\ge\|z\|_2\}\) and \(\mathcal Q_{m+2}^{r}=\{(u,v,z):u,v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|z\|_2^2\}\). For affine \(z(x)=Ax+b\),
\[
\|z(x)\|_2\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(t,z(x))\in\mathcal Q_{m+1}.
\]
For \(s>0\), the quadratic-over-linear atom has the representation
\[
\frac{\|z(x)\|_2^2}{s}\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(t/2,s,z(x))\in\mathcal Q_{m+2}^{r}.
\]
Consequently, epigraph constraints for Euclidean norms, affine residual norms, and quadratic-over-linear expressions admit direct second-order-cone formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean norms use a Lorentz-cone epigraph, while quadratic-over-linear expressions use a rotated Lorentz cone.
assumptions_latex: \(z(x)=Ax+b\) is affine.
\(s>0\) for the finite quadratic-over-linear expression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed norm and quadratic-over-linear epigraphs are respectively \(\mathcal Q\)- and \(\mathcal Q^r\)-representable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and both cone normalizations fit this atom-family topic. An authoritative locator is still required for the Lorentz- and rotated-Lorentz-cone epigraph equivalences.

children.title: Exponential-Cone Atoms

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Cone Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed exponential-cone representations of exponential and log-sum-exp epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w):v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\le w\}.
\]
Then the exponential epigraph satisfies \(e^x\le t\) if and only if \((x,1,t)\in K_{\exp}\). Moreover, for \(x\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n e^{x_i}\right)\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\mathbb R_+^n:\ (x_i-t,1,z_i)\in K_{\exp}\ \text{for every }i,\quad \sum_{i=1}^n z_i\le1.
\]
These equivalences give exact conic epigraph formulations, including boundary points through closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponential and log-sum-exp epigraphs have exact lifts using one exponential cone per exponential term.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R\) for the scalar epigraph or \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) for log-sum-exp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exponential and log-sum-exp inequalities are equivalent to the displayed \(K_{\exp}\)-constraints.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exponential and log-sum-exp lifts are internally consistent and fit the leaf, including use of the closed exponential cone. No source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Entropy Cone Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential-cone epigraph of the closed scalar relative-entropy atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the closed relative-entropy atom by
\[
\operatorname{rel\_entr}(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
x\log(x/y),&x>0,\ y>0,\\
0,&x=0,\ y\ge0,\\
+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Using \(K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(u,v,w):v>0,\ v\exp(u/v)\le w\}\), its epigraph is
\[
\operatorname{rel\_entr}(x,y)\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(-t,x,y)\in K_{\exp}.
\]
For vectors, the separable relative entropy \(\sum_i\operatorname{rel\_entr}(x_i,y_i)\) is represented by one such cone constraint per coordinate and a linear inequality summing the epigraph variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed scalar relative entropy is represented exactly by placing the negated epigraph variable and its arguments in the exponential cone.
assumptions_latex: \(x,y,t\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rel\_entr}(x,y)\le t\Longleftrightarrow(-t,x,y)\in K_{\exp}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed scalar relative-entropy convention and exponential-cone representation fit the terminal container, but they lack an inspectable authoritative citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Power-Cone Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-dimensional power-cone representation of weighted geometric products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed parameter \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define
\[
K_{\alpha}=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ u^{\alpha}v^{1-\alpha}\ge|w|\}.
\]
The hypograph of the weighted geometric product is represented exactly by
\[
t\le x^{\alpha}y^{1-\alpha},\quad x\ge0,\quad y\ge0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(x,y,t)\in K_{\alpha},\quad t\ge0.
\]
Likewise, the two-sided constraint \(|t|\le x^{\alpha}y^{1-\alpha}\) is equivalent simply to \((x,y,t)\in K_{\alpha}\). The exponent \(\alpha\) is fixed cone data rather than an optimization variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed weighted geometric product has a direct power-cone hypograph; the cone also represents its symmetric absolute-value form.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\le x^{\alpha}y^{1-\alpha},\ t\ge0\Longleftrightarrow(x,y,t)\in K_{\alpha},\ t\ge0\).

notation.meaning: three-dimensional power cone with exponent alpha

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-parameter power-cone representation is mathematically consistent and the representation kind fits the leaf. No source with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Mean Cone Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted geometric-mean hypographs and their recursive power-cone lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(w_i>0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=1\). The weighted geometric mean
\[
g_w(x)=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{w_i},\qquad x\in\mathbb R_+^n,
\]
is concave, and its hypograph cone is
\[
G_w=\{(x,t):x\in\mathbb R_+^n,\ t\ge0,\ t\le g_w(x)\}.
\]
An exact lift is obtained recursively: combine two nonnegative factors \(a,b\) through \((a,b,z)\in K_{\alpha}\), which enforces \(z\le a^{\alpha}b^{1-\alpha}\), and choose each fixed \(\alpha\) from the aggregate weights of the corresponding binary-tree branches. The root variable is constrained below by \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted geometric-mean hypograph is convex and admits an exact recursive lift through fixed-parameter power cones.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i\ge0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_w\) is a convex cone and has a finite recursive representation using power cones \(K_{\alpha}\).

notation.meaning: power cone with fixed exponent alpha

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The geometric-mean hypograph and recursive power-cone lift fit the container, but the exact arbitrary-weight binary-tree construction is not supported by an inspectable source.

children.title: Cone-Parameter Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Parameter Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper parameter ranges and closed boundary faces of exponential and power cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The power cone
\[
K_{\alpha}=\{(u,v,w):u,v\ge0,\ u^{\alpha}v^{1-\alpha}\ge|w|\}
\]
has the intended nondegenerate three-dimensional form only for \(0<\alpha<1\). At \(\alpha=0\) or \(\alpha=1\), one nonnegative coordinate drops from the product, producing a degenerate limiting cone rather than an interior power-cone parameter. For the exponential cone,
\[
K_{\exp}=\{(u,v,w):v>0,\ v e^{u/v}\le w\}\cup\{(u,0,w):u\le0,\ w\ge0\}.
\]
Omitting the second set loses the closed face at \(v=0\), so conic formulations must use the closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power exponents must lie strictly between zero and one; the exponential cone also requires its explicit zero-perspective boundary face.
assumptions_latex: The power-cone exponent is fixed.
The exponential cone is interpreted as a closed cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proper range is \(0<\alpha<1\), and \(K_{\exp}\) includes \(\{(u,0,w):u\le0,\ w\ge0\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate, and the exponential-cone boundary face is stated correctly. The endpoint conventions for the power cone and the closed exponential-cone formula require a cited authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric-matrix representation of a quadratic function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the canonical symmetric coefficient matrix, homogeneous representation, quadratic-form specialization, and constant Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be a polynomial of degree at most two, represented as \(q(x)=x^\top Ax+c^\top x+d\). With \(H=A+A^\top\in\mathbb S^n\), one has \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Hx+c^\top x+d\) and \(q(x)=\tfrac12\begin{bmatrix}x\\1\end{bmatrix}^{\!\top}\begin{bmatrix}H&c\\c^\top&2d\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\1\end{bmatrix}\). Moreover, \(\nabla^2q(x)=H\). When \(c=0\) and \(d=0\), \(q\) is a quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every real quadratic function can use a symmetric matrix for its quadratic coefficient and can be written as a homogeneous quadratic expression in the augmented vector (x,1). Its Hessian is that symmetric coefficient, and setting the linear and constant terms to zero gives a quadratic form.

knowledge_statements.title: Complex Quadratic-Form Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued quadratic forms on complex vectors under Hermitian curvature conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\) be Hermitian and define \(q(z)=z^*Hz\), which is real-valued. Viewing \(\mathbb C^n\) as \(\mathbb R^{2n}\),
\[
q\text{ is convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H\succeq0,
\qquad
q\text{ is concave}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H\preceq0.
\]
When \(H=R^*R\), one has \(q(z)=\|Rz\|_2^2\), where the norm includes real and imaginary components, so the epigraph is rotated-second-order-cone representable after realification. For a non-Hermitian matrix \(A\), the real part of \(z^*Az\) depends only on \((A+A^*)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complex Hermitian quadratic form is convex exactly for a positive-semidefinite matrix and can then be represented after realification.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\) is Hermitian.
\(z\in\mathbb C^n\) is identified with its real and imaginary parts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\mapsto z^*Hz\) is convex if and only if \(H\succeq0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-complement epigraph of the jointly convex matrix-fractional function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), define \(f(x,Y)=x^{\mathsf T}Y^{-1}x\). This function is jointly convex, and the Schur complement gives
\[
f(x,Y)\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{pmatrix}Y&x\\x^{\mathsf T}&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
\]
Its closed extension to \(Y\succeq0\) is \(x^{\mathsf T}Y^{\dagger}x\) when \(x\in\operatorname{range}(Y)\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise. For this extension, the same block positive-semidefinite constraint characterizes the epigraph, including singular boundary matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matrix-fractional function is jointly convex, and its closed epigraph is exactly one block positive-semidefinite constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(Y\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), or \(Y\succeq0\) under the stated closed extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}Y^{-1}x\le t\Longleftrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}Y&x\\x^{\mathsf T}&t\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\) for \(Y\succ0\).

children.title: Quadratic Curvature Regimes
children.top_down_role: Convex, concave, affine, indefinite, plus parameter-dependent classifications induced by coefficient matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Curvature Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete curvature classification of unrestricted real quadratic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
f(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Px+q^{\mathsf T}x+r,
\]
let \(S=(P+P^{\mathsf T})/2\). The Hessian is \(2S\), so the curvature regimes are
\[
S\succeq0\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is convex},
\qquad
S\preceq0\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is concave}.
\]
If \(S\) has both a positive and a negative eigenvalue, then \(f\) is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^n\). If \(S=0\), then \(f\) is affine. These conclusions concern the unrestricted ambient space; restriction to an affine subspace replaces \(S\) by its compression to feasible directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric quadratic coefficient determines curvature: positive semidefinite is convex, negative semidefinite concave, indefinite neither, and zero affine.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(r\in\mathbb R\).
The default domain is \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inertia of \(S=(P+P^{\mathsf T})/2\) gives the complete unrestricted curvature classification of \(f\).

notation.meaning: symmetric part of the quadratic coefficient

children.title: Quadratic Domain Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Indefinite coefficients, singular matrices, incompatible dimensions, plus unsupported variable-dependent matrix arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain and curvature boundaries for real quadratic and matrix-fractional atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), the quadratic atom \(q_Q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx\) is finite on \(\mathbb R^n\), convex exactly when \(Q\succeq0\), and concave exactly when \(Q\preceq0\). For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\in\mathbb S^n\), the matrix-fractional expression \(x^{\mathsf T}Y^{-1}x\) has domain \(Y\succ0\). Its closed extended-value form is \(x^{\mathsf T}Y^\dagger x\) when \(Y\succeq0\) and \(x\in\operatorname{range}(Y)\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Indefinite \(Q\), or an inverse expression outside its positive-definite domain, violates the corresponding convex-atom specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic curvature is determined by definiteness. Matrix-fractional atoms require a positive-definite denominator, with a closed pseudoinverse extension on positive-semidefinite matrices satisfying the range condition.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\) and \(Y\in\mathbb S^n\).
All vectors and matrices are real and finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_Q\) is convex iff \(Q\succeq0\), while the closed matrix-fractional domain is \(\{(x,Y):Y\succeq0,\ x\in\operatorname{range}(Y)\}\).

children.title: Spectral-Value Atom Family
children.top_down_role: Extremal and aggregated spectral-value families.

children.title: Extremal Eigenvalue Atoms
children.top_down_role: Largest or smallest eigenvalue scalarizations for symmetric or Hermitian matrix expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremal Eigenvalue Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature and variational forms of extremal eigenvalues on symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), \(\lambda_{\max}(X)=\max_{\|u\|_2=1}u^{\mathsf T}Xu\) is convex and monotone in the Loewner order, whereas \(\lambda_{\min}(X)=\min_{\|u\|_2=1}u^{\mathsf T}Xu\) is concave and Loewner-monotone. Let \(p\ge1\), let \(X(\cdot):\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb S^n\) be affine, and let \(z\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\). Then \(\lambda_{\max}(X(z))\le t\) is equivalent to \(X(z)\preceq tI_n\), and \(\lambda_{\min}(X(z))\ge t\) is equivalent to \(X(z)\succeq tI_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest eigenvalue is convex, the smallest is concave, and their level-set constraints for symmetric affine matrix maps have direct semidefinite representations.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^n\).
\(X(\cdot):\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb S^n\) is affine when the level-set representations are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\max}\) is convex, \(\lambda_{\min}\) is concave, and their indicated level sets are semidefinite representable.

children.title: Ordered Eigenvalue Atoms
children.top_down_role: Selected or aggregated ordered eigenvalues under supported curvature regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered Eigenvalue Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ky Fan representations distinguish valid convex eigenvalue sums from interior ordered eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1(X)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(X)\). For \(1\le k\le n\), the Ky Fan sum satisfies \[\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(X)=\max\{\operatorname{tr}(U^{\mathsf T}XU):U\in\mathbb R^{n\times k},\ U^{\mathsf T}U=I_k\}.\] Hence the sum of the \(k\) largest eigenvalues is convex. The sum of the \(k\) smallest eigenvalues is concave by applying this identity to \(-X\). For \(1<k<n\), the individual ordered eigenvalue \(\lambda_k\) is generally neither convex nor concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sums of the largest ordered eigenvalues have a variational maximum representation and are convex; interior individual eigenvalues generally have neither curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^n\).
Eigenvalues are ordered nonincreasingly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(X)\) is convex, while an interior \(\lambda_k(X)\) is generally neither convex nor concave.

children.title: Extremal Singular-Value Atoms
children.top_down_role: Largest or selected singular-value scalarizations for rectangular matrix expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremal Singular-Value Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature and variational characterization of largest and smallest singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(\sigma_{\max}(X)=\max\{u^{\mathsf T}Xv:u\in\mathbb R^m,\ v\in\mathbb R^n,\ \|u\|_2=\|v\|_2=1\}=\|X\|_2\); therefore it is a convex norm. Writing \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), when \(m\ge n\) one has \(\sigma_{\min}(X)=\sigma_r(X)=\min\{\|Xv\|_2:v\in\mathbb R^n,\ \|v\|_2=1\}\), with the transposed analogue when \(m<n\). On the unrestricted matrix space, \(\sigma_{\min}\) is generally neither convex nor concave, so it is not a globally valid convex or concave atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest singular value is the convex spectral norm. The smallest singular value has a minimum-gain representation but generally has no global convexity or concavity.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
Singular values are ordered nonincreasingly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\max}\) is convex, whereas \(\sigma_{\min}\) is generally neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).

notation.meaning: i-th largest singular value of X

children.title: Singular-Value Sum Atoms
children.top_down_role: Nuclear, Ky Fan, plus related aggregated singular-value constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value Sum Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational and curvature specification of Ky Fan singular-value sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with singular values \(\sigma_1(X)\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r(X)\), where \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), define \(K_k(X)=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i(X)\) for \(1\le k\le r\). Then \[K_k(X)=\max\{\operatorname{tr}(U^{\mathsf T}XV):U\in\mathbb R^{m\times k},\ V\in\mathbb R^{n\times k},\ U^{\mathsf T}U=V^{\mathsf T}V=I_k\}.\] Thus \(K_k\) is a unitarily invariant convex norm. Its endpoints are \(K_1(X)=\|X\|_2\) and \(K_r(X)=\|X\|_*\), the spectral and nuclear norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of the largest k singular values is a convex Ky Fan norm with an orthonormal-factor variational representation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
\(1\le k\le\min\{m,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_k\) is a convex unitarily invariant norm with the displayed maximum representation.

notation.meaning: sum of the k largest singular values

children.title: Spectral Multiplicity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Repeated eigenvalue or singular-value cases affecting smoothness, recovery, plus diagnostic interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Multiplicity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability and subdifferentials at simple and repeated extremal spectral values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), let \(E_{\max}\) be the eigenspace associated with \(\lambda_{\max}(X)\). If this eigenvalue is simple with unit eigenvector \(u\in\mathbb R^n\), then \(\lambda_{\max}\) is differentiable at \(X\) and \(\nabla\lambda_{\max}(X)=uu^{\mathsf T}\). In general, let \(d=\dim E_{\max}\) and let \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) have orthonormal columns spanning \(E_{\max}\). Then \[\partial\lambda_{\max}(X)=\{UZU^{\mathsf T}:Z\in\mathbb S^d,\ Z\succeq0,\ \operatorname{tr}Z=1\}.\] Thus multiplicity greater than one causes nondifferentiability while retaining a computable convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple largest eigenvalue has a rank-one gradient. At multiplicity, differentiability fails and the subdifferential consists of trace-one positive-semidefinite matrices supported on the top eigenspace.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^n\).
\(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) has orthonormal columns spanning the maximal eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\max}\) is differentiable exactly in the simple-eigenvalue regime, with the stated subdifferential in every multiplicity regime.

children.title: Spectral Structure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Nonsymmetric eigenvalue inputs, unsupported ordering requests, incompatible value spaces, plus uncertified spectral selections.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Structure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural limits on applying ordered eigenvalue atoms to matrix expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Ordered real-eigenvalue atoms require a symmetric real matrix, or a Hermitian complex matrix. If this structure is absent, eigenvalues need not be real or continuously orderable, and the convexity rules for \(\lambda_{\max}\), \(\lambda_{\min}\), and Ky Fan eigenvalue sums do not apply. For example, \(R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) is real but nonsymmetric and has eigenvalues \(i\) and \(-i\), so neither a largest nor a smallest real eigenvalue exists. Singular-value atoms remain well-defined for arbitrary rectangular matrices but obey different curvature rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordered eigenvalue atoms require symmetric or Hermitian inputs. A nonsymmetric real matrix can have complex eigenvalues, destroying real ordering and the associated convexity rules.
assumptions_latex: Eigenvalue ordering uses the ordinary order on real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside symmetric or Hermitian structure, ordered eigenvalue atoms are not valid without a separately defined extension.

children.title: Spectral Scalarization Atom Family

children.title: Trace Atoms
children.top_down_role: Affine trace scalarizations plus trace compositions over compatible matrix expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Trace Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine scalarization of square matrix expressions by the trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X,Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), the trace atom satisfies \(\operatorname{tr}(aX+bY)=a\operatorname{tr}(X)+b\operatorname{tr}(Y)\). Consequently it is both convex and concave. If \(X,Y\in\mathbb S^n\), then \(\operatorname{tr}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i(X)\), and \(X\preceq Y\) implies \(\operatorname{tr}(X)\le\operatorname{tr}(Y)\). For fixed \(C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), the weighted trace \(X\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(C^{\mathsf T}X)\) is likewise affine on \(\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trace and fixed weighted trace are affine scalarizations. On symmetric matrices, trace equals the eigenvalue sum and respects positive-semidefinite ordering.
assumptions_latex: All traced matrices are square and dimensionally compatible.
\(C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is fixed in the weighted-trace expression.
Both matrices in a Loewner-order comparison belong to \(\mathbb S^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{tr}\) and \(X\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(C^{\mathsf T}X)\) are affine scalar-valued atoms.

notation.meaning: sum of the diagonal entries of X

children.title: Log-Determinant Atoms
children.top_down_role: Concave spectral scalarizations over positive-definite matrix domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Determinant Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concavity, domain, and derivative of the log-determinant scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the extended-value log-determinant atom on \(\mathbb S^n\) by \(f(X)=\log\det X\) for \(X\succ0\) and \(f(X)=-\infty\) otherwise. On \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\), \(f\) is strictly concave and Loewner-increasing, with differential \(Df(X)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}H)\). Equivalently, \(-\log\det X\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and is assigned \(+\infty\) outside that domain. Thus a disciplined composition must establish positive definiteness of its matrix argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log determinant is strictly concave and increasing on positive-definite matrices; its negative is strictly convex. Outside positive definiteness, the extended-value atom is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \(X,H\in\mathbb S^n\).
Finite evaluation and differentiation require \(X\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log\det X\) is strictly concave on \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\), with \(Df(X)[H]=\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}H)\).

notation.meaning: directional differential of f at X in direction H

children.title: Determinant-Root Atoms
children.top_down_role: Concave determinant-root scalarizations over positive-semidefinite matrix domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Determinant-Root Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concave homogeneous determinant scalarization on the positive-semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\), define \(d(X)=(\det X)^{1/n}\). The determinant-root atom is nonnegative, positively homogeneous, Loewner-increasing, and concave: for \(X,Y\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(0\le\theta\le1\), \[d(\theta X+(1-\theta)Y)\ge\theta d(X)+(1-\theta)d(Y).\] It is continuous on \(\mathbb S_+^n\), including singular matrices where \(d(X)=0\). Its standard concave extended-value convention assigns \(-\infty\) to arguments outside \(\mathbb S_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nth root of determinant is a nonnegative, homogeneous, increasing, concave function on positive-semidefinite matrices, with value zero on singular matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
\(0\le\theta\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\mapsto(\det X)^{1/n}\) is concave and positively homogeneous on \(\mathbb S_+^n\).

children.title: Matrix Geometric-Mean Atoms
children.top_down_role: Order-sensitive means of positive-definite or positive-semidefinite matrix arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Geometric-Mean Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted positive-definite matrix geometric mean and its principal structural properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A,B\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), the weighted matrix geometric mean is \[A\#_tB=A^{1/2}\bigl(A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}\bigr)^tA^{1/2}.\] It satisfies \(A\#_0B=A\), \(A\#_1B=B\), joint Loewner monotonicity, and joint matrix concavity in \((A,B)\). For every invertible \(S\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), it also satisfies \[(S^{\mathsf T}AS)\#_t(S^{\mathsf T}BS)=S^{\mathsf T}(A\#_tB)S.\] For commuting \(A\) and \(B\), it reduces to \(A^{1-t}B^t\). The definition extends continuously to \(A,B\in\mathbb S_+^n\) as the limit of \((A+\varepsilon I_n)\#_t(B+\varepsilon I_n)\) when \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted matrix geometric mean is defined by a congruence-normalized matrix power; it is jointly concave and monotone, is invariant under invertible congruences, and reduces to the scalar-like product for commuting matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\).
The congruence identity uses an invertible \(S\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\#_tB\) is a jointly matrix-concave and jointly Loewner-monotone mean with congruence invariance and a continuous positive-semidefinite extension.

notation.meaning: principal spectral matrix power of positive-definite X

children.title: Trace-Mean Scalarizations
children.top_down_role: Scalar objectives or constraints formed by tracing supported matrix-mean constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Trace-Mean Scalarizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized trace-power means as spectral scalarizations of positive-semidefinite matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(p>0\), define the normalized trace mean \(M_p(X)=\bigl(n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(X^p)\bigr)^{1/p}\). Equivalently, \(M_p(X)\) is the scalar power mean of the nonnegative eigenvalues of \(X\). The map \(M_p\) is positively homogeneous and Loewner-increasing. It is concave for \(0<p\le1\) and convex for \(p\ge1\). Its continuous limit at \(p=0\) on \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\) is \(M_0(X)=(\det X)^{1/n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized trace-power means apply scalar power means to matrix eigenvalues. They are concave up to order one, convex from order one, and converge to determinant root at order zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\).
\(p>0\), with the limit \(p\to0\) restricted to \(X\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_p\) is concave for \(0<p\le1\), convex for \(p\ge1\), and \(M_0(X)=(\det X)^{1/n}\).

notation.meaning: spectral power of a positive-semidefinite matrix

children.title: Determinant Domain Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Singular, indefinite, nonsymmetric, non-Hermitian, plus unsupported matrix-domain cases.

knowledge_statements.title: Determinant Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts the disciplined domains of log-determinant and determinant-root atoms with the unrestricted determinant polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 2\), define the extended-value log-determinant atom on \(\mathbb S^n\) by \(g(X)=\log\det X\) when \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and \(g(X)=-\infty\) otherwise. Then \(g\) is concave and its finite domain is \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\). The function \(h(X)=(\det X)^{1/n}\), restricted to \(\mathbb S_+^n\), is real-valued and concave. By contrast, the polynomial \(X\mapsto\det X\) is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb S^n\). Thus disciplined determinant scalarizations require their declared positive-definite or positive-semidefinite domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under its extended-value atom convention, log-determinant has the positive-definite cone as its finite domain. Determinant-root is concave on the positive-semidefinite cone, while the unrestricted determinant polynomial is neither convex nor concave.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}_{\mathrm{finite}}g=\mathbb S_{++}^n\), and \(h(X)=(\det X)^{1/n}\) is concave on \(\mathbb S_+^n\).

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices.

children.title: Semidefinite-Lifted Matrix Functions
children.top_down_role: Matrix-function families represented through linear matrix inequalities or semidefinite lifts.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite-Lifted Matrix Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional epigraph representation by projection of an affine semidefinite slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=n(n+1)/2\), and let \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R\) be fixed linear coordinates that uniquely determine \(X\in\mathbb S^n\). An extended-real-valued matrix function \(f:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is semidefinite-lifted when there exist an integer \(q\ge0\) and real symmetric matrices \(F_0,F_t,F_1,\ldots,F_N,G_1,\ldots,G_q\) of a common order such that \[\operatorname{epi}f=\left\{(X,t)\in\mathbb S^n\times\mathbb R:\exists y\in\mathbb R^q,\ F_0+tF_t+\sum_{i=1}^N\xi_i(X)F_i+\sum_{j=1}^q y_jG_j\succeq0\right\}.\] Consequently, \(f(X)\le t\) holds exactly when suitable auxiliary variables \(y\) satisfy the displayed affine linear matrix inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite-lifted matrix function has an epigraph equal to the projection of an affine positive-semidefinite constraint in the matrix coordinates, epigraph variable, and auxiliary variables.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
All coefficient matrices are real symmetric and have a common order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)\le t\iff\exists y\in\mathbb R^q:\ F_0+tF_t+\sum_{i=1}^N\xi_i(X)F_i+\sum_{j=1}^q y_jG_j\succeq0\).

children.title: Affine Sets
children.top_down_role: Convex sets described through affine equalities or affine images.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine sets characterized by affine combinations or linear equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is affine if for every \(x,y\in C\) and every \(\theta\in\mathbb R\), one has \(\theta x+(1-\theta)y\in C\). Equivalently, there exist \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\) and a linear subspace \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) such that \(C=x_0+L\). In finite dimensions this is also equivalent to an equation representation \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}\) for some matrix \(A\) and vector \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine set contains every affine combination of two of its points and is equivalently a translated linear subspace or linear-equation solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ affine}\iff C=x_0+L\iff C=\{x:Ax=b\}\).

notation.meaning: A linear subspace of the ambient Euclidean space.

children.title: Polyhedral Sets
children.top_down_role: Convex sets represented through finite systems of linear inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex polyhedra represented by finitely many affine equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral if there exist finite-dimensional data \(A,b,C,d\) such that
\[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\},\]
where the vector inequality is componentwise. Thus a polyhedral set is an intersection of finitely many closed halfspaces and affine hyperplanes; in particular, it is closed and convex. Empty sets and the whole space are included by allowing inconsistent or vacuous systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral set is the solution set of finitely many affine equalities and componentwise affine inequalities; it is closed and convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Ball Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed balls of arbitrary norms in finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(\mathbb R^n\), let \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(r\ge0\). The corresponding closed norm ball is
\[B_{\|\cdot\|}(c,r)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x-c\|\le r\}.\]
It is closed and convex. For \(r>0\), it equals \(c+rB_{\|\cdot\|}(0,1)\); for \(r=0\), it is the singleton \(\{c\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed norm ball contains points within norm distance r of its center; every such ball is closed and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(\|\cdot\|\) is a norm on \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(c\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(r\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\|\cdot\|}(c,r)=\{x:\|x-c\|\le r\}\) is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: Closed ball of radius r centered at c in the specified norm.

children.title: Representation Relations Across Elementary Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Relations Across Elementary Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusions and standard conic representations linking affine, polyhedral, and common norm-ball sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every affine set \(\{x:Ax=b\}\) is polyhedral. The balls of the \(\ell_1\)- and \(\ell_\infty\)-norms are polyhedral, since
\[\|x\|_1\le r\iff\exists u:\ -u\le x\le u,\ \mathbf1^Tu\le r,\]
and \(\|x\|_\infty\le r\iff-r\mathbf1\le x\le r\mathbf1\). The Euclidean ball satisfies \(\|x-c\|_2\le r\iff(r,x-c)\in\mathcal Q^{n+1}\), so it is second-order-cone representable; for \(n\ge2\), it is not polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine sets and one- and infinity-norm balls are polyhedral, while Euclidean balls are second-order-cone representable and generally nonpolyhedral.
assumptions_latex: For the nonpolyhedral conclusion, \(n\ge2\) and \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{affine}\subseteq\text{polyhedral}\), while \(\ell_2\)-balls are representable over \(\mathcal Q^{n+1}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order-Cone Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard Lorentz cone and its affine inverse images used in conic-quadratic modeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The second-order cone, or Lorentz cone, in \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\) is
\[\mathcal Q^{n+1}=\{(t,x):\|x\|_2\le t\}.\]
It is a closed, convex, pointed, self-dual cone with nonempty interior \(\{(t,x):\|x\|_2<t\}\). A second-order-cone set is any set describable as an affine inverse image or finite product of such cones, possibly followed by projection through auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order cone consists of scalar-vector pairs whose scalar dominates the vector's Euclidean norm; affine lifts define second-order-cone sets.
assumptions_latex: The ambient inner product is the standard Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal Q^{n+1}=\{(t,x):\|x\|_2\le t\}\) is closed, convex, pointed, and self-dual.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotated-Cone Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotated Lorentz cone under the convention \(2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The rotated second-order cone in \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\) is
\[\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\}.\]
It is a closed convex cone. A rotated-cone set is an affine inverse image, finite product, or lifted projection of rotated second-order cones. The fixed factor \(2\) is part of the convention and must be adjusted when translating formulations using \(uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rotated second-order cone models nonnegative products dominating squared Euclidean norms, with an explicit factor-two convention.
assumptions_latex: The factor-two normalization \(2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}=\{(u,v,w):u,v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\}\) is a closed convex cone.

notation.meaning: Rotated second-order cone with factor-two normalization.

children.title: Cone-Isomorphism Relations
children.top_down_role: Representation-level correspondence between standard and rotated cone forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Isomorphism Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit linear isomorphism between Lorentz and rotated Lorentz cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the invertible linear map \(T:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n+1}\) by \[T(u,v,w)=\left(u+v,\ u-v,\ \sqrt2w\right).\] Under the normalization \(\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}=\{(u,v,w):u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\}\), one has \[(u,v,w)\in\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\iff T(u,v,w)\in\mathcal Q^{n+2}.\] Hence \(T\) maps the rotated second-order cone bijectively onto the standard second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum-difference transformation with square-root-two scaling maps the factor-two-normalized rotated second-order cone bijectively onto the standard second-order cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\) uses the normalization \(2uv\ge\|w\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\mathcal Q_r^{n+2})=\mathcal Q^{n+2}\).

notation.meaning: Rotated second-order cone with factor-two normalization.

children.title: Conic-Quadratic Modeling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model structures favoring either standard or rotated cone representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Quadratic Modeling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognizes constraints admitting finite affine lifts over standard or rotated second-order cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A feasible set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is conic-quadratic representable when there exist auxiliary variables \(y\), affine equations, and finitely many affine maps \(F_k\) such that
\[x\in C\iff\exists y:\ Ax+By=b,\quad F_k(x,y)\in\mathcal Q^{m_k}\ \text{or}\ F_k(x,y)\in\mathcal Q_r^{m_k}\quad\text{for every }k.\]
This regime includes affine constraints, Euclidean-norm inequalities, and convex quadratic inequalities that possess such a cone lift. A generic indefinite quadratic inequality does not qualify merely because it is quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is conic-quadratic when affine equations and finitely many standard or rotated second-order-cone constraints represent its feasible set after lifting.
assumptions_latex: All affine maps and lifting spaces are finite-dimensional.
Each cone constraint uses a standard or rotated second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is conic-quadratic representable exactly when it has the displayed finite affine cone lift.

children.title: Positive-Semidefinite Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Semidefinite Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The symmetric positive-semidefinite cone defined by quadratic-form nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The positive-semidefinite cone is
\[\mathbb S_+^n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:z^TXz\ge0\text{ for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\}.\]
Equivalently, \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) exactly when every eigenvalue of \(X\) is nonnegative. This set is a closed, convex, pointed, self-dual cone under the trace inner product \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\), and its interior is the positive-definite cone \(\mathbb S_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-semidefinite cone contains symmetric matrices with nonnegative quadratic forms, equivalently nonnegative eigenvalues, and is closed, convex, pointed, and self-dual.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^n\) carries the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb S_+^n=\{X:z^TXz\ge0\ \forall z\}\) and \((\mathbb S_+^n)^*=\mathbb S_+^n\).

notation.meaning: Real symmetric n by n matrices.

children.title: Matrix-Order Sets
children.top_down_role: Convex sets expressed through Loewner-order comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Order Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loewner-order intervals and upper or lower sets generated by the semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X,Y\in\mathbb S^n\), the Loewner order is defined by
\[X\preceq Y\iff Y-X\in\mathbb S_+^n.\]
Accordingly, for fixed \(L,U\in\mathbb S^n\), the lower set \(\{X:X\preceq U\}\), upper set \(\{X:L\preceq X\}\), and interval \([L,U]_{\preceq}=\{X:L\preceq X\preceq U\}\) are convex and closed. The interval is nonempty exactly when \(L\preceq U\). Each is an affine inverse image of the positive-semidefinite cone or a product of two such cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Loewner-order sets impose positive-semidefinite matrix differences; their upper sets, lower sets, and intervals are closed and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(L,U,X,Y\in\mathbb S^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([L,U]_{\preceq}\neq\varnothing\iff L\preceq U\), and every displayed order set is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: Loewner order, meaning Y minus X is positive semidefinite.
Closed interval in the Loewner order.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Matrix Slices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine inverse images of the positive-semidefinite cone in finite-dimensional symmetric-matrix space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb S^m\), and define the affine matrix map \(L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb S^m\) by \(L(x)=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\). An affine matrix slice is a set of the form \[S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:L(x)\succeq0\}=L^{-1}(\mathbb S_+^m).\] Since \(\mathbb S_+^m\) is a closed convex cone and \(L\) is affine, \(S\) is a closed convex set, possibly empty or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine matrix slice consists of points making an affine symmetric matrix positive semidefinite; it is a closed convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(A_i\in\mathbb S^m\) for \(i=0,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=L^{-1}(\mathbb S_+^m)\) is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: real symmetric matrices of order m

knowledge_statements.title: Order-to-Cone Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loewner-order constraints represented as positive-semidefinite cone membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X,Y\in\mathbb S^m\), the Loewner order is represented by \[X\preceq Y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Y-X\in\mathbb S_+^m.\] Consequently, for affine symmetric-matrix maps \(F,G:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb S^m\), the matrix-order constraint \(F(x)\preceq G(x)\) is exactly the conic constraint \(G(x)-F(x)\in\mathbb S_+^m\). In particular, \(F(x)\preceq0\) corresponds to \(-F(x)\in\mathbb S_+^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric-matrix inequality is equivalent to requiring its ordered difference to belong to the positive-semidefinite cone.

\(F\) and \(G\) are affine symmetric-matrix maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential-Cone Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed three-dimensional exponential cone and its affine inverse images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exponential cone is the closed convex cone \[K_{\exp}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:y>0,\ y\exp(x/y)\le z\}.\] Equivalently, \[K_{\exp}=\{(x,y,z):y>0,\ y\exp(x/y)\le z\}\cup\{(x,0,z):x\le0,\ z\ge0\}.\] An exponential-cone set is any affine inverse image \(\{u:A u+b\in K_{\exp}^q\}\), where \(q\) is a positive integer; every such set is convex and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential cone closes the perspective epigraph of the exponential function; affine inverse images of its products form exponential-cone sets.
assumptions_latex: \(q\in\mathbb N\) is positive.
\(u\mapsto Au+b\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{u:Au+b\in K_{\exp}^q\}\) is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of q exponential cones

knowledge_statements.title: Power-Cone Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-dimensional power cones with fixed exponent and their affine inverse images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), the three-dimensional power cone is \[K_{\mathrm{pow}}^{\alpha}=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ x^{\alpha}y^{1-\alpha}\ge |z|\}.\] A power-cone set is an affine inverse image \(\{u:Au+b\in\prod_{j=1}^qK_{\mathrm{pow}}^{\alpha_j}\}\), where every \(\alpha_j\in(0,1)\). Such a set is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power cone bounds an absolute coordinate by a weighted geometric mean; affine inverse images of products of these cones are convex.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha_j\in(0,1)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,q\).
\(u\mapsto Au+b\) is affine.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-dual convention for closed convex cones and corresponding membership constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), its positive dual is \[K^*=\{y\in\mathbb R^d:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\] The set \(K^*\) is always a closed convex cone. If \(K\) is closed and convex, then \(K^{**}=K\). A dual-cone variant of a conic set is an affine inverse image \(\{u:Au+b\in K^*\}\); it is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone contains vectors having nonnegative inner product with every primal-cone vector; closed convex cones equal their biduals.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is a cone.
For the bidual equality, \(K\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*\) is closed and convex, and \(K^{**}=K\) when \(K\) is closed and convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Extension Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common semantic fields required by custom atom and set registrations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Shared extension metadata are consistent when they specify a fixed output shape, an effective domain \(D\), parameter-dependent dimension rules, and all semantic attributes used by composition checking.
