For a set \(C\), declared convexity, ambient dimension, and parameter restrictions must agree with its membership representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared metadata must consistently describe shapes, domains, parameters, signs, curvature, monotonicity, and convex-set membership semantics.
assumptions_latex: All declarations refer to the same registered object and parameter values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every declared semantic attribute must hold on the declared domain and agree with the canonical representation.

notation.meaning: range of the registered atom over its domain

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The consistency requirements are plausible, but the asserted shared metadata schema and mandatory fields are implementation-specific. An authoritative DCM extension-schema source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Interface Trust Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Separation between user-supplied declarations and trusted library behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Interface Trust Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional soundness boundary for user-supplied semantic declarations and canonicalizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a disciplined-model validator and \(E\) a registered extension. Acceptance of a model containing \(E\) certifies convexity only conditionally: every semantic declaration made by \(E\) must be true, and its canonicalization must be equivalent to the declared graph or set. Thus \[V(M,E)=\mathrm{accept}\ \land\ \mathrm{Valid}(E)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M\text{ has the certified convex semantics}.\] Acceptance alone gives no such implication when extension metadata or graph equivalence remain unverified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validator remains sound for custom extensions only when their semantic declarations and canonicalizations are trusted or independently verified.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is sound for its built-in trusted library.
\(M\) uses the registered extension \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(M,E)=\mathrm{accept}\) certifies convex semantics only under \(\mathrm{Valid}(E)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-soundness principle fits the trust-boundary leaf, but the formal meanings of Valid(E), certified convex semantics, and the validator's extension guarantees are not sourced and may vary by implementation.

children.title: Semantic Metadata Validation
children.top_down_role: Consistency checking for declared domains, curvature, signs, and monotonicity.

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Metadata Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency predicate for domains, curvature, signs, shapes, and monotonicity declarations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a declared atom \(f:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}\), semantic metadata pass validation only if: \(D\) and all shapes are well-defined; every declared sign bound contains \(f(D)\); the declared convexity or concavity inequality holds for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\); and each declared argument monotonicity holds whenever two domain points differ only in that argument. Parameter conditions must imply these properties and must be decidable before composition analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metadata validation checks that domains and shapes are coherent and that declared signs, curvature, monotonicity, and parameter restrictions are mathematically true.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is the declared effective domain.
All compared argument tuples belong to \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metadata are accepted only if every declared semantic predicate holds throughout \(D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leaf and condition content kind align, but the exact validation protocol is uncited and implementation-sensitive. The use of a codomain containing both extended infinities also requires a source-backed convention before the curvature and sign conditions can be assessed reliably.

children.title: Graph-Representation Validation
children.top_down_role: Correctness and solver-compatibility checking for custom canonicalizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Representation Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness and solver-compatibility conditions for custom conic canonicalizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proposed convex-atom canonicalization \(G(x,t,z)\in K\) passes graph-representation validation precisely when \[t\ge f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\;G(x,t,z)\in K\] over the declared domain, with the analogous hypograph equivalence for a concave atom and membership equivalence for a custom set. Moreover, \(G\) must be affine in optimization variables, dimensions must agree, every cone factor of \(K\) must be supported by the selected solver, and parameter specialization must preserve these properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph validation requires exact graph equivalence, affine canonicalization, consistent dimensions, and cones supported by the selected solver.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and its domain are fixed by the extension metadata.
\(K\) is the canonicalization's product cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonicalization is valid exactly when graph equivalence and solver-compatibility conditions both hold.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record addresses both exact graph equivalence and solver compatibility as required by the leaf, but the claim that these conditions are precisely sufficient depends on the modeling system, solver interface, and parameter-specialization rules. No authoritative source or locator is provided.

children.title: Epigraph Representations
children.top_down_role: Graph representations oriented toward convex-valued atoms.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), where \(X\) is a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi} f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)\le t\}\), and \(f(x)=\inf\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real epigraph representation used to replace an upper bound on a convex expression.

source_refs.locator: 3. Basic Concepts of Convex Optimization p. 115

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an extended-real-valued function \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), its epigraph is \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)\le t\}.\] Thus the inequality \(f(x)\le t\) is represented exactly by membership \((x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\). The function value is recovered by \[f(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{R}:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\},\] with the infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). Moreover, \(f\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper bound on a function is equivalent to membership in its epigraph; the function value is the lowest admissible height, and convexity equals convexity of the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Basic Concepts of Convex Optimization p. 115

children.title: Hypograph Representations
children.top_down_role: Graph representations oriented toward concave-valued atoms.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\), where \(X\) is a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{hypo} f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:t\le f(x)\}\), and \(f(x)=\sup\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{hypo}f\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real hypograph representation used to replace a lower bound on a concave expression.

source_refs.locator: 3. Basic Concepts of Convex Optimization p. 115

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an extended-real-valued function \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\), its hypograph is \[\operatorname{hypo}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:t\le f(x)\}.\] Thus the inequality \(t\le f(x)\) is represented exactly by membership \((x,t)\in\operatorname{hypo}f\). The function value is recovered by \[f(x)=\sup\{t\in\mathbb{R}:(x,t)\in\operatorname{hypo}f\},\] with the supremum of the empty set interpreted as \(-\infty\). Moreover, \(f\) is concave if and only if \(\operatorname{hypo}f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower bound on a function is equivalent to membership in its hypograph; the function value is the greatest admissible height, and concavity equals hypograph convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Hypograph Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Basic Concepts of Convex Optimization p. 115

children.title: Orientation Duality
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between epigraph and hypograph orientations.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is extended-real-valued.
\(g=-f\), with the corresponding extended-real sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\iff(x,-t)\in\operatorname{hypo}g\), hence \(\operatorname{epi}f=R^{-1}(\operatorname{hypo}(-f))\) for \(R(x,t)=(x,-t)\).

notation.meaning: Sign-reversal map in the graph-height coordinate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign reversal exchanges epigraph and hypograph orientations and exchanges convexity with concavity.

source_refs.locator: 3. Basic Concepts of Convex Optimization p. 115

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=-f\) and let \(R:X\times\mathbb{R}\to X\times\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(R(x,t)=(x,-t)\). Then \[(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -t\le g(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R(x,t)\in\operatorname{hypo}g.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{epi}f=R^{-1}(\operatorname{hypo}(-f))\) and \(\operatorname{hypo}f=R^{-1}(\operatorname{epi}(-f))\). Because \(R\) is an invertible linear map, epigraph convexity of \(f\) is equivalent to hypograph convexity of \(-f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating both a function and its height coordinate converts epigraph membership into hypograph membership, while converting convex functions into concave functions.
knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Duality

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Basic Concepts of Convex Optimization p. 115

children.title: Graph-Orientation Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where graph orientation conflicts with source curvature or constraint placement.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Orientation Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wrong graph orientation is generally nonconvex; on a convex domain, simultaneous epigraph and hypograph convexity characterizes affine real-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x)=x^2\), the hypograph \(\operatorname{hypo}f\) is nonconvex. For \(h:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(h(x)=-x^2\), the epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}h\) is nonconvex. Thus a lower graph orientation for a convex expression, or an upper graph orientation for a concave expression, generally fails convex graph canonicalization. More generally, if \(D\) is convex and \(\varphi:D\to\mathbb{R}\) has both a convex epigraph and a convex hypograph relative to \(D\times\mathbb{R}\), then \(\varphi\) is affine on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic has a nonconvex hypograph, and a concave quadratic has a nonconvex epigraph. On a convex domain, both orientations are convex only for a real-valued affine function.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a convex subset of a real vector space when the affine boundary is invoked.
\(\varphi:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The wrong graph orientation is generally nonconvex; if both graph orientations are convex on \(D\), then \(\varphi\) is affine on \(D\).

notation.meaning: Convex domain used in the affine boundary statement.

children.title: Partial-Optimization Representations
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations using auxiliary optimization variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Optimization Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact attained partial-minimization lift; without attainment, projection may omit boundary heights and closure qualifications may be necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, and define \(g:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) by \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). Assume \(g(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in X\), and assume that whenever \(g(x)<+\infty\), some \(y\in Y\) attains the infimum. Then \[\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:\exists y\in Y,\ F(x,y)\le t\}=\pi_{x,t}(\operatorname{epi}F).\] Hence \(g(x)\le t\) is implemented exactly by introducing \(y\) and imposing \(F(x,y)\le t\). If \(F\) is convex, then \(g\) is convex; closedness of the projected epigraph requires additional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every finite fiberwise infimum is attained and no fiber value is negative infinity, partial minimization is represented exactly by projecting the joint epigraph. Convexity is preserved, but closedness is not automatic.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, and convex.
For every \(x\in X\), \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)>-\infty\).
Whenever \(g(x)<+\infty\), the infimum is attained by some \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:\exists y\in Y,\ F(x,y)\le t\}=\pi_{x,t}(\operatorname{epi}F)\).

notation.meaning: Projection retaining the original variable and epigraph height.

source_refs.locator: 3.3. Partial Minimization of Convex Functions p. 122

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3. Partial Minimization of Convex Functions p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unattained Infimum Omits the Epigraph Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp example showing the necessity of attainment for exact boundary projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(y)=e^y\), \(g=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R}F(y)=0\), but the infimum is unattained and \[\{t:\exists y,\ e^y\le t\}=(0,+\infty)\ne[0,+\infty)=\operatorname{epi}g.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential function approaches zero without attaining it, so projection loses exactly the epigraph boundary height zero.
assumptions_latex: \(F(y)=e^y\) for \(y\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{t:\exists y,\ F(y)\le t\}=(0,+\infty)\ne\operatorname{epi}(\inf_yF)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unattained Infimum Omits the Epigraph Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Boundary for Unattained Partial Infima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the projected joint epigraph from the value-function epigraph without fiberwise attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\) and \(P=\{(x,t):\exists y,\ F(x,y)\le t\}\). Then \[P\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g,\qquad \{(x,t):g(x)<t\}\subseteq P,\qquad \overline P=\overline{\operatorname{epi}g}.\] At a point with finite \(g(x)\), \((x,g(x))\in P\) exactly when the fiberwise infimum is attained. If \(g\) is proper convex and its lower-semicontinuous hull \(\operatorname{cl}g\) is proper, then \(\overline P=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without fiberwise attainment, projection may omit finite boundary points of the value-function epigraph, although its closure recovers the closed epigraph under the stated proper-convex assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
For the final closed-epigraph identity, \(g\) and \(\operatorname{cl}g\) are proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline P=\overline{\operatorname{epi}g}\), and finite boundary membership in \(P\) is equivalent to fiberwise attainment.

notation.meaning: Projection of the joint epigraph onto retained variables and height.
Lower-semicontinuous convex closure of the value function.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Boundary for Unattained Partial Infima

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugacy restricts the eliminated variable's dual coordinate to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). Whenever the extended-real conjugates are well defined, \[g^*(u)=F^*(u,0)\qquad(u\in X^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a partial infimum is the joint conjugate evaluated at zero in the eliminated variable's dual coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\) are interpreted in extended-real arithmetic.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the joint function.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate of a Partial Infimum

children.title: Cone-Membership Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations of nonlinear expressions through standard cone memberships.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Membership Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of an exact lifted conic epigraph representation for a scalar extended-real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) be a closed convex cone. A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) has an exact lifted \(K\)-cone epigraph representation if there are an integer \(r\ge 0\), matrices \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times n}\) and \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times r}\), and vectors \(b,d\in\mathbb{R}^q\) such that, for every \((x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\), \[f(x)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^r\ \text{such that}\ Ax+bt+Cz+d\in K.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is the projection onto \((x,t)\) of an affine inverse image of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epigraph is exactly cone representable when it is the projection of an affine cone-membership feasible set in the original, height, and auxiliary variables.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) is a closed convex cone.
\(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
\(A\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times n}\), \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times r}\), and \(b,d\in\mathbb{R}^q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \((x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\), \(f(x)\le t\iff\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^r:\ Ax+bt+Cz+d\in K\).

notation.meaning: Closed convex cone used by the representation.
Affine data of compatible explicitly stated dimensions.

children.title: Set-Lift Representations
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations for named convex sets.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq X\times Z\) is a convex set in finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\pi_X(Q)=\{x\in X:\exists z\in Z,\ (x,z)\in Q\}\) is the set represented by the lift \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional existential set lift and projection, independent of any particular cone or matrix structure.

source_refs.locator: 3. Basic Concepts of Convex Optimization p. 115

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq X\) has a set-lift representation through \(Q\subseteq X\times Z\) when \[S=\pi_X(Q)=\{x\in X:\exists z\in Z,\ (x,z)\in Q\}.\] The variable \(z\) is auxiliary and is removed by projection. If \(Q\) is convex, then \(S\) is convex. Conversely, every convex \(S\) admits the trivial lift \(Q=S\times\{0\}\); useful lifts impose a simpler description on \(Q\) than is available directly for \(S\). Exactness refers only to equality after projection and does not imply preservation of representation size or analytic regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set lift represents a set as the projection of a higher-dimensional feasible set; convexity survives projection, while simplicity and closedness require separate assessment.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Lift Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Basic Concepts of Convex Optimization p. 115

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimization Preservation Under an Exact Set Lift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization consequence of exact equality with a lifted projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S=\pi_X(Q)\) and \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), then \[\inf_{x\in S}\varphi(x)=\inf_{(x,z)\in Q}\varphi(x),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}\varphi(x)=\pi_X\!\left(\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,z)\in Q}\varphi(x)\right),\] where the argmin sets are empty when the infimum is unattained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact set lift preserves objectives depending only on original variables, including optimal values and projected minimizers.
assumptions_latex: The lifted objective \(\varphi(x)\) is independent of the auxiliary variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and lifted optimal values agree, and their argmin sets agree after projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Preservation Under an Exact Set Lift

children.title: Matrix-Lift Representations
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations introducing structured matrix variables or constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(F_0,F_1,\ldots,F_n,G_1,\ldots,G_r\in\mathbb{S}^m\) are real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{x:\exists z,\ F_0+\sum_i x_iF_i+\sum_jz_jG_j\succeq0\}\) is a matrix-lift representation of \(S\).

notation.meaning: Space of real symmetric matrices of order m.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite matrix lift, also called a spectrahedral-shadow representation.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has a positive-semidefinite matrix-lift representation of order \(m\) if symmetric matrices exist for which \[S=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^r,\ F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_i+\sum_{j=1}^r z_jG_j\succeq0\right\}.\] The lifted set in \((x,z)\) is a spectrahedron, and \(S\) is its projection, hence a spectrahedral shadow. The representation is convex because the positive-semidefinite cone is convex and both affine inverse images and linear projections preserve convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix lift expresses a set as the projection of a linear matrix inequality feasible region, making the represented set a convex spectrahedral shadow.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Lift Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure operations for finite positive-semidefinite matrix-lift representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Finite-dimensional spectrahedral shadows are closed under finite Cartesian products, finite intersections, affine inverse images, and linear images. Multiple LMI lifts can be combined through \[M_i(x,z_i)\succeq0\ (i=1,\ldots,k)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{diag}(M_1(x,z_1),\ldots,M_k(x,z_k))\succeq0.\] These operations preserve convexity but do not ensure closedness after projection or linear imaging.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix lifts combine through block-diagonal LMIs and remain matrix lifts under standard finite affine operations, but their images need not be closed.
assumptions_latex: All spaces and matrix pencils are finite-dimensional.
Each input set has a finite positive-semidefinite matrix lift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite products, intersections, affine inverse images, and linear images of spectrahedral shadows are spectrahedral shadows.

notation.meaning: The symmetric affine pencil in the ith lift.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Calculus of Matrix Lifts

children.title: Spectral Lifts
children.top_down_role: Matrix-based lifts for supported spectral quantities.

assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb{S}^m\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\max}(X)\le t\iff tI-X\succeq0\), so \(\operatorname{epi}\lambda_{\max}=\{(X,t):tI-X\succeq0\}\).

notation.meaning: Largest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical semidefinite epigraph lift for the maximum eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real symmetric matrix \(X\in\mathbb{S}^m\), the spectral theorem gives \[\lambda_{\max}(X)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad tI-X\succeq0.\] Consequently, \[\operatorname{epi}\lambda_{\max}=\{(X,t)\in\mathbb{S}^m\times\mathbb{R}:tI-X\succeq0\}.\] This is an affine positive-semidefinite cone membership representation with no auxiliary matrix beyond the affine slack \(tI-X\). It establishes convexity of \(X\mapsto\lambda_{\max}(X)\) and permits a maximum-eigenvalue upper bound to be canonicalized as a linear matrix inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The largest eigenvalue is at most a scalar exactly when that scalar times the identity minus the matrix is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Lifts

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite lift for sums of the largest eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\in\mathbb S^m\), \(1\le k\le m\), and \(\lambda_1(X)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_m(X)\), then \[\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(X)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists s\in\mathbb R,\ Z\in\mathbb S^m:\ Z\succeq0,\ Z-X+sI\succeq0,\ ks+\operatorname{tr}Z\le t.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the sum of the largest k eigenvalues has an exact semidefinite lift using one scalar and one PSD auxiliary matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^m\).
\(1\le k\le m\) is an integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The existential LMI system is equivalent to \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i(X)\le t\).
knowledge_statements.title: Ky Fan Eigenvalue-Sum Epigraph Lift

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orientation counterpart to the maximum-eigenvalue epigraph for real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S^m\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\), \[\lambda_{\min}(X)\ge t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X-tI\succeq0.\] Thus \(\operatorname{hypo}\lambda_{\min}=\{(X,t):X-tI\succeq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower bound on the smallest eigenvalue is exactly one positive-semidefinite constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^m\).
\(t\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\min}(X)\ge t\iff X-tI\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of a real symmetric matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Eigenvalue Hypograph Lift

children.title: Lift Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting equivalence between source objects and lifted representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Lift Equivalence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional equivalence concerns projected feasibility only; it does not identify formulation structure or regularity of the lifted sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_1\subseteq X\times Z_1\) and \(Q_2\subseteq X\times Z_2\). The two lifts are extensionally equivalent exactly when \[\pi_X(Q_1)=\pi_X(Q_2).\] This equality does not imply equal auxiliary dimension, cone family, matrix order, constraint count, constraint qualifications, closedness of the lifted sets \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\), or dual attainment behavior. Because the projections are equal, the represented set itself necessarily has the same closedness status in both representations. However, even a closed convex lifted set can have a nonclosed projection, so closedness of a lift does not by itself establish closedness of the represented set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal projections make two lifts feasibility-equivalent, but do not equate their dimensions, cone types, lifted-set regularity, or dual behavior. The common projected set has one shared closedness status, which need not follow from closedness of either lift.
assumptions_latex: \(X\), \(Z_1\), and \(Z_2\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(Q_1\subseteq X\times Z_1\) and \(Q_2\subseteq X\times Z_2\) are lifted feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifts are extensionally equivalent exactly when \(\pi_X(Q_1)=\pi_X(Q_2)\); this equality does not identify their formulation structure or lifted-set regularity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States what projection equivalence preserves in optimization and what it does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\pi_X(Q_1)=\pi_X(Q_2)=S\), then for every \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \[\inf_{(x,z_1)\in Q_1}\varphi(x)=\inf_{x\in S}\varphi(x)=\inf_{(x,z_2)\in Q_2}\varphi(x),\] and, when minima exist, both lifted argmin sets project to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}\varphi(x)\). Projection equality implies no corresponding result for auxiliary-dependent objectives or auxiliary witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent lifts preserve objectives depending only on original variables, but need not preserve auxiliary-dependent costs or witnesses.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_i\subseteq X\times Z_i\) for \(i=1,2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Original-variable optimal values and projected minimizers agree across the lifts; auxiliary-dependent objectives need not agree.

children.title: Function-Value Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Preservation of source-level function values by graph implementations.

knowledge_statements.title: Function-Value Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise value-correctness condition for an upper-bound graph implementation with existential auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be sets, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and let \(\Gamma(x,t,z)\) be a feasibility predicate for \((x,t,z)\in X\times\mathbb{R}\times Z\). Define \[\widehat f(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{R}:\exists z\in Z,\ \Gamma(x,t,z)\},\] where the infimum may initially lie in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\) and the infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). The implementation is function-value equivalent to \(f\) if and only if \[\widehat f(x)=f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Equality of the implemented epigraph with \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is sufficient but stronger: value equivalence can hold even if an unattained boundary height is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted graph implementation is value-equivalent when the infimum of its feasible heights over the auxiliary domain recovers the original function at every input.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the input set and \(Z\) is the auxiliary-variable set.
\(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
\(\Gamma(x,t,z)\) is a predicate on \(X\times\mathbb{R}\times Z\).
The infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implementation is function-value equivalent if and only if \(f(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{R}:\exists z\in Z,\ \Gamma(x,t,z)\}\) for every \(x\in X\).

children.title: Feasibility Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Preservation of feasible source decisions under canonical representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based feasibility correctness for simultaneous canonicalization of inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p,q\) be nonnegative integers, let \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,p\), and let \(h_j:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,q\). Define \[S=\{x\in X:f_i(x)\le0\ \text{for every }i,\ h_j(x)=0\ \text{for every }j\}.\] For each \(i\), let \(Z_i\) be an auxiliary domain and let \(\Gamma_i(x,z_i)\) be a predicate on \(X\times Z_i\). With \(Z=\prod_{i=1}^p Z_i\) and \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_p)\), define \[\widehat S=\{(x,z)\in X\times Z:\Gamma_i(x,z_i)\ \text{for every }i,\ h_j(x)=0\ \text{for every }j\}.\] The canonicalization is feasibility equivalent if and only if \[S=\pi_X(\widehat S)=\{x\in X:\exists z\in Z,\ (x,z)\in\widehat S\}.\] A sufficient local condition is \(f_i(x)\le0\iff\exists z_i\in Z_i,\ \Gamma_i(x,z_i)\) for every \(x\in X\) and every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonicalization preserves feasibility exactly when projection of the lifted feasible set onto the original variables reproduces the original feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(p,q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\).
\(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,p\).
\(h_j:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,q\).
For each \(i\), \(Z_i\) is an auxiliary domain and \(\Gamma_i\) is a predicate on \(X\times Z_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is preserved if and only if \(S=\pi_X(\widehat S)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological boundary for finite-dimensional extended formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(F=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^2:x\ge0,\ z\ge0,\ xz\ge1\}\) is closed and convex, but \(\operatorname{proj}_xF=(0,\infty)\), which is not closed. Thus finite-dimensional projection preserves convexity but not closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex lifted feasible set can have a nonclosed source-coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is closed and convex},\qquad \operatorname{proj}_xF=(0,\infty)\text{ is not closed}.

notation.meaning: Lifted feasible set in the counterexample.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Need Not Survive Projection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural property after eliminating auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) is convex, then \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xF\) is convex. Consequently, an exact convex graph expansion cannot project to a nonconvex source feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection preserves convexity, so a convex lift has a convex projected feasible set.
assumptions_latex: F\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_xF\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Under Extended-Variable Projection

The lifted graph constraints exactly represent every expanded atom, including its domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S=\operatorname{proj}_x(F)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ (x,z)\in F\}.\]

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the source formulation.
Feasible set of the lifted formulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact graph expansion with existentially quantified auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the feasible set defined by the source constraints, and let \(F\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) be the feasible set after replacing every supported atom by an exact graph implementation. Functional feasibility is preserved precisely when \[x\in S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^p\text{ such that }(x,z)\in F.\] Thus auxiliary variables may enlarge the ambient space but cannot add or remove any feasible source-variable assignment after projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact graph expansion preserves feasibility when projecting the lifted feasible set onto the original variables gives exactly the source feasible set.

children.title: Equivalence Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation defects that break value or feasibility preservation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates function-value equivalence from projected-domain equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^2\), replace the exact epigraph condition \(t\ge x^2\) by \(t\ge0\). Both formulations project onto all \(x\in\mathbb R\), but \(\inf\{t:t\ge0\}=0\neq x^2\) whenever \(x\neq0\). Thus domain or feasibility correspondence does not imply function-value equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation can preserve every feasible input while changing the represented function value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,t):t\ge0\}=\mathbb R=\operatorname{dom}f,\qquad \inf_{t\ge0}t\neq f(x)\ \text{for }x\neq0.
knowledge_statements.title: Value Failure Without Feasibility Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic classification of feasibility errors from inexact graph implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the source feasible set and \(F\) a lifted feasible set. An outer approximation satisfies \(S\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xF\), with strict inclusion producing false feasible source assignments. An inner approximation satisfies \(\operatorname{proj}_xF\subseteq S\), with strict inclusion discarding valid source assignments. Exact feasibility equivalence holds precisely when both inclusions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer approximations add false feasible points, inner approximations remove valid points, and exactness requires both inclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\operatorname{proj}_xF\iff S\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_xF\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{proj}_xF\subseteq S.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer and Inner Approximation Failures

assumptions_latex: A claimed canonicalization replaces an exact graph constraint by a strict relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{proj}_x(F_{\mathrm{lift}})\ne S_{\mathrm{source}},\] so functional feasibility equivalence fails.

notation.meaning: Lifted feasible set under the relaxed implementation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete failure caused by an inexact exponential epigraph implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the source constraint \(e^x\le 0\), whose feasible set is empty. If the exponential epigraph \(t\ge e^x\) is incorrectly replaced by the single tangent relaxation \(t\ge 1+x\), canonicalization gives \(t\le 0\) and \(t\ge 1+x\). The lifted point \((x,t)=(-2,0)\) is feasible, although no source point is feasible. Hence replacing an exact graph, domain condition, or equivalence-preserving constraint by a proper relaxation can strictly enlarge the projected feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalence fails when an exact graph is relaxed: a tangent approximation makes an impossible exponential constraint feasible after lifting.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalence Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the leaf, and the tangent-relaxation example is internally correct. An inspectable source is nevertheless required for this canonicalization failure example because the record provides neither a citation nor standard-field rationale.

children.title: Domain Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Preservation of explicit and implicit domains under expansion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recursive Domain of an Atom Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local domain rule that exact graph expansion must preserve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=f(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\), interpreted with extended-real domain semantics, \[\operatorname{dom}h=\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i\right)\cap\{x:(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.\] Consequently, an exact recursive graph expansion must encode every inner domain and the outer atom's domain condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composed atom is defined only where every inner expression is defined and their value tuple belongs to the outer atom's domain.
assumptions_latex: h(x)=f(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\text{ uses extended-real domain semantics.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}h=\left(\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}g_i\right)\cap\{x:g(x)\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.

notation.meaning: Effective domain of an extended-real function or atom.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Domain of an Atom Composition

assumptions_latex: The graph implementation of each atom is exact and includes all implicit domain restrictions.
Explicit source constraints are copied or equivalently transformed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D=\operatorname{proj}_x(\widehat D).\]

notation.meaning: Source-variable domain satisfying explicit and implicit restrictions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain preservation for exact finite-dimensional graph expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) contain exactly those source assignments satisfying all explicit constraints and every implicit atom domain. Let \(\widehat D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\) contain the expanded assignments satisfying the canonical constraints and their graph-domain conditions. Correct expansion requires \[x\in D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^p\text{ with }(x,z)\in\widehat D.\] In particular, expansion must neither discard boundary points admitted by the source semantics nor admit points where a source expression is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact expansion preserves both written constraints and implicit atom domains under projection onto the source variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Domain Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property matches the stated role and consistently includes explicit and implicit domains, but the exact graph-domain semantics on which the projection identity depends are not supported by any source.

children.title: Primal-Variable Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationships between source variables and lifted variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued correspondence for source coordinates explicitly embedded in an exact lifted formulation; auxiliary extensions need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq X\) and \(\widehat S\subseteq X\times Z\) be source and lifted feasible sets satisfying \(S=\pi_X(\widehat S)\). Then every lifted feasible point projects to a source feasible point, every source feasible point has at least one lifted extension, and no uniqueness of that extension is required. Let \(g:S\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(\widehat g:\widehat S\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) satisfy \(\widehat g(x,z)=g(x)\) for all \((x,z)\in\widehat S\). If \(X^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}g(x)\) and \(\widehat X^\star=\operatorname*{argmin}_{(x,z)\in\widehat S}\widehat g(x,z)\), then \(\pi_X(\widehat X^\star)=X^\star\), including the case in which both optimizer sets are empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact projection gives a surjective correspondence from lifted feasible points to source feasible points, and objective preservation makes the same projection map the lifted optimizer set exactly onto the source optimizer set; auxiliary extensions may be nonunique.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\pi_X(\widehat S)\).
\(\widehat g(x,z)=g(x)\) for every \((x,z)\in\widehat S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_X(\widehat S)=S,\qquad \pi_X(\widehat X^\star)=X^\star.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Variable Correspondence

children.title: Dual-Information Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Representation-dependent recovery and interpretation of dual information.

assumptions_latex: A source equality \(Ax=b\) is represented as \(T(Ax-b)=0\).
The matrix \(T\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y=T^{\mathsf T}\lambda,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y=A^{\mathsf T}T^{\mathsf T}\lambda.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative linear-equality case illustrating representation-dependent dual recovery.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the source equality \(Ax=b\), suppose a lifted representation uses \(T(Ax-b)=0\), where \(T\) has full column rank. A lifted multiplier \(\lambda\) contributes \(A^{\mathsf T}T^{\mathsf T}\lambda\) to stationarity, so the corresponding source multiplier is \(y=T^{\mathsf T}\lambda\). Conversely, every source multiplier has a lifted preimage because \(T^{\mathsf T}\) is surjective. Lifted multipliers may be nonunique when \(T^{\mathsf T}\) has a nontrivial kernel; therefore raw dual coordinates are representation dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual multipliers transform by the adjoint of the residual map; recovered source multipliers can be unique even when lifted multipliers are not.

assumptions_latex: The decision vector is \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: Equality coefficient matrix and right-hand side.
Canonical decision vector, possibly containing auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite systems of affine equalities in a polyhedral canonical form.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.2 Dual to a linear programming program: Origin p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear-equality target is a constraint block of the form \[Au=b,\] where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) contains the canonical decision and auxiliary variables. Its feasible set is an affine subspace when consistent and is empty otherwise. Scalar affine equalities are obtained by taking \(m=1\), and multiple equality blocks may be stacked without changing the represented set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-equality target is a finite affine system equating a matrix-vector product to a fixed right-hand side.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear-inequality target is a constraint block \[Gu\le h,\] where \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times n}\), \(h\in\mathbb{R}^q\), and the inequality is componentwise. Equivalently, its \(i\)-th row requires \(g_i^{\mathsf T}u\le h_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\). The represented feasible set is an intersection of finitely many closed halfspaces and is therefore a closed convex polyhedron, possibly empty or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-inequality target is a finite componentwise affine system whose feasible set is a polyhedron.

children.title: Polyhedral-Cone Targets
children.top_down_role: Canonical targets using general polyhedral cone blocks.

assumptions_latex: The cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) is a closed convex polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[h-Gu\in K.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine membership constraints over finite-dimensional polyhedral cones.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral-cone target is an affine conic constraint \[h-Gu\in K,\] where \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) is a closed convex polyhedral cone. Because such a cone is the intersection of finitely many homogeneous halfspaces, there exists a matrix \(W\) such that \(K=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^q:Ws\ge0\}\). Consequently, the target is equivalent to the finite linear-inequality system \(W(h-Gu)\ge0\), although retaining cone membership can preserve useful block structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral-cone target constrains an affine residual to a polyhedral cone and can be expanded into finitely many linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral-Cone Targets

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Descriptions of a Polyhedral Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-cone formulas for the H- and V-representations used by polyhedral targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=\{s:Ws\ge0\}\), then \[K^{*}=\{W^{\mathsf T}\lambda:\lambda\ge0\}.\] If \(K=\{R\theta:\theta\ge0\}\), then \[K^{*}=\{y:R^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\}.\] Hence duality exchanges finite H- and V-descriptions and preserves polyhedrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duality exchanges the halfspace and generator descriptions of a polyhedral cone.
assumptions_latex: Dual cones use the nonnegative Euclidean pairing.
\(W\) and \(R\) give exact descriptions of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ polyhedral}\Longrightarrow K^{*}\text{ polyhedral}.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Descriptions of a Polyhedral Cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minkowski-Weyl Forms of a Polyhedral Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generator and homogeneous-halfspace forms underlying polyhedral-cone targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-dimensional convex cone \(K\) is polyhedral iff it is finitely generated. Thus finite matrices \(W,R\) exist with \[K=\{s:Ws\ge0\}=\{R\theta:\theta\ge0\}.\] Consequently, \(r(u)\in K\) is represented either by \(Wr(u)\ge0\) or by \(r(u)=R\theta\), \(\theta\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every polyhedral cone has finite homogeneous inequality and conic-generator descriptions, producing two exact target forms.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is polyhedral}\iff K\text{ is finitely generated}.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns generate the cone

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski-Weyl Forms of a Polyhedral Cone

children.title: Linear-to-Polyhedral Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Representation choices connecting explicit linear constraints with polyhedral cones.

assumptions_latex: All vector inequalities use the nonnegative orthant ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Gu\le h\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h-Gu\in\mathbb{R}_+^q,\qquad Au=b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b-Au\in\{0\}^m.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion between affine systems and orthant or zero-cone membership.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Componentwise affine inequalities and equalities are conic constraints over polyhedral cones: \[Gu\le h\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h-Gu\in\mathbb{R}_+^q,\] and \[Au=b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b-Au\in\{0\}^m.\] Conversely, if a polyhedral cone has an inequality description \(K=\{s:Ws\ge0\}\), then \(h-Gu\in K\) is equivalent to \(W(h-Gu)\ge0\). These conversions preserve the feasible set exactly, though their multiplier coordinates and sparsity patterns may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear equalities and inequalities are zero-cone and nonnegative-orthant constraints; any described polyhedral-cone constraint expands back into linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-to-Polyhedral Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Geometry of the primal and dual problems p. 53

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted conversion between componentwise inequalities and equality-plus-orthant form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(G\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\) and \(h\in\mathbb R^q\), \[Gu\le h\iff\exists s\in\mathbb R_+^q:\ Gu+s=h.\] For each feasible \(u\), the slack is uniquely \(s=h-Gu\). A free vector may also be represented as \(v=v^+-v^-\) with \(v^+,v^-\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear inequalities are exactly equalities with nonnegative slacks, while free variables can be split into differences of nonnegative variables.
assumptions_latex: Vector inequalities use componentwise ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{u:Gu\le h\}=\operatorname{proj}_u\{(u,s):Gu+s=h,\ s\ge0\}.

notation.meaning: nonnegative vectors representing a free vector

knowledge_statements.title: Slack-Variable Correspondence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex quadratic-program target has the form \[\underset{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}{\operatorname{minimize}}\ \frac12u^{\mathsf T}Pu+q^{\mathsf T}u+r\quad\text{subject to}\quad Au=b,\quad Gu\le h,\] where \(P\in\mathbb{S}_+^n\). Positive semidefiniteness makes the objective convex, while the constraints define a polyhedron. A canonicalization may introduce auxiliary variables, but it is a quadratic-program target only when the retained nonlinear structure is quadratic and every remaining constraint is affine.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical representation using three-dimensional power cones with fixed exponents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define the power cone \[K_{\mathrm{pow}}^{\alpha}=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ |z|\le x^{\alpha}y^{1-\alpha}\}.\] A power-cone target is an affine conic program \[\operatorname{minimize}_{u}\ c^{\mathsf T}u\quad\text{subject to}\quad Au+b\in K,\] where \(K\) is a Cartesian product containing blocks \(K_{\mathrm{pow}}^{\alpha_j}\). Thus \(|z|\le x^{\alpha}y^{1-\alpha}\), with \(x,y\ge0\), is represented exactly by \((x,y,z)\in K_{\mathrm{pow}}^{\alpha}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Conversion Does Not Establish Exact Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact cone compatibility and approximation-based routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an unsupported required cone block is replaced by a formulation having a different projected feasible set or objective epigraph, the replacement is an approximation, relaxation, or restriction rather than an exact conversion. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a canonical problem \(P\) and an exact conversion library. If \(\mathcal S'\) retains every direct cone capability and exact conversion available under \(\mathcal S\), then \((P,\mathcal S)\) cone-compatible implies \((P,\mathcal S')\) cone-compatible. The converse can fail when \(\mathcal S'\) supports a required block unavailable under \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact compatibility persists when cone capabilities and exact conversions are enlarged, but the converse can fail.

Cone-Compatibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility condition for emitting a canonical cone target supported by a solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal B(P)\) be the multiset of cone blocks required by a canonicalization of source problem \(P\), and let \(\mathcal S\) be the solver-supported cone families and dimensions. The pair \((P,\mathcal S)\) is cone-compatible precisely when every \(B\in\mathcal B(P)\) either belongs to \(\mathcal S\) or admits an exact finite-dimensional conversion into a product of cones in \(\mathcal S\). Compatibility additionally requires that all converted affine maps and domains preserve the source feasible set under projection and preserve objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem and solver are cone-compatible when every required block is supported directly or exactly convertible without changing projected feasibility or objective values.
assumptions_latex: A canonical cone-block multiset \(\mathcal B(P)\) has been determined.
Solver capabilities \(\mathcal S\) include supported cone families and dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((P,\mathcal S)\text{ is compatible}\iff \forall B\in\mathcal B(P),\ B\text{ is supported or exactly convertible into cones in }\mathcal S\).

children.title: Source-Problem Normalization
children.top_down_role: Normalization of objectives, constraints, attributes, and value spaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the system-independent algebraic portion of source-problem normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A maximization objective \max f_0(x) is equivalently written as \min -f_0(x). A constraint g(x)\ge0 is equivalently written as -g(x)\le0, while g(x)\le0 and h(x)=0 retain their orientations. Recording the objective-sign change gives a bijection between feasible points and preserves optimizers, with normalized and source optimal values related by sign reversal for a converted maximization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective sense and inequality orientation can be standardized exactly by sign changes while recording the corresponding source-value map.
assumptions_latex: All sign changes are performed in the extended-real sense on the declared domains.
The normalization records whether the source objective was maximized or minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in F}f_0(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}(-f_0(x)),\qquad p_{\min(-f_0)}=-p_{\max(f_0)}.

notation.meaning: Unchanged source feasible set after orientation normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Sense and Constraint-Orientation Normalization
Source-Problem Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization preceding atom expansion and cone conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a disciplined convex problem with typed variables, objective \(f_0\), and constraints. First convert maximization to minimization by negating its objective. Rewrite inequalities as \(f_i(x)\le0\), equalities as \(h_j(x)=0\), and attributes as explicit domains or retained metadata. Resolve shapes, broadcasts, constants, parameters, and value spaces, then construct a directed acyclic expression graph with shared subexpressions represented once. Reject the input if dimensions, domains, or curvature-sign composition rules are inconsistent. Output the normalized graph and a recovery map to the original variables and objective sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalization standardizes objective sense, constraint orientation, domains, shapes, and expression sharing, while retaining a map back to the source problem.
assumptions_latex: The input uses a finite expression graph of registered atoms.
Variable and parameter attributes have declared value spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{norm}}\) has standardized syntax and is equivalent to the source problem under the recorded recovery map.

With constant-time template lookup and append operations, atom expansion requires \[O\!\left(N+\sum_v s_v\right)\] time and emits \(O(\sum_v s_v)\) scalar data, before optional algebraic simplification. If shared subexpressions are expanded separately by occurrence, \(N\) and the sum are taken over occurrences.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a normalized directed acyclic expression graph. Traverse its nodes in topological order. Replace the atom occurrence by \(t_a\), reusing one expansion for shared nodes. Choose an epigraph, hypograph, or equality graph according to the atom curvature and monotonic context. Output an affine expression graph together with the accumulated graph constraints and a map from auxiliary variables to source nodes.
