knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Time Chordal Recognition and Zero-Fill Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supplies the standard recognition and certificate route for the zero-fill regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maximum cardinality search produces a vertex ordering of an adjacency-list graph \(G=(V,E)\) in \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time. Using the convention that vertices are placed from last to first as they are selected, the resulting ordering is a perfect elimination ordering exactly when its later-neighbor clique test succeeds at every vertex. Thus the procedure recognizes chordality and returns a zero-fill ordering when one exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum cardinality search, followed by the perfect-elimination test, recognizes chordal graphs and returns a zero-fill ordering in linear time.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph represented by adjacency lists.
Selected vertices are placed from last to first in the reported ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{MCS}}=O(|V|+|E|),\quad G\text{ chordal}\iff\text{the reported ordering passes the perfect-elimination test}.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Time Chordal Recognition and Zero-Fill Ordering

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes easy zero-fill recognition from optimal positive-fill ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected graph \(G\) and nonnegative integer \(k\), deciding whether at most \(k\) edges can be added to make \(G\) chordal is NP-complete. Equivalently, computing an elimination ordering with minimum added fill is NP-hard, while the fill produced by a proposed ordering can be computed and verified in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognizing zero fill is tractable, but finding a minimum-fill ordering is NP-hard and its decision form is NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph.
\(k\) is a nonnegative integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(G,k):\operatorname{fill}(G)\le k\}\text{ is NP-complete}.

notation.meaning: minimum number of edges required in a chordal completion of G

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Fill-In Complexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes exactly when an undirected sparsity graph admits a zero-fill ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G\), an elimination ordering \(\pi\) produces no fill if and only if every vertex's neighbors occurring later in \(\pi\) form a clique; such a \(\pi\) is a perfect elimination ordering. Consequently, \(G\) admits a zero-fill ordering if and only if \(G\) is chordal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-fill orderings are exactly perfect elimination orderings, and they exist exactly for chordal graphs.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph.
Elimination joins every pair of later neighbors of the eliminated vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_\pi=\varnothing\iff\pi\text{ is a perfect elimination ordering};\qquad \exists\pi:F_\pi=\varnothing\iff G\text{ is chordal}.

notation.meaning: edges added under elimination ordering pi

knowledge_statements.title: Chordality and Zero-Fill Elimination

children.title: Decomposition Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Alignment of canonical structure with block-oriented solver processing.

assumptions_latex: The source model has local blocks \(x_k\), local functions \(f_k\), and an explicit coupling set \(C\).
Canonicalization produces local lifted variables \((x_k,u_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility holds when \(\widehat F=\{(x,u):(x_k,u_k)\in\widehat F_k\ \forall k,\ x\in C\}\) and \(f(x)=\sum_k f_k(x_k)\).

notation.meaning: canonical local feasible set for block k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers separable canonicalization with explicit retained coupling.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonicalization is compatible with the source decomposition when \(f(x)=\sum_k f_k(x_k)\) remains separable and its feasible set can be written as \(\widehat F=\{(x,u):(x_k,u_k)\in\widehat F_k\text{ for every }k,\ x\in C\}\). Thus all newly introduced variables, rows, and cone blocks are local to one \(k\), while every cross-block relation is confined to the original designated coupling set \(C\). This form permits independent local evaluations or solves coordinated only through \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonicalization is decomposition compatible when every new object remains local to one source block and all cross-block interaction stays in the designated coupling set.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Compatibility

children.title: Symmetry Preservation
children.top_down_role: Retention of useful invariances in canonical representations.

assumptions_latex: A group \(G\) acts linearly on original variables through \(\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}(X)\).
The original objective and feasible set are invariant under \(\rho(G)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Symmetry is preserved when a lifted action \(\widehat\rho\) satisfies \(R\widehat\rho(g)=\rho(g)R\) and leaves the canonical objective and feasible set invariant for every \(g\in G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses equivariance of primal recovery as the preservation criterion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R:\widehat X\to X\) recover original variables. Canonicalization preserves \(G\)-symmetry if there exists a linear action \(\widehat\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}(\widehat X)\) such that \(R\widehat\rho(g)=\rho(g)R\) for every \(g\in G\), the canonical feasible set is invariant under \(\widehat\rho(g)\), and the canonical objective has the same value at \(z\) and \(\widehat\rho(g)z\). Consequently, each lifted orbit recovers to an original orbit, and symmetry reduction may be performed consistently in either representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetry is preserved when the group has an invariant lifted action that commutes with primal recovery and leaves the canonical objective unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Preservation

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4 Symmetries, Dual Cones, and Facial Structure p. 167
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness Does Not Imply Equivariant Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact source recovery and preservation of source symmetry by a particular lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact projection of a lifted feasible set onto a \(G\)-invariant source problem does not by itself supply a lifted group action. Symmetry is preserved by the chosen representation only when an action on lifted variables leaves its feasible set and objective invariant and intertwines recovery with the source action. If no such action exists in the declared representation class, the lift is exact but not symmetry preserving.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact lift need not preserve visible symmetry; preservation additionally requires an invariant lifted action compatible with recovery.
assumptions_latex: The source problem is invariant under \(\rho(G)\).
A lifted representation, recovery map, and admissible class of lifted actions are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{exact recovery}\not\Rightarrow\text{equivariant lifted recovery}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Does Not Imply Equivariant Representation

children.title: Symmetry Reduction
children.top_down_role: Representations that quotient or compress repeated symmetric structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of fixed-point restriction for invariant nonconvex feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=\{1,-1\}\) act on \(\mathbb R\) by sign change and let \(F=\{-1,1\}\). Although \(F\) and \(f(x)=x^2\) are \(G\)-invariant, the orbit average of either feasible point is \(0\notin F\), and \(F\cap\operatorname{Fix}(G)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the invariant nonconvex set {-1,1}, orbit averaging produces the infeasible fixed point 0.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts by \(x\mapsto -x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\cap\operatorname{Fix}(G)=\varnothing\quad\text{although }F\text{ is }G\text{-invariant}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Boundary for Orbit Averaging

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Haar-averaging extension of finite-group fixed-point reduction for convex invariant problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a compact group \(G\) act continuously and linearly on a finite-dimensional space \(X\), let \(F\subseteq X\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and \(G\)-invariant, and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex and \(G\)-invariant. With normalized Haar measure \(\mu\), define \(Rx=\int_G g x\,d\mu(g)\). Then \(Rx\in F\cap\operatorname{Fix}(G)\) and \(f(Rx)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). Consequently, minimization may be restricted to \(F\cap\operatorname{Fix}(G)\) without changing its infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Haar averaging maps every feasible point of a compact-group-invariant convex problem to a fixed feasible point with no larger invariant convex objective.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is compact and acts continuously and linearly on finite-dimensional \(X\).
\(F\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and invariant.
\(f\) is convex and invariant, and the orbit integral is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in F}f(x)=\inf_{x\in F\cap\operatorname{Fix}(G)}f(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Group Fixed-Point Reduction
Symmetry Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit-based reduction of a finite-dimensional conic canonicalization invariant under a finite group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act linearly and orthogonally on \(\mathbb R^n\) through matrices \(P_g\). Consider a conic program whose objective, feasible set, and cone representation are invariant under every \(P_g\). Define the Reynolds operator \(R=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}P_g\). For every feasible \(x\), the point \(Rx\) is feasible, has the same objective value when the objective is invariant and affine, and lies in \(\operatorname{Fix}(G)=\{z:P_gz=z\ \forall g\in G\}\). Hence optimization may be restricted to \(\operatorname{Fix}(G)\) and parameterized by a basis of that subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A group-invariant convex conic problem can be restricted to the fixed-point subspace by averaging each feasible point over its symmetry orbit.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and acts orthogonally on \(\mathbb R^n\).
The feasible conic representation is convex and \(G\)-invariant.
The affine objective satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}P_gx=c^{\mathsf T}x\) for every \(g\in G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x=\inf_{x\in F\cap\operatorname{Fix}(G)}c^{\mathsf T}x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-group averaging preserves invariant convex feasible sets and affine objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-group averaging statement is mathematically standard and fits Symmetry Reduction, but no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Redundancy Detection
children.top_down_role: Identification of duplicated variables, constraints, or cone blocks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Farkas Certificate for Redundant Linear Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact redundancy certificate for one inequality relative to a nonempty polyhedron containing inequalities and equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear inequality is redundant over a nonempty polyhedron exactly when retained inequalities and equalities admit a compatible Farkas multiplier certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Hx=h\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Certificate for Redundant Linear Inequalities

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Redundant Affine Equality in a Consistent Equality Subsystem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tests whether one affine equality is implied by the remaining affine equalities alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within a consistent affine equality subsystem, an equality is redundant exactly when its augmented row lies in the span of the retained augmented rows.
assumptions_latex: The retained equality subsystem \(R_{-i}x=q_{-i}\) is consistent.
No additional inequalities are used in this test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [r_i^{\mathsf T}\ q_i]\in\operatorname{rowspan}[R_{-i}\ q_{-i}]\iff r_i^{\mathsf T}x=q_i\text{ is implied by the retained equalities}.

notation.meaning: coefficient matrix after deleting equality i
right-hand side of the retained equalities

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Affine Equality in a Consistent Equality Subsystem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes deletion-preserving redundancy from uniform inactivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty retained feasible set \(F_{-i}\) and candidate inequality \(g_i(x)\le0\), weak redundancy is equivalent to \(\sup_{x\in F_{-i}}g_i(x)\le0\). The stronger condition \(\sup_{x\in F_{-i}}g_i(x)<0\) gives uniform positive slack. When the supremum equals zero, the inequality remains weakly redundant but need not have uniform slack and may be active if the supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A redundant inequality need not be uniformly inactive; only a strictly negative maximum violation certifies uniform slack.
assumptions_latex: \(F_{-i}\ne\varnothing\).
The supremum is interpreted in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{F_{-i}}g_i<0\Rightarrow\text{uniform slack},\qquad \sup_{F_{-i}}g_i=0\Rightarrow\text{weak redundancy without guaranteed uniform slack}.

notation.meaning: feasible set after omitting the candidate inequality

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Versus Weak Redundancy Boundary
Redundancy Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact implication test for redundant affine constraints in a convex canonical representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_{-i}=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j\text{ for }j\ne i,\ Hx=h,\ Ax+s=b,\ s\in K\}\), where all displayed constraints except \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) are retained. The omitted inequality is redundant exactly when \(F_{-i}\subseteq\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\}\). Equivalently, if the auxiliary convex problem is well posed, redundancy holds exactly when \(\sup_{x\in F_{-i}}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i)\le0\). A strictly positive optimum or an unbounded-above auxiliary problem certifies nonredundancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality is redundant precisely when maximizing its violation subject to all other constraints produces a nonpositive value.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The auxiliary supremum is interpreted in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\text{ is redundant}\iff\sup_{x\in F_{-i}}(a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i)\le0\).

notation.meaning: feasible set after omitting constraint i
closed convex cone in the canonical representation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: redundancy is logical implication and can be tested by maximal violation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximal-violation characterization is precise and the condition kind fits the leaf, but the record has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Redundancy Elimination
children.top_down_role: Removal of unnecessary canonical structure without changing source semantics.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Individually Redundant Constraints Cannot Necessarily Be Deleted Simultaneously
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary requiring redundancy to be retested against the currently retained family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1=C_2=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\). Relative to \((C_1,C_2)\), each constraint is redundant because deleting either one leaves \(\{0\}\). Deleting both constraints simultaneously, however, leaves the unconstrained set \(\mathbb R\). Thus constraints certified redundant relative to the original family cannot generally all be removed without updating the family after each deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two duplicate constraints are each individually redundant, but deleting both at once changes the feasible set; certified deletion must update the retained family.
assumptions_latex: An empty constraint intersection is interpreted as the whole decision space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_{i=1}^2C_i=\{0\},\qquad\bigcap_{i\in\varnothing}C_i=\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.title: Individually Redundant Constraints Cannot Necessarily Be Deleted Simultaneously
Redundancy Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion procedure preserving the feasible set and objective of a canonical conic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite indexed constraint family \((C_i)_{i\in I}\), initialize \(J\leftarrow I\). For each selected \(i\in J\), test whether \(\bigcap_{j\in J\setminus\{i\}}C_j\subseteq C_i\), using an exact implication test or a valid certificate. If the inclusion holds, set \(J\leftarrow J\setminus\{i\}\); otherwise retain \(i\). Stop after every remaining index has been tested against the current family and output \((C_j)_{j\in J}\). Every deletion preserves the current intersection, so the output feasible set equals \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\), although the retained irredundant family may depend on processing order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly delete constraints certified as implied by the others; each certified deletion preserves the feasible set and objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
Every deletion is supported by an exact or sound implication certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{j\in J}C_j=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\).

notation.meaning: feasible set defined by constraint i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: deleting a logically implied constraint preserves the intersection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deletion algorithm and preservation conclusion are sound, but an authoritative presolve or redundancy-elimination source with a specific locator is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This defines redundancy rather than its elimination and is therefore assigned to the Redundancy Detection sibling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite family \((C_i)_{i\in I}\), constraint \(i\) is redundant exactly when \(\bigcap_{j\ne i}C_j\subseteq C_i\), equivalently when deleting it leaves the intersection unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is redundant exactly when removing it leaves the feasible set unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
All \(C_i\) belong to a common decision space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: i\text{ redundant}\iff\bigcap_{j\ne i}C_j=\bigcap_{j\in I}C_j.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant and Irredundant Constraint Families

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is sequential certified deletion, preservation after each deletion, finite termination, order dependence, and the failure of simultaneous deletion. The proposed redundancy definition is deferred to Redundancy Detection. Symmetry reduction and variable or auxiliary elimination are excluded as sibling or external scopes.

children.title: Representation Conditioning Regimes
children.top_down_role: Numerical behavior introduced or amplified by representation choices.

children.title: Representation Scaling
children.top_down_role: Magnitude balancing introduced through canonical representation choices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A diagonal matrix-balancing heuristic for canonical affine data; admissibility of row factors on cone blocks must be checked separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), alternately scale each nonzero row by the reciprocal of its current selected norm and each nonzero column by the reciprocal of its current selected norm. Accumulating the positive diagonal factors gives matrices \(D\) and \(E\) and a scaled matrix \(DAE\). Each half-step normalizes the objects processed at that half-step; finite termination or simultaneous equilibration is not guaranteed without additional assumptions. Zero rows and columns are detected rather than inverted, and a conic row factor may be used only when it preserves the associated cone block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating diagonal row and column normalization is an equilibration heuristic; zero supports and cone compatibility require explicit handling, and generic convergence is not automatic.
assumptions_latex: The selected row and column norms are fixed.
Only nonzero row and column norms are inverted.
Every applied conic row scaling preserves its cone block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_{k+1}=D_kA_kE_k\text{ at a complete iteration, with the processed rows or columns normalized at their respective half-steps.}
knowledge_statements.title: Iterative Row-and-Column Equilibration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates objective normalization from constraint, variable, and slack scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any feasible set \(F\), objective \(f:F\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\alpha>0\), minimizing \(f\) and minimizing \(\alpha f\) produce the same minimizers. Their infimal values satisfy \(p_\alpha^*=\alpha p^*\) whenever the extended-real product is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying an objective by a positive scalar preserves minimizers while scaling its infimal value.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}\alpha f(x),\qquad p_\alpha^*=\alpha p^*.

notation.meaning: infimal value after positive objective scaling

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Objective Rescaling
Representation Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive diagonal scaling of an affine conic representation without changing its represented solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the conic system \(Ax+s=b\), \(s\in K\), with objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\). Let \(D\) and \(E\) be invertible positive diagonal matrices such that \(DK=K\). Under the substitution \(x=E\hat x\) and \(\hat s=Ds\), the system becomes \((DAE)\hat x+\hat s=Db\), \(\hat s\in K\), with objective \((E^{\mathsf T}c)^{\mathsf T}\hat x\). The map \((\hat x,\hat s)\mapsto(E\hat x,D^{-1}\hat s)\) is bijective, so scaling changes numerical magnitudes but not feasibility or corresponding objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compatible invertible row and variable scalings yield a bijective conic formulation with identical feasibility and corresponding objective values.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and \(E\) are invertible positive diagonal matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\hat x,\hat s)\text{ is scaled-feasible}\iff(E\hat x,D^{-1}\hat s)\text{ is original-feasible})\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: invertible compatible changes of variables preserve conic feasibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatible invertible scaling equivalence is mathematically coherent and fits the representation leaf, but it lacks an inspectable conic-scaling citation.

children.title: Numerical Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of canonical data to finite-precision numerical processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation-based conditioning of the solution map for a locally well-posed canonical representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\) collect the numerical data of a canonical convex program and let \(S(d)\) be its nonempty solution set. At data \(d_0\), the representation is locally Lipschitz well-conditioned if there exist \(L<\infty\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(d\) with \(\lVert d-d_0\rVert\le\varepsilon\), the perturbed problem has a solution and \(\operatorname{dist}(S(d),S(d_0))\le L\lVert d-d_0\rVert\), where distance is the excess or Hausdorff distance specified for the solution-set convention. The least admissible \(L\) is a local absolute condition modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representation is locally well-conditioned when sufficiently small data perturbations cause proportionally small changes in its solution set.
assumptions_latex: \(S(d_0)\) is nonempty.
Fixed norms and a fixed solution-set distance are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(S(d),S(d_0))\le L\lVert d-d_0\rVert\text{ locally for some }L<\infty\).

notation.meaning: solution set associated with data d

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: numerical conditioning is local sensitivity of solutions to data perturbations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed conditioning notion depends materially on whether excess or Hausdorff distance is used and on the direction of excess. A source and fixed convention are needed before the mathematical definition can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Cone-Specific Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scaling considerations associated with different cone families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tracks the dual variable paired with a cone slack under a cone-compatible scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone, let \(D\) be invertible with \(DK=K\), and set \(\widehat s=Ds\). If \(y\in K^*\), define \(\widehat y=D^{-\mathsf T}y\). Then \(\widehat y\in K^*\), \(\langle\widehat y,\widehat s\rangle=\langle y,s\rangle\), and complementarity is preserved in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone-compatible primal scaling induces inverse-adjoint dual scaling, preserving dual feasibility and complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
\(D\) is invertible and \(DK=K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s\in K,\ y\in K^*,\ \langle y,s\rangle=0\iff Ds\in K,\ D^{-\mathsf T}y\in K^*,\ \langle D^{-\mathsf T}y,Ds\rangle=0.

notation.meaning: inverse-adjoint scaling applied to the dual variable

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Transformation Under Cone Automorphisms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies admissible invertible linear scalings for orthant, Lorentz, and real positive-semidefinite cone blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear automorphisms of \(\mathbb R_+^n\) are precisely the positive monomial matrices. Every automorphism of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) has the form \(X\mapsto MXM^{\mathsf T}\) for a nonsingular \(M\). For \(\mathcal Q^n=\{(t,u):t\ge\lVert u\rVert_2\}\) and \(J=\operatorname{diag}(1,-I)\), its automorphisms are \(z\mapsto\alpha Lz\), where \(\alpha>0\), \(L^{\mathsf T}JL=J\), and \(L\mathcal Q^n=\mathcal Q^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthant blocks permit positive monomial transformations, PSD blocks permit nonsingular congruences, and Lorentz blocks permit positive Lorentz transformations preserving the chosen cone component.
assumptions_latex: All maps are real, linear, and invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DK=K\text{ exactly when }D\text{ belongs to the stated automorphism family for the selected standard cone }K.
knowledge_statements.title: Automorphisms of Standard Cone Blocks
Cone-Specific Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible scaling must preserve the product-cone geometry of the canonical representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\) be the product cone of a canonical program. A block scaling \(D=\operatorname{diag}(D_1,\ldots,D_m)\) is cone-compatible when each \(D_i\) is invertible and \(D_iK_i=K_i\). Positive coordinatewise scaling is admissible for a nonnegative-orthant block. A positive scalar multiple of the identity is admissible for every cone block. More general scalings are admissible only when they are automorphisms of the corresponding cone. Consequently, arbitrary diagonal equilibration cannot be applied inside a cone block unless it preserves that cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling is valid blockwise only through invertible maps preserving each cone; arbitrary coordinate equilibration may destroy cone membership.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is represented as a finite product of closed convex cones.
Every block map \(D_i\) is invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DK=K\iff D_iK_i=K_i\text{ for every }i\).

notation.meaning: scaling applied to cone block i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a transformed slack remains equivalent exactly under cone automorphisms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The blockwise cone-automorphism restriction is plausible and fits the leaf, but the exact admissible scaling regimes require an authoritative cone-automorphism source.

children.title: Conditioning Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation regimes prone to severe numerical degradation.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of stable canonical solutions as a displayed problem family approaches a feasibility-status boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R}x\) subject to \(\varepsilon x\ge 1\). Its unique optimizer is \(x_\varepsilon=1/\varepsilon\). Although the displayed coefficient changes from \(\varepsilon\) to \(0\) by magnitude \(\varepsilon\), the optimizer diverges and the limiting system \(0\cdot x\ge 1\) is infeasible. Hence, in the displayed coordinates and absolute coefficient metric, no finite Lipschitz condition modulus for the solution map is uniform as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the displayed coordinates, conditioning fails near the feasibility boundary because a vanishing constraint coefficient makes the optimizer diverge while the limiting problem becomes infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
Conditioning is measured using absolute perturbations of the displayed coefficient and the original coordinate \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-1}\to+\infty\text{ while the problem at }\varepsilon=0\text{ is infeasible}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit scalar family directly exhibits unbounded solution sensitivity in the stated coordinates

children.title: Parameter-Dependence Expression Classes
