children.title: Parameter-Free Expressions
children.top_down_role: Expressions whose canonical data do not depend on mutable parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Expressions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic parameter-independence within a disciplined parametrized expression grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an expression grammar with optimization variables \(x\), declared parameters \(\theta\), numerical constants, and atoms. An expression \(e\) is parameter-free when its expression tree contains no parameter leaf, equivalently when \(\operatorname{Params}(e)=\varnothing\). Such an expression can be evaluated solely from optimization variables and numerical constants and therefore defines a mapping independent of \(\theta\). Parameter-freeness is syntactic: accidental cancellation producing a parameter-independent mapping does not qualify unless canonical simplification removes every parameter occurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter-free expression syntactically contains no parameter leaf; this guarantees parameter-independent evaluation, while accidental semantic cancellation alone does not qualify.
assumptions_latex: A fixed expression tree and parameter declaration are given.
All evaluations lie in the declared domains of their atoms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\text{ is parameter-free}\iff\operatorname{Params}(e)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: parameter leaves occurring in the expression tree

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: syntactic absence of parameter leaves guarantees parameter-independent evaluation

children.title: Parameter-Affine Expressions
children.top_down_role: Expressions with affine dependence on permitted parameter data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic characterization of parameter-affinity on a convex declared domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be convex and let \(e:\Theta\to V\) contain no optimization-variable leaf. Then \(e\) is affine on \(\Theta\) if and only if, for every \(\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \(e(t\theta_1+(1-t)\theta_2)=t e(\theta_1)+(1-t)e(\theta_2)\). In a DPP system this semantic identity is necessary, but syntactic membership may additionally require a derivation under the approved grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable-free expression is semantically affine exactly when it preserves all convex combinations of parameter values; DPP acceptance may also require a syntactic certificate.
assumptions_latex: \Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p\text{ is convex}.
e\text{ contains no optimization-variable leaf}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e\text{ affine on }\Theta\iff e(t\theta_1+(1-t)\theta_2)=t e(\theta_1)+(1-t)e(\theta_2)\ \forall\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta,\ t\in[0,1].
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Combination Characterization
Parameter-Affine Expressions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DPP expression class affine in declared parameters and independent of optimization variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) denote declared parameters. An expression \(e\) is parameter-affine when it contains no optimization-variable leaf and, on its declared parameter domain, has the form \(e(\theta)=E\theta+e_0\) for a parameter-independent linear map \(E\) and constant \(e_0\). Thus numerical constants and individual parameter leaves are parameter-affine, as are dimensionally valid sums and parameter-independent affine transformations of such expressions. A syntactically nonlinear combination of parameters is not parameter-affine merely because particular parameter values make it numerically affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter-affine expression contains no optimization variables and is an affine function of the declared parameters throughout their domain.
assumptions_latex: \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) is the declared parameter domain.
Expression dimensions are fixed and compatible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\text{ is parameter-affine}\iff e(\theta)=E\theta+e_0\text{ and }e\text{ contains no variable leaf}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: parameter-affine DPP expressions are affine in parameters and variable-free

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic affine form is plausible, but the exact DPP class is grammar-dependent and no official definition with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Expression-Class Closure
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships governing how the two expression classes combine.

knowledge_statements.title: Expression-Class Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure rules for parameter-free and parameter-affine DPP expression classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be the parameter-free expressions and \(\mathcal A\) the parameter-affine expressions. Dimensionally compatible sums satisfy \(\mathcal F+\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal F\), \(\mathcal A+\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal A\), and \(\mathcal F+\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal A\) when the member of \(\mathcal F\) is variable-free. Parameter-independent affine maps preserve both classes. For the DPP product rule, a product is admissibly affine when one factor is constant, or when one factor is parameter-affine and the other is parameter-free; its ordinary curvature and variable dependence are then determined by the surrounding disciplined grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DPP classes are closed under compatible addition and parameter-independent affine maps, with products allowed only under the disciplined parameter rule.
assumptions_latex: All operations are dimensionally valid.
Every atom satisfies its ordinary disciplined convexity composition rule.
Parameter classes are assigned syntactically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F+\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal F\text{ and }\mathcal A+\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal A\), with products restricted by the DPP product rule.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stated rules reflect the usual DPP parameter product grammar

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact DPP product and closure rules are implementation-specific and the statement mixes parameter-class closure with ordinary curvature. An authoritative grammar source is needed to determine the correct formulation.

children.title: Nonaffine Dependence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Parameter interactions lying outside reusable affine canonicalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonaffine Dependence Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic boundary excluding nonlinear dependence on declared parameters from the parameter-affine class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta\) be a scalar parameter whose domain contains a nondegenerate interval. The expressions \(\theta^2\), \(\exp(\theta)\), and \(1/\theta\) on a positive interval are not parameter-affine because none equals \(a\theta+b\) throughout its domain. Likewise, the product \(\theta_1\theta_2\) is not jointly affine when the parameter domain contains a two-dimensional open set. Such expressions cross the DPP parameter-affinity boundary even if their values are constants during one solve or happen to agree with an affine function at finitely many sampled parameter values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squares, reciprocals, exponentials, and products of independently varying parameters are nonaffine and lie outside the parameter-affine DPP class.
assumptions_latex: Each stated parameter domain has nonempty relative interior.
Parameter-affinity is required throughout the declared domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta^2,\exp(\theta),1/\theta\notin\mathcal A\text{ and }\theta_1\theta_2\notin\mathcal A\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: listed functions fail the defining affine identity on nondegenerate domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The examples are mathematically nonaffine on the stated nondegenerate domains and fit a failure-boundary leaf, but no official DPP source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Parameter Attribute-Domain Contracts
children.top_down_role: Sign, positivity, symmetry, and definiteness declarations for mutable data.

children.title: Parameter Sign Attributes
children.top_down_role: Sign-related declarations attached to mutable scalar or array data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementation-independent relations among zero, nonnegative, and nonpositive parameter domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For real arrays of fixed shape, the componentwise weak-sign domains satisfy \(\mathbb R_+^p\cap\mathbb R_-^p=\{0\}\). Hence a zero domain implies both nonnegative and nonpositive metadata, while simultaneous nonnegative and nonpositive requirements force every entry to zero. Neither weak sign requirement implies a strict sign requirement because the zero array belongs to both weak orthants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative and nonpositive domains intersect only at zero; weak sign metadata does not certify strict positivity or negativity.
assumptions_latex: Sign order is interpreted componentwise on real arrays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb R_+^p\cap\mathbb R_-^p=\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Sign Attribute Lattice
Parameter Sign Attributes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Declared sign domains used by disciplined curvature and monotonicity analysis of parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real scalar or array parameter \(\theta\), a nonnegative sign attribute imposes \(\theta\in\mathbb R_+^p\), a nonpositive attribute imposes \(\theta\in\mathbb R_-^p\), and a positive or negative attribute imposes the corresponding strict componentwise inequalities when the modeling system supports strict domains. An unsigned parameter has domain \(\mathbb R^p\). Every assigned numerical value must belong to the declared domain. Curvature and monotonicity rules may use the declared attribute, but they must not infer a stronger sign solely from a current numerical value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter sign attribute declares its admissible componentwise sign domain, and every assigned value must satisfy that declaration.
assumptions_latex: \(\theta\) is a declared real parameter with fixed dimension \(p\).
Sign constraints are interpreted componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{value}(\theta)\in\operatorname{dom}(\theta)\), with \(\operatorname{dom}(\theta)\) determined by its declared sign attribute.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sign attributes are domain contracts used by disciplined composition analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Nonnegative and nonpositive domain contracts are standard, but positive and negative attributes do not universally impose strict domains. Official modeling-system documentation is needed to fix the exact semantics.

children.title: Parameter Matrix Attributes
children.top_down_role: Symmetry or definiteness declarations attached to mutable matrix data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences and nonconsequences of positive-semidefinite parameter metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P\in\mathbb S^n\), \(P\succeq0\) is equivalent to \(x^{\mathsf T}Px\ge0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and implies \(P_{ii}\ge0\) for every \(i\). It does not imply entrywise nonnegativity: \(\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}\succeq0\). Thus positive-semidefinite metadata supplies Loewner-order information, not a componentwise nonnegative sign declaration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive semidefiniteness controls quadratic forms and diagonal entries but does not make every matrix entry nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: P\in\mathbb S^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\succeq0\implies P_{ii}\ge0\ \forall i,\qquad P\succeq0\not\implies P\ge0\text{ entrywise}.

notation.meaning: P is positive semidefinite in Loewner order.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Attributes and Entrywise Sign

assumptions_latex: The parameter is real-valued with a fixed declared shape \(m\times n\).
Matrix attributes are interpreted as constraints on every numerical parameter assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every admissible value lies in the intersection of the matrix domains declared for the parameter.

notation.meaning: Matrix parameter and its numerical value

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard matrix-attribute domain contract in disciplined parametrized modeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real matrix parameters with structural and semidefinite attributes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix parameter \(P\) of shape \(m\times n\) has an attribute domain \(\mathcal D(P)\subseteq\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). The symmetric, positive-semidefinite, and negative-semidefinite attributes require \(m=n\) and respectively impose \(X=X^{\mathsf T}\), \(X=X^{\mathsf T}\) with \(X\succeq0\), and \(X=X^{\mathsf T}\) with \(X\preceq0\). A diagonal attribute requires \(m=n\) and \(X_{ij}=0\) for \(i\ne j\). Declaring several compatible attributes replaces their domains by their intersection. A numerical assignment \(\widehat P\) is admissible exactly when \(\widehat P\in\mathcal D(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix attributes restrict every parameter value to the corresponding structural or cone domain; simultaneous compatible attributes impose the intersection of their domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Matrix Attributes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Parameter Matrix Attributes leaf and is internally coherent, but no cited source supports the exact set of available matrix attributes or the claim that several compatible attributes may always be combined by domain intersection. That behavior is implementation- and version-dependent, so an authoritative DPP/modeling-system locator is required.

children.title: Parameter Value Domains
children.top_down_role: Admissible value regions associated with declared parameter metadata.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain Contracts Are Not Modeled Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishing parameter assignment validity from optimization-variable feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be a parameter with declared domain \(\mathcal D_p\). An assignment \(\widehat p\notin\mathcal D_p\) violates the parameter contract before the instantiated optimization problem is analyzed. Adding a modeled constraint involving \(p\) cannot make that assignment admissible because \(p\) is supplied data, not an optimization variable. Admitting \(\widehat p\) requires changing the declaration or parameterization and revalidating the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invalid parameter value cannot be repaired by a model constraint; parameter-domain validation precedes optimization feasibility.
assumptions_latex: p is supplied data and is not an optimization variable.
\mathcal D_p is fixed by the parameter declaration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat p\notin\mathcal D_p\implies\widehat p\text{ is not an admissible model instance}.

notation.meaning: Declared numerical domain of parameter p.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Contracts Are Not Modeled Constraints

assumptions_latex: Each parameter has a fixed shape and a declared collection of scalar or matrix attributes.
Assignments are finite real arrays of that shape.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A parameter assignment is valid exactly when it belongs to its declared value domain.

notation.meaning: Declared value domain of the parameter

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard parameter-domain contract in disciplined modeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical domains induced by parameter declarations and attributes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameter \(p\) with declared shape, its value domain \(\mathcal D_p\) is the set of numerical arrays of that shape satisfying all declared attributes. Thus a nonnegative declaration imposes entrywise \(x_i\ge0\), a nonpositive declaration imposes entrywise \(x_i\le0\), and a positive declaration imposes entrywise \(x_i>0\). Structural matrix declarations additionally impose their associated symmetry, sparsity, or cone conditions. A supplied value \(\widehat p\) is a valid realization of \(p\) if and only if \(\widehat p\in\mathcal D_p\). The declaration is fixed while parameter values may vary within \(\mathcal D_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter may vary only over arrays of its declared shape satisfying every sign, positivity, structural, and cone attribute attached to it.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Value Domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Parameter Value Domains leaf, and its notation and quantifiers are adequate. However, no source establishes the stated declaration semantics, especially whether a positive attribute means strict entrywise positivity rather than nonnegativity or another implementation-specific domain convention.

children.title: Attribute-Domain Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency between assigned parameter values and declared metadata.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic implication and equivalence among dimensionally meaningful attribute domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let attributes \(a\) and \(b\) induce domains \(\mathcal D_a\) and \(\mathcal D_b\) in one fixed-shape ambient space. If \(\mathcal D_a\subseteq\mathcal D_b\), adding \(b\) to a declaration already containing \(a\) does not change its mathematical value domain. Two attribute collections are semantically equivalent exactly when their domain intersections coincide. These set-theoretic facts do not require a modeling frontend to accept every redundant combination syntactically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attribute is semantically redundant when its domain contains the domain already imposed; equal intersections define equivalent mathematical contracts, although frontend syntax may be stricter.
assumptions_latex: All compared attributes are dimensionally meaningful in the same fixed-shape ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal D_a\subseteq\mathcal D_b\implies\mathcal D_a\cap\mathcal D_b=\mathcal D_a.

notation.meaning: Domains induced by attributes a and b.

knowledge_statements.title: Attribute Implication and Redundancy

assumptions_latex: A parameter has a fixed shape and finitely many declared attributes.
Each attribute determines a subset of the ambient array space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The declaration is consistent if and only if \(\mathcal D_p\ne\varnothing\), and each assignment is accepted if and only if it lies in \(\mathcal D_p\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: consistency is nonemptiness of the intersection of declared attribute domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static consistency of parameter declarations and dynamic validity of assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A(p)\) be the attributes declared for parameter \(p\), and let each \(a\in A(p)\) induce a domain \(\mathcal D_a\) in the fixed-shape ambient space. Define \(\mathcal D_p=\bigcap_{a\in A(p)}\mathcal D_a\). The declaration is attribute-domain consistent exactly when \(\mathcal D_p\ne\varnothing\) and every attribute is dimensionally meaningful; for example, symmetry or semidefiniteness requires a square matrix. A numerical assignment \(\widehat p\) is consistent with the declaration exactly when \(\widehat p\in\mathcal D_p\). Consequently, incompatible declarations or an out-of-domain assignment violate the parameter contract independently of the model's curvature analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declared attributes are consistent when their dimensionally valid domains have nonempty intersection; an assigned value is consistent precisely when it belongs to that intersection.
knowledge_statements.title: Attribute-Domain Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is appropriate for Attribute-Domain Consistency and is mathematically coherent as an abstract intersection-domain contract. A source is still required because actual DPP systems may reject attribute combinations syntactically even when the corresponding mathematical intersection is nonempty, so nonemptiness alone may not characterize accepted declarations.

children.title: Parameter-Interaction Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Grammatical boundaries on products and nonlinear transformations involving parameters.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Affinity Does Not Imply DPP Compliance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of fixed-instance curvature checking to certify the DCP-based DPP interaction grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R\) be a decision variable and \(\theta_1,\theta_2\in\mathbb R\) declared parameters. For every fixed \((\theta_1,\theta_2)\), \(e(x;\theta_1,\theta_2)=\theta_1\theta_2x\) is affine in \(x\). Its displayed expression tree is nevertheless not DPP-compliant: the subexpression \(\theta_1\theta_2\) multiplies two parameter-affine factors, neither of which is parameter-free.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Theta1 times theta2 times x is affine for every fixed parameter pair but violates the DPP product grammar by multiplying two parameter-dependent factors.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is an optimization variable.
\(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) are separately declared parameters.
The displayed expression graph is analyzed without replacing \(\theta_1\theta_2\) by a new parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall(\theta_1,\theta_2),\ e(\cdot;\theta_1,\theta_2)\text{ is affine},\qquad e\text{ is not DPP-compliant}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Affinity Does Not Imply DPP Compliance

assumptions_latex: Expressions are analyzed under the DCP-based disciplined parametrized programming grammar.
A parameter-affine expression contains parameters affinely and no variables; a parameter-free expression contains no parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A product is DPP-admissible only in the stated cases, and other parameter-dependent nonlinear interactions require an equivalent admissible reformulation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard DCP-based DPP product and composition restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DCP-based restrictions on products and nonlinear parameter interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the DCP-based DPP grammar, a product \(uv\) is admissible when it is already admissible under ordinary DCP, or when one factor is parameter-affine and the other is parameter-free. Hence a product of two parameter-dependent factors is excluded, as is a parameter-dependent factor multiplied by an expression that depends jointly on variables and parameters. More generally, each nonlinear atom \(f(u_1,\ldots,u_k)\) must satisfy its DCP curvature and monotonicity composition rule while also obeying the atom's DPP parameter restrictions. Parameter-dependent nonlinear interactions outside these rules are not DPP-compliant even when every fixed parameter realization defines a convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DPP permits only grammatically controlled parameter interactions; notably, its special product rule pairs a parameter-affine factor with a parameter-free factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Interaction Restrictions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local topic fit, but the exact DCP-based DPP product rule must be checked against an authoritative DPP definition. The sentence excluding every product of two parameter-dependent factors may be broader than the formal rule because parameter-free status and parameter-affine classification require precise recursive definitions and implementation conventions.

children.title: DPP Variants
children.top_down_role: Parameter disciplines associated with convex and log-log convex source grammars.

children.title: DCP-Based DPP
children.top_down_role: Parameter restrictions layered over ordinary DCP models.

assumptions_latex: The model is DCP-compliant when parameters are treated as constants.
Parameter signs and domains are fixed declarations rather than inferred from current values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is DCP-based DPP exactly when every expression satisfies both ordinary DCP and the additional parameter grammar.

notation.meaning: Source model with variable x and parameter vector theta

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of DCP-based disciplined parametrized programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DPP obtained by adding parameter grammar to ordinary DCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parametrized model \(M(x;\theta)\), with \(\theta\in\Theta\), is DCP-based disciplined parametrized programming compliant when every objective and constraint expression is accepted by the ordinary DCP composition rules after parameters are treated as constants, and every parameter occurrence additionally satisfies the DPP parameter grammar. In particular, parameters are classified as parameter-affine, their declared signs determine valid monotonicity reasoning, and products or other atoms involving parameters must satisfy the DPP-specific interaction restrictions. Compliance is a syntactic property of the expression graph and declared domains, uniform over \(\theta\in\Theta\), rather than a conclusion obtained by separately checking convexity at sampled parameter values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DCP-based DPP consists of ordinary DCP models whose complete expression graphs also satisfy fixed, uniform restrictions on how declared parameters may occur.
knowledge_statements.title: DCP-Based DPP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is the correct role for DCP-Based DPP, and the statement captures the intended syntactic and uniform character. Acceptance requires an authoritative locator defining parameter-affine expressions, treatment of parameters as affine expressions, and the additional DPP composition rules.

children.title: DGP-Based DPP
children.top_down_role: Positive-parameter restrictions layered over disciplined geometric models.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: DGP-based DPP condition for a power atom whose exponent may be a declared parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a DGP power atom \(u^p\), DPP requires \(p\) to be either a numerical constant or a single declared parameter, not a composite parameter expression. If \(p\) is a parameter, the base \(u\) must be parameter-free. Equivalently, the base and exponent may not both depend on parameters. These restrictions are additional to the ordinary DGP domain and log-log-curvature rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DGP power may use a parameter exponent only with a parameter-free base, and the exponent must be a constant or one declared parameter rather than a parameter expression.
assumptions_latex: The power atom is analyzed under the DGP-based DPP grammar.
All quantities requiring logarithmic coordinates satisfy their declared positive domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\text{ parameter-dependent}\implies p\text{ is a declared parameter and }\operatorname{Params}(u)=\varnothing.

notation.meaning: base expression of the power atom

knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized-Power Restriction

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DGP Validity Does Not Imply DGP-DPP Compliance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of fixed-instance DGP checking for a power with parameter-dependent base and exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta>0\) and \(p\) be declared parameters. For each fixed admissible pair, \(\theta^p\) is a positive numerical constant and hence is admissible in a fixed DGP instance. The displayed power atom is not DGP-based DPP compliant because both its base and exponent are parameter-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter raised to a parameter power is a valid positive constant after substitution but violates DGP-DPP because both base and exponent depend on parameters.
assumptions_latex: \(\theta\) is a declared positive parameter.
\(p\) is a declared parameter admissible as an exponent.
The displayed power atom is retained in the expression graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta^p\text{ is fixed-instance DGP-admissible but not DGP-based DPP compliant}.\)

notation.meaning: positive parameter used as the base

knowledge_statements.title: DGP Validity Does Not Imply DGP-DPP Compliance

assumptions_latex: All variables and parameters used by the geometric model are positive on their declared domains.
The model is DGP-compliant under the logarithmic change of variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is DGP-based DPP exactly when its log-transformed expression graph satisfies the corresponding parameter-affine discipline uniformly over positive parameter values.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: DGP-based DPP is DPP applied through the logarithmic DGP representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive DPP models interpreted through disciplined geometric programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive parametrized geometric model in variables \(x\) and parameters \(\theta\) is DGP-based disciplined parametrized programming compliant when it is accepted by the DGP grammar and, after the coordinate change \(u=\log x\) and \(\eta=\log\theta\), its transformed convex expression graph satisfies the applicable DPP parameter restrictions. Products and positive powers are interpreted through their log-log curvature rules. Any atom whose logarithmic representation would create a forbidden nonlinear interaction between parameter-dependent arguments is excluded. Compliance is uniform over the declared positive domain of \(\theta\), and is not established merely because each fixed realization happens to be a valid geometric program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DGP-based DPP applies disciplined parameter restrictions to positive geometric models through their logarithmic convex representation, uniformly over declared positive parameter values.
knowledge_statements.title: DGP-Based DPP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the DGP-Based DPP topic, but its characterization through the log-transformed graph may omit or blur the formal DGP-specific rules for parametrized powers and parameter exponents. An authoritative DPP/DGP locator is needed to determine the exact mathematical statement.

children.title: Affine-Solver-Affine Representation
children.top_down_role: The central compiled representation family for DPP models.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Affine-solver-affine form

children.title: Parameter-to-Canonical-Data Map
children.top_down_role: Compiled dependence of solver data on source parameters.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Evaluation of the Compiled Data Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic and storage cost of evaluating an already compiled affine parameter-to-data operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the compiled map is \(d(\theta)=R[\theta^{\mathsf T},1]^{\mathsf T}\) and \(R\) is stored sparsely, one canonical-data update is a sparse matrix-vector product requiring \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(R))\) arithmetic operations and \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(R))\) operator storage. This bound excludes symbolic canonicalization and solver execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An already compiled sparse affine data map can be evaluated in time and storage linear in the number of stored operator entries.
assumptions_latex: A fixed affine compilation operator \(R\) is available.
\(R\) is evaluated using a standard sparse matrix-vector product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{update}}=O(\operatorname{nnz}(R)),\qquad M_{\mathrm{operator}}=O(\operatorname{nnz}(R)).

notation.meaning: Number of stored nonzero entries in the compilation operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Evaluation of the Compiled Data Map

assumptions_latex: A fixed DPP-compliant source problem has been canonicalized to a fixed cone-program structure.
All source parameters are stacked into a vector with an appended constant coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical solver data depend affinely on the source parameters through a fixed sparse linear operator.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: affine parameter-to-data map is the first affine stage of the ASA representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine compilation from source parameters to fixed-format solver data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a canonical cone-program form and a DPP-compliant source expression graph. Stack all numerical parameter entries into \(\theta\in\mathbb R^p\), and stack the canonical objective, constraint, and offset data into \(d(\theta)\in\mathbb R^q\). Then compilation admits a fixed matrix \(R\in\mathbb R^{q\times(p+1)}\) such that \[d(\theta)=R\begin{bmatrix}\theta\\1\end{bmatrix}.\] The sparsity pattern, dimensions, and row interpretation of \(R\) are fixed by the source graph and canonical form. Changing \(\theta\) therefore updates canonical numerical data without repeating symbolic canonicalization, provided the new value remains in the declared parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After one symbolic compilation, fixed sparse linear data map source parameters, plus a constant coordinate, to the numerical data expected by the solver.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-to-Canonical-Data Map

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is well matched to the Parameter-to-Canonical-Data Map leaf, and the affine formula is properly delimited. The central affine-map claim is nontrivial and needs a specific ASA/DPP theorem or section establishing it for the stated fixed canonical form and data vectorization.

children.title: Canonical Solver Interface
children.top_down_role: The solver-facing component of the compiled representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary compatibility conditions for dispatching compiled data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let canonical data \(d\) specify a problem over \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\). Dispatch is valid only if the solver or an exact bridge supports every \(K_i\), dimensions match the canonical schema, numerical and sparsity encodings are accepted, and primal-dual sign and coordinate conventions agree with the result decoder. Otherwise dispatch must be rejected or preceded by an exact supported bridge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical data may be dispatched only when cone capabilities, dimensions, encodings, and result conventions match, possibly through an exact bridge.
assumptions_latex: The compiled problem has a declared canonical schema.
Solver capabilities and conventions are known to the dispatcher.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dispatch}(d)\text{ is valid}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{requirements}(d)\subseteq\operatorname{supported\ capabilities}.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Solver Compatibility Contract

assumptions_latex: Canonicalization fixes a conic problem structure and cone \(K\).
The numerical data supplied to the solver have the required dimensions and cone-compatible layout.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solver interface maps canonical data to a canonical primal-dual solution or to an explicit termination status.

notation.meaning: Canonical objective, constraint matrix, and right-hand side
Canonical primal, equality dual, and cone slack variables
Closed convex cone and its dual

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: abstract primal-dual conic solver interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract conic solver boundary used by the compiled representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For canonical data \((c,A,b)\), the solver-facing problem is \[\underset{z}{\operatorname{minimize}}\;c^{\mathsf T}z\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad Az+s=b,\quad s\in K.\] On successful termination, the canonical solver interface returns primal-dual data \((z,y,s)\) satisfying the solver's accuracy tolerances, with dual feasibility \(A^{\mathsf T}y+c=0\) and \(y\in K^*\), together with objective and status information. If no qualifying solution is produced, it returns an explicit status such as infeasible, unbounded, inaccurate, or failed. The interface consumes only canonical numerical data and does not inspect source-level expressions or parameter semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical solver receives fixed-format cone-program data and returns a canonical primal-dual result, accuracy information, and an explicit termination status.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Solver Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A representation is appropriate for the Canonical Solver Interface. The primal form and displayed feasibility equations are coherent under one dual-sign convention, but the dual cone, multiplier sign, returned coordinates, accuracy guarantees, and status taxonomy vary across canonical forms and solvers; a specific source is required.

children.title: Canonical-to-Source Solution Map
children.top_down_role: Compiled recovery of source-model variables and outputs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for recovery to be independent of equivalent canonical representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let admissible canonical solutions form \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^r\), with \(w_1\sim w_2\) exactly when \(w_1-w_2\in N\), where \(N\) is a linear subspace. An affine rule \(R(w)=Sw+t\) is constant on equivalence classes in \(W\) if and only if \[N\cap(W-W)\subseteq\ker S.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine recovery is well defined on canonical equivalence classes exactly when its linear part annihilates every admissible ambiguity.
assumptions_latex: Canonical ambiguity is represented by a linear subspace \(N\).
Recovery is affine on the selected coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\text{ descends to }W/{\sim}\iff N\cap(W-W)\subseteq\ker S.

notation.meaning: Linear part and offset of recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Well-Defined Affine Recovery Criterion

assumptions_latex: Canonicalization introduced auxiliary variables but retained a fixed correspondence with source variables.
A canonical solution compatible with the compiled problem has been returned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Source outputs are recovered by a fixed affine map from canonical solution coordinates.

notation.meaning: Stacked source-variable values and requested outputs

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: affine recovery is the second affine stage of the ASA representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine recovery of source-level quantities from canonical solver coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w\in\mathbb R^r\) stack the canonical primal-dual coordinates required to recover source-model variables and requested outputs. For a fixed compiled expression graph, there are fixed \(S\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) and \(t\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \[x_{\mathrm{src}}=Sw+t.\] The map discards purely auxiliary coordinates, reverses fixed vectorizations, and evaluates only affine recovery relations recorded during canonicalization. It is applied only when the solver result contains the coordinates required by the requested source outputs. Thus repeated solves with different admissible parameter values reuse the same recovery operator, while solver statuses lacking a solution are propagated without fabricating source-variable values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed affine recovery operator selects and reshapes canonical solution coordinates to reconstruct source variables and requested outputs after each successful solve.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical-to-Source Solution Map

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record has the correct representation role and matches the solution-recovery leaf. The claim that all source variables and requested outputs are recovered by one fixed affine map is nontrivial and may depend on what counts as an output and on the canonicalizer, so it requires an authoritative ASA locator.

children.title: Directional-Adjoint Interface Pair
children.top_down_role: Interfaces used by neighboring sensitivity and differentiation topics.

children.title: Directional Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Forward sensitivity interfaces exposed around reusable canonicalization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between directional evaluation and a Jacobian-vector product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a selected map \(F\) is one-sided directionally differentiable at \(\theta\), then \(F'(\theta;\alpha h)=\alpha F'(\theta;h)\) for \(\alpha\ge0\), but additivity in \(h\) need not hold. A single Jacobian-vector interface \(F'(\theta;h)=Jh\) for every \(h\) exists only when the directional derivative is linear in direction; Fréchet differentiability is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional derivatives are positively homogeneous but need not form one linear Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: A single-valued local selection \(F\) is fixed.
The one-sided directional derivative exists in the directions considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'(\theta;\alpha h)=\alpha F'(\theta;h)\ (\alpha\ge0),\quad F'(\theta;\cdot)=J(\cdot)\iff F'(\theta;\cdot)\text{ is linear}.

notation.meaning: Single linear Jacobian operator, when it exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Linearity Boundary

assumptions_latex: The canonical solution map is directionally differentiable at the current canonical data.
The parameter-to-data and solution-recovery maps are affine and fixed locally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The directional interface computes the Jacobian-vector product \(D(R\circ S\circ C)(\theta)[\dot\theta]\) by forward composition through the three stages.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: forward directional interface is the chain-rule Jacobian-vector product through ASA stages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-mode differentiation through compilation, solve, and recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the source solution map be \(F=R\circ S\circ C\), where \(C\) maps parameters to canonical data, \(S\) maps canonical data to a selected canonical solution, and \(R\) recovers source outputs. Given a base parameter \(\theta\) and direction \(\dot\theta\), compute \(d=C(\theta)\), \(\dot d=DC(\theta)[\dot\theta]\), a selected solution \(w=S(d)\), and \(\dot w=DS(d)[\dot d]\). Return \[\dot x=DR(w)[\dot w]=DF(\theta)[\dot\theta].\] Because \(C\) and \(R\) are affine, their directional derivatives are their fixed linear parts; only the solver stage requires local sensitivity analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional interface pushes a parameter perturbation forward through affine compilation, the differentiated solver, and affine recovery to obtain a source-solution perturbation.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind for the forward directional interface, and the chain-rule construction is internally consistent. The existence and computation of the selected solver derivative require precise regularity, uniqueness or selection, and cone-program sensitivity hypotheses that are not sourced here.

children.title: Adjoint Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Reverse sensitivity interfaces exposed around reusable canonicalization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bilinear identity validating a reverse operator against a forward linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L:X\to Y\) be linear and \(A:Y\to X\) be a candidate adjoint under declared inner products. Then \(A=L^*\) if and only if \[\langle Lu,v\rangle_Y=\langle u,Av\rangle_X\quad\text{for all }u\in X,\ v\in Y.\] Testing spanning sets is sufficient. Random nonspanning tests are diagnostics, not exact certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse operator is the adjoint exactly when it satisfies the defining inner-product identity.
assumptions_latex: The spaces and inner products are fixed.
The forward operator \(L\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A=L^*\iff\forall u,v,\ \langle Lu,v\rangle_Y=\langle u,Av\rangle_X.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Consistency Test

assumptions_latex: The selected canonical solution map is differentiable, or has a specified linearization, at the current data.
The spaces carry Euclidean inner products compatible with the chosen vectorizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adjoint interface returns \(DF(\theta)^*\bar x\), the vector-Jacobian product with respect to source parameters.

notation.meaning: Cotangent at the recovered source output

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reverse-mode adjoint is the transposed chain rule through ASA stages
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse-mode differentiation through recovery, solve, and compilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=R\circ S\circ C\) be the locally linearized source solution map. Given an output cotangent \(\bar x\), initialize \(\bar w=DR(w)^*\bar x\), propagate through the solver as \(\bar d=DS(d)^*\bar w\), and return \[\bar\theta=DC(\theta)^*\bar d=DF(\theta)^*\bar x.\] Here \(^*\) denotes the adjoint with respect to the declared inner products. For affine \(C\) and \(R\), the two outer adjoints are multiplication by fixed transposed linear operators. The solver adjoint must correspond to the same local solution selection and vectorization conventions used by the forward directional interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adjoint interface propagates an output cotangent backward through recovery, solver sensitivity, and compilation to produce a parameter vector-Jacobian product.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct role for the adjoint interface, and the reverse chain is consistent with the forward notation. A source must specify when the solver linearization exists, how a solution selection is fixed, and under which inner products and vectorizations the stated adjoints are valid.

children.title: Canonical-Data Interface Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary connecting parameter data, canonical data, and neighboring sensitivity systems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate and pairing contract across canonical data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let canonical data lie in an inner-product space \(D\), and let \(L:\Theta\to D\) be the compilation linearization. A forward boundary sends \(\dot d=L\dot\theta\); a reverse boundary sends \(\bar d\in D\) back as \(L^*\bar d\). The two are compatible exactly when they use the same coordinate layout and pairings, so \[\langle L\dot\theta,\bar d\rangle_D=\langle\dot\theta,L^*\bar d\rangle_\Theta\] for all \(\dot\theta,\bar d\). Any scaling, vectorization, or metric change requires the corresponding transformation on the other side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward tangents and reverse cotangents share a boundary only when their layouts and pairings satisfy the adjoint identity.
assumptions_latex: Canonical-data and parameter coordinates have declared inner products.
Both interfaces use the same compiled data layout.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{compatibility}\iff\forall\dot\theta,\bar d,\ \langle L\dot\theta,\bar d\rangle_D=\langle\dot\theta,L^*\bar d\rangle_\Theta.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-Cotangent Boundary Compatibility

assumptions_latex: The source model has a fixed DPP compilation and fixed canonical data layout.
Differentiation is performed at a parameter value for which a canonical solution selection is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compilation interface exposes perturbations only as canonical-data tangents and returns sensitivities only as canonical-data cotangents.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical numerical data form the abstraction boundary between modeling and solver differentiation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between source-level compilation and solver-level sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=C(\theta)\) be the canonical data produced from source parameters. The canonical-data boundary requires the modeling layer to pass the solver only \(d\) and, for forward differentiation, \(\dot d=DC(\theta)[\dot\theta]\). The solver layer returns a canonical solution and, when requested, its directional response or the canonical-data cotangent \(\bar d\). Reverse propagation to parameters is then performed by \(\bar\theta=DC(\theta)^*\bar d\). Source expression nodes, parameter attributes, and canonicalization rules remain outside the solver interface; cone layout, scaling conventions, and canonical solution coordinates remain inside it. Both sides must use the same fixed vectorization and inner-product conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical numerical data and their tangents or cotangents form the strict boundary between source-model compilation and solver sensitivity calculations.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical-Data Interface Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the Canonical-Data Interface Boundary leaf and cleanly separates modeling-layer and solver-layer quantities. The asserted strict boundary and ownership of scaling, cone layout, and solution coordinates are architectural conventions rather than universal mathematical facts, so they require a source for the intended ASA implementation or specification.

children.title: Nondifferentiable Interface Regimes
children.top_down_role: Solution-map regimes limiting directional or adjoint information.

knowledge_statements.title: Nondifferentiable Interface Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for derivative and adjoint interfaces of compiled parameter-to-data maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the compiled canonical-data map be \(D:\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^m\). At \(\theta\in\Theta\), a classical directional-adjoint pair requires a linear derivative \(J=D'(\theta)\) satisfying \(D(\theta+h)=D(\theta)+Jh+o(\lVert h\rVert)\). If only directional derivatives \(D'(\theta;h)\) exist and their dependence on \(h\) is nonlinear, no single matrix \(J\) represents all directions; consequently, no unique adjoint map \(v\mapsto J^{\mathsf T}v\) is defined. Any returned branch derivative or generalized Jacobian element must therefore be labeled as a selection rather than the derivative of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a kink, direction-dependent linearizations need not form one Jacobian, so a unique adjoint interface is unavailable without an explicit derivative selection.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is defined on a neighborhood of \(\theta\).
The interface requests a classical linear derivative and its transpose.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonlinear dependence of \(D'(\theta;h)\) on \(h\) precludes a unique directional-adjoint pair at \(\theta\).

notation.meaning: Candidate classical Jacobian of the data map.

source_refs.locator: 3 Nonsmooth Convex Optimization p. 139

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Nonsmooth Convex Optimization p. 139

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection semantics for a locally Lipschitz compiled data map at a nondifferentiable point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\theta\), and let \(\Omega_D\) be its differentiability set. Its Clarke generalized Jacobian is \[\partial_C D(\theta)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\lim_{k\to\infty}D'(\theta_k):\theta_k\to\theta,\ \theta_k\in\Omega_D\right\},\] with only existing limits included. Choosing \(J\in\partial_C D(\theta)\) defines the selected linear maps \(h\mapsto Jh\) and \(v\mapsto J^{\mathsf T}v\), but neither is the intrinsic classical derivative or adjoint of \(D\) unless classical differentiability with derivative \(J\) is separately established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Clarke generalized Jacobian supplies possible linearization selections, not an intrinsic derivative-adjoint pair at a kink.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\theta\).
The interface explicitly permits a generalized-derivative selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\in\partial_C D(\theta)\Longrightarrow (Jh,J^{\mathsf T}v)\text{ is selection-dependent unless }D'(\theta)=J\text{ classically}.

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of the compiled data map.
Set where the data map is classically differentiable.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Jacobian Interface Selection

children.title: Repeated-Solve Compilation
children.top_down_role: Reuse mechanisms for parameterized families with fixed symbolic structure.

children.title: Compiled Data-Map Reuse
children.top_down_role: Reuse of parameter-to-canonical-data transformations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic cost of applying a stored affine parameter-to-canonical-data map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(M\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}\) in \(d(\theta)=d_0+M\theta\), standard sparse matrix-vector evaluation forms one data vector in \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(M)+q)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(q)\) output storage. Dense evaluation costs \(O(qp)\) arithmetic operations. These bounds exclude compilation, solver setup, and optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying a compiled sparse affine data map takes work linear in its stored nonzeros plus output size; compilation and solving are excluded.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) and \(d_0\) are already compiled and stored.
Standard sparse or dense matrix-vector arithmetic is used.
\(q\) is the stacked canonical-data length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{eval}}=O(\operatorname{nnz}(M)+q)\text{ sparsely},\qquad T_{\mathrm{eval}}=O(qp)\text{ densely}.

notation.meaning: number of stored nonzeros in the compiled map

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Data-Map Evaluation Cost
Compiled Data-Map Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine parameter-to-data representation used in repeated solves of a fixed DPP problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed compiled problem with parameter vector \(\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), suppose the stacked numerical canonical data satisfy \[d(\theta)=d_0+M\theta.\] The compiler may store \(d_0\) and \(M\) once. For every new admissible parameter value \(\theta_k\), canonical data are obtained by the matrix-vector evaluation \(d_k=d_0+M\theta_k\), without re-traversing the expression graph or reconstructing the parameter-to-data transformation. This reuse applies only while the compiled parameter ordering, canonical-data ordering, and structural template remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compiled affine map converts each new parameter vector directly into canonical numerical data while the ordering and structural template remain fixed.
assumptions_latex: \(d(\theta)\) is affine in the declared parameters.
Parameter and canonical-data orderings are fixed across solves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The same stored pair \((d_0,M)\) generates \(d(\theta_k)\) for every admissible repeated-solve instance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine compiled-data representation fits the container and is mathematically coherent, but no inspectable DPP compilation source is supplied.

children.title: Canonical Structure Reuse
children.top_down_role: Reuse of dimensions, sparsity patterns, cone layouts, and inverse mappings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of fixed-template reuse across parameter instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a compiled canonical template. If a parameter change alters a canonical variable or constraint dimension, index ordering, required cone family or block dimension, or a support pattern represented by \(T\), numerical substitution into \(T\) is not an exact canonicalization of the new instance. A compatible template must be constructed unless \(T\) already contains a fixed superstructure whose inactive entries and blocks preserve projected feasibility and objective values exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A change to unreserved dimensions, indexing, cone layout, or structural support crosses the reuse boundary and requires recompilation.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) has fixed dimensions, indexing, cone layout, and represented support.
Canonicalization must preserve projected feasibility and objective values exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{unrepresented structural mutation}\implies\text{numerical substitution into }T\text{ is insufficient}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Structural Mutation Requires Recompilation
Canonical Structure Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural invariance of a compiled cone-program template across parameter values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the parameterized cone program \[\min_x\ c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad A(\theta)x+b(\theta)\in K.\] If parameter substitution changes only stored numerical entries, while the dimensions of \(x\), the row and column index sets, the permitted sparsity patterns of \(A(\theta)\), and the ordered product-cone decomposition of \(K\) remain fixed, then one canonical template can be reused for all admissible \(\theta\). The associated map that recovers modeled variables from canonical variables is reusable when its indexing and reconstruction rules are likewise parameter-independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical template is reusable when dimensions, index sets, sparsity patterns, cone layout, and inverse reconstruction rules do not change with parameters.
assumptions_latex: Only numerical canonical entries vary with \(\theta\).
Canonical indexing and cone ordering are parameter-independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One canonical structure and inverse reconstruction map serve every admissible parameter instance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly describes fixed-template reuse, but its compiler and inverse-map claims require an authoritative DPP source with a specific locator.

children.title: Solver-State Reuse Interface
children.top_down_role: Transfer of compatible numerical state across parameter instances.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Warm Starts Preserve the Canonical Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary separating initialization state from mathematical problem data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed canonical data \(d_k\), importing prior state \(s_{k-1}\) is a warm start only when it changes initialization but not the objective, constraints, cones, or termination predicates defining the solve. The exact feasible and optimizer sets are then independent of whether the state is imported. The imported state is not a feasibility or optimality certificate unless its components separately satisfy the applicable residual and cone-membership tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A genuine warm start changes initialization rather than the optimization problem, and imported state is not automatically a solution certificate.
assumptions_latex: The canonical problem data and mathematical termination predicates are fixed.
The warm-start interface does not reinterpret state fields as problem data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Feas}(d_k,s_{k-1})=\operatorname{Feas}(d_k),\qquad\operatorname{Opt}(d_k,s_{k-1})=\operatorname{Opt}(d_k).
review_flags: Concrete state fields and scaling conventions remain solver-specific.
knowledge_statements.title: Warm Starts Preserve the Canonical Problem
Solver-State Reuse Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Warm-start transfer between compatible instances of one compiled canonical problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a fixed canonical template, new data \(d_k\), and an optional prior solver state \(s_{k-1}\). Verify that \(s_{k-1}\) matches the current variable dimensions, constraint dimensions, cone ordering, scaling convention, and solver-specific state schema. If compatible, initialize the numerical solver with \(s_{k-1}\); otherwise use its default initialization. Run the solver on \(d_k\) until its prescribed termination test holds, return the primal-dual result, and export a new state \(s_k\) only through the solver's declared warm-start interface. Compatibility permits reuse but does not by itself guarantee fewer iterations or convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transfer prior numerical state only after validating structural and solver-specific compatibility; otherwise initialize normally, and make no unconditional speedup claim.
assumptions_latex: The canonical structural template is unchanged.
The solver exposes explicit state import and export operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a solve result and a compatible exported state \(s_k\), without asserting a universal performance improvement.

notation.meaning: Canonical numerical data for solve k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the interface container, but compatibility checks and exported solver state are solver-specific and unsupported by a cited warm-start specification.

children.title: DPP Applicability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Parameter dependencies that prevent reusable affine compilation or stable solution-map interfaces.

children.title: Nonaffine Parameter Interactions
children.top_down_role: Parameter products, inverses, and transformations outside the DPP grammar.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonaffine Parameter Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DPP boundary caused by nonlinear dependence of canonical data on declared parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta\) denote declared parameters and let \(d(\theta)\) denote stacked canonical numerical data. A compiled affine data interface requires \(d(\theta)=d_0+M\theta\). Expressions producing products of independently varying parameters, reciprocals such as \(1/\theta_i\), or nonlinear transformations such as \(\exp(\theta_i)\) generally violate this requirement because their parameter dependence is not affine on any open domain. Such an expression may define a convex problem after \(\theta\) is fixed, yet it lies outside the affine parameter grammar required for direct DPP data-map compilation unless the nonlinear quantity is supplied as a separate precomputed parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter products, reciprocals, and nonlinear transforms generally defeat affine compiled data maps, even when each fixed-parameter problem remains convex.
assumptions_latex: The relevant parameters vary independently on a domain with nonempty interior.
Compilation requires an affine map from declared parameters to canonical data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A genuinely nonaffine parameter interaction is outside this DPP compilation interface unless it is externalized as parameter data.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is plausible and locally appropriate, but the asserted DPP affine-data grammar and treatment of nonlinear parameter expressions require an authoritative source.

children.title: Parameter-Dependent Preprocessing
children.top_down_role: Canonicalization requiring nonlinear factorization or transformation of parameter data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness conditions when nonlinear preprocessing output is promoted to explicit model input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q=T(\theta)\) be computed outside the compiled model and suppose the downstream canonical-data map is \(d(q)=d_0+Mq\). Treating \(q\) as the declared parameter reproduces the intended instance at \(\theta\) only when the supplied value satisfies \(q=T(\theta)\), has the declared shape, and lies in every atom and canonical-form domain assumed during compilation. Under those conditions, \[d_{\mathrm{intended}}(\theta)=d(T(\theta))=d_0+MT(\theta).\] The compiled downstream interface does not itself certify the equality \(q=T(\theta)\) or the validity of the preprocessing operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Externalizing a nonlinear transform restores affine downstream compilation only under consistency, shape, and domain checks that the compiled model does not perform automatically.
assumptions_latex: The symbolic model is compiled with \(q\) as an independent declared parameter.
The downstream canonical data depend affinely on \(q\).
The intended source semantics require \(q=T(\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q=T(\theta)\ \text{and domain compatibility}\Longrightarrow d_{\mathrm{intended}}(\theta)=d_0+MT(\theta).

notation.meaning: Preprocessed input supplied to the compiled model.

knowledge_statements.title: Externalized Preprocessing Contract
Parameter-Dependent Preprocessing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary where canonicalization must recompute a nonlinear transformation of parameter data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose canonicalization needs a derived coefficient \(q=T(\theta)\), where \(T\) is nonlinear, for example a matrix factor satisfying \(L(\theta)L(\theta)^{\mathsf T}=P(\theta)\). If each new \(\theta\) requires recomputing \(T(\theta)\) before canonical data can be assembled, then the original declared-parameter interface is not a reusable affine data map. Reuse can be restored only by treating \(q\) as externally computed input, with its domain conditions validated, or by providing a separate compiled representation of \(T\). The cost and differentiability of that preprocessing are not covered by the canonical solver interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear parameter preprocessing, such as refactorizing a matrix, lies outside direct affine data-map reuse unless its result becomes explicit input.
assumptions_latex: The canonical coefficient depends on a nonlinear transformation \(T\).
The transformation must be reevaluated when \(\theta\) changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Direct reuse of the original affine parameter-to-data map does not include the preprocessing step \(T\).

children.title: Parameter-Dependent Structural Changes
children.top_down_role: Changes in dimensions, domains, sparsity patterns, or reduction structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding bounded structural alternatives in one parameter-independent canonical envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every instance embeds in fixed variable and constraint dimensions and a fixed ordered cone product. If activation changes only canonical numerical coefficients, while inactive coordinates are fixed and inactive constraints become tautologies without changing index sets, cone types, or cone sizes, then all instances have one structural signature \(S(\theta)=S_0\). This construction does not cover parameter-dependent shapes, index sets, cone types, or unbounded structural variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded structural alternatives can share one template when embedded in fixed dimensions and controlled numerically without changing canonical index or cone structure.
assumptions_latex: A finite parameter-independent envelope exists for every variable, constraint, and cone-block dimension.
Activation changes numerical canonical data only and preserves every index set, cone type, and cone size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(\theta)=S_0\quad\text{for all admissible }\theta.

notation.meaning: Canonical structural signature at parameter value theta.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Envelope Structural Reformulation
Parameter-Dependent Structural Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of one-template reuse when parameter values alter canonical combinatorial structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(\theta)\) collect the canonical variable dimension, constraint dimension, sparsity index sets, ordered cone-block types and sizes, and inverse-reduction indexing. A single compiled canonical structure is reusable on a parameter domain \(\Theta\) only if \(S(\theta)=S_0\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta\). If a parameter value activates a different dimension, domain, sparsity pattern, cone layout, or reduction branch, then the existing template does not represent that instance. The model must instead be reformulated with fixed structure, partitioned into structurally constant regimes, or recompiled when the regime changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One compiled template cannot cover parameter values that change dimensions, sparsity, cone blocks, domains, or reduction branches.
assumptions_latex: A compiled template fixes all canonical index sets and cone blocks.
At least one component of \(S(\theta)\) changes across the parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No single fixed canonical structure represents every instance in \(\Theta\).

notation.meaning: Complete structural signature of the canonical instance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary statement fits the structural-change container, but the asserted compilation boundary lacks a DPP structural-reuse source.

children.title: Nonsmooth Set-Valued Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity boundaries caused by degeneracy or nonunique solutions.

children.title: Set-Valued Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Parameter regimes with multiple admissible source solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Solution Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimizer correspondence for a parameterized optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(\Theta\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(F:\Theta\rightrightarrows X\) be the feasible-set correspondence, and let \(f:X\times\Theta\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). The solution map is the correspondence \[S(\theta)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F(\theta)} f(x,\theta)=\{x\in F(\theta):f(x,\theta)=v(\theta)\},\] where \(v(\theta)=\inf_{y\in F(\theta)}f(y,\theta)\). It is set-valued at \(\theta\) when \(S(\theta)\) contains more than one optimizer, and it is empty when the infimum is not attained or the problem is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solution map assigns each parameter all attaining optimizers; it may contain multiple points or be empty.
assumptions_latex: The extended-real objective and feasible-set correspondence are defined for every \(\theta\in\Theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S:\Theta\rightrightarrows X\) is the optimizer correspondence determined by \(f\) and \(F\).

notation.meaning: Set of optimizers at parameter value theta.
Feasible set at parameter value theta.

source_refs.locator: 3 Nonsmooth Convex Optimization p. 139

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Nonsmooth Convex Optimization p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Structure of Convex Optimizer Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity, closedness, and uniqueness of the optimizer set at a fixed parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\theta\). If \(F(\theta)\) is convex and \(f(\cdot,\theta)\) is convex on \(F(\theta)\), then every nonempty \(S(\theta)\) is convex. If additionally \(F(\theta)\) is closed and \(f(\cdot,\theta)\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(S(\theta)\) is closed. If \(f(\cdot,\theta)\) is strictly convex on \(F(\theta)\), then \(S(\theta)\) contains at most one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed convex problem has a convex optimizer set; closed feasibility and lower semicontinuity give closedness, while strict convexity gives at most one optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\theta)\) is convex and \(f(\cdot,\theta)\) is convex for the convexity conclusion.
Closedness additionally requires closed \(F(\theta)\) and lower-semicontinuous \(f(\cdot,\theta)\).
Strict convexity is required only for the uniqueness conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(\theta)\neq\varnothing\Longrightarrow S(\theta)\text{ is convex, with the stated closedness and uniqueness refinements}.

notation.meaning: Optimizer set at the fixed parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Structure of Convex Optimizer Sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Berge Regularity of the Solution Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard continuity regime for a compact-valued parameterized feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(\Theta\) be finite-dimensional metric spaces. Suppose \(F:\Theta\rightrightarrows X\) is nonempty compact-valued and continuous at \(\theta_0\), and \(f\) is continuous on a neighborhood of \(\{(x,\theta_0):x\in F(\theta_0)\}\) relative to \(\operatorname{gph}F\). Then the value function is continuous at \(\theta_0\), and \(S\) is nonempty compact-valued and upper hemicontinuous at \(\theta_0\). If \(S(\theta_0)=\{x_0\}\), every optimizer sequence \(x_k\in S(\theta_k)\) with \(\theta_k\to\theta_0\) converges to \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Berge's compactness and continuity assumptions, optimizers exist, the value is continuous, and the solution correspondence is upper hemicontinuous; uniqueness yields local sequential stability.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty compact-valued and continuous at \(\theta_0\).
\(f\) is continuous on the relevant feasible graph near \(\theta_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\text{ is continuous at }\theta_0,\qquad S\text{ is nonempty compact-valued and upper hemicontinuous at }\theta_0.
knowledge_statements.title: Berge Regularity of the Solution Correspondence

children.title: Nonsmooth Solution Maps
children.top_down_role: Parameter regimes where selected solutions vary nonsmoothly.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Solution Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar convex family whose unique optimizer is not differentiable in the parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\), consider \[S(\theta)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\left(\frac12x^2-\theta x+|x|\right).\] Strong convexity gives a unique optimizer, and the optimality condition \(0\in x-\theta+\partial|x|\) yields \[S(\theta)=\begin{cases}\{\theta-1\},&\theta>1,\\ \{0\},&|\theta|\leq 1,\\ \{\theta+1\},&\theta<-1.\end{cases}\] Thus the single-valued optimizer selection is continuous and Lipschitz but is not differentiable at \(\theta=-1\) or \(\theta=1\). Uniqueness alone therefore does not guarantee a classically differentiable solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Soft thresholding gives a unique, continuous optimizer that has kinks at two parameter values, disproving uniqueness as a sufficient differentiability condition.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(\theta\) are real scalars.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique solution map fails to be differentiable at \(\theta=\pm1\).

children.title: Degeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural degeneracy associated with unstable or nonunique solution behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of optimizer uniqueness and stable sensitivity at a degenerate parameter value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}\), consider \[S(\theta)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{-1\leq x\leq1}\theta x.\] Direct minimization gives \[S(\theta)=\begin{cases}\{-1\},&\theta>0,\\ [-1,1],&\theta=0,\\ \{1\},&\theta<0.\end{cases}\] At \(\theta=0\), every feasible point is optimal, so the optimizer is nonunique and the objective has no growth away from any selected solution. Moreover, the unique optimizers on the two neighboring parameter regimes approach different limits. Hence no selection agreeing with the unique optimizer for every nonzero \(\theta\) can be continuous at the degenerate value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar linear program has one optimizer on either side of zero but an entire optimal interval at zero, destroying continuous sensitivity.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(\theta\) are real scalars.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degeneracy at \(\theta=0\) prevents a continuous optimizer selection consistent with all nearby unique solutions.

notation.meaning: Optimizer correspondence of the parameterized linear program.
