children.title: Sensitivity Interface Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on reusable sensitivity information near pathological solution maps.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Intrinsic Jacobian for a Locally Multivalued Optimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical derivative output when the optimizer correspondence is not a local function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\Theta\rightrightarrows X\) be an optimizer correspondence. If \(S\) is not single-valued on any neighborhood of \(\theta_0\), it is not a classical function on such a neighborhood and therefore has no intrinsic classical Jacobian \(DS(\theta_0)\). A derivative can instead be associated with an explicitly specified differentiable local selection \(s(\theta)\in S(\theta)\); such a derivative belongs to the selection and need not be shared by other selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally multivalued optimizer correspondence has no intrinsic classical Jacobian; derivatives belong to specified local selections.
assumptions_latex: The requested output is a classical Jacobian of the optimizer map.
The optimizer correspondence is not single-valued on any neighborhood of \(\theta_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DS(\theta_0)\text{ is not intrinsically defined; only }Ds(\theta_0)\text{ for a specified selection may be defined}.
knowledge_statements.title: No Intrinsic Jacobian for a Locally Multivalued Optimizer

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient regularity for a classical local primal-dual sensitivity interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable near \((z_0,\theta_0)\), satisfy \(R(z_0,\theta_0)=0\), and have nonsingular \(R_z(z_0,\theta_0)\). Then there are neighborhoods and a unique continuously differentiable branch \(z(\theta)\) through \((z_0,\theta_0)\) satisfying \(R(z(\theta),\theta)=0\), with \[Dz(\theta_0)=-R_z(z_0,\theta_0)^{-1}R_\theta(z_0,\theta_0).\] If the residual equation locally characterizes the selected primal-dual optimizer, this is a valid classical sensitivity output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable residual with an invertible solution Jacobian defines a unique local differentiable solution branch and the inverse-Jacobian sensitivity formula.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is continuously differentiable near \((z_0,\theta_0)\).
\(R_z(z_0,\theta_0)\) is nonsingular.
The residual equation locally characterizes the selected primal-dual optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dz(\theta_0)=-R_z(z_0,\theta_0)^{-1}R_\theta(z_0,\theta_0).
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Implicit Sensitivity Regime
Sensitivity Interface Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions separating classical solution derivatives from generalized or set-valued sensitivity outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a parameterized convex problem have KKT residual \(R(z,	heta)=0\), where \(z\) collects the primal and dual variables. A classical local sensitivity interface may return \(Dz(\theta)=-R_z(z,\theta)^{-1}R_\theta(z,\theta)\) only when the selected solution is locally single-valued, \(R\) is differentiable on the active regime, and \(R_z(z,\theta)\) is nonsingular. If any condition fails because of multiple solutions, an active-set transition, nonsmooth residuals, or degeneracy, the formula does not define a unique classical derivative. The interface must then report failure or explicitly return a directional, generalized, or set-valued sensitivity object.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Implicit KKT differentiation requires a locally unique regular solution; degeneracy, kinks, or multiple solutions require failure or generalized sensitivity output.
assumptions_latex: The KKT system is a locally valid characterization of the selected solution.
A classical derivative is the requested interface output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inverse-Jacobian sensitivity formula is valid only under differentiability, local single-valuedness, and nonsingularity of \(R_z\).

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the KKT residual with respect to the solution vector.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary is directionally correct, but mere differentiability of the KKT residual is not generally enough for the stated implicit sensitivity conclusion; an appropriate continuous-differentiability or strict-differentiability hypothesis and an authoritative sensitivity source are needed.

children.title: Log-Log Geometry
children.top_down_role: Function and domain classes induced by logarithmic coordinates.

children.title: Positive-Domain Semantics
children.top_down_role: Strictly positive variables, parameters, and atom values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set geometry induced by logarithmic coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(D\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\) is log-convex if \(\log D\) is convex. Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), the componentwise geometric interpolation \(x^\theta y^{1-\theta}\) belongs to \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive set is log-convex exactly when it is closed under componentwise geometric interpolation.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is log-convex}\iff x^\theta y^{1-\theta}\in D\quad\forall x,y\in D,\ \theta\in[0,1].
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Convex Positive Domains

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization consequence of excluding zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strict positivity does not imply a positive lower bound or attainment. For example, \(\inf\{x:x\in\mathbb R_{++}\}=0\), but no feasible point attains the infimum. In logarithmic coordinates the same infimum is approached only as \(u\to-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-domain problem may approach zero at infinity in log coordinates without attaining it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x>0}x=0,\qquad\operatorname*{argmin}_{x>0}x=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Open-Boundary Nonattainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic constructions preserving log-convex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Arbitrary intersections and Cartesian products of log-convex subsets of positive orthants are log-convex. If \(D\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\) is log-convex and \(C\) is convex, then \(D\cap\{x:A\log x+b\in C\}\) is log-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersections, products, and convex affine constraints in log coordinates preserve log-convex domains.
assumptions_latex: All sets lie in compatible strictly positive orthants.
C\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \log D\text{ remains convex under the stated constructions}.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Domain Set Calculus
Positive-Domain Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain convention enabling logarithmic transformation in disciplined geometric programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In disciplined geometric programming, every scalar variable, parameter, and admissible atom value that is transformed logarithmically has domain \(\mathbb{R}_{++}=\{t\in\mathbb{R}:t>0\}\). For a positive vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), logarithmic coordinates are \(u=\log x\), with the logarithm applied componentwise, and the inverse coordinates are \(x=\exp u\). Consequently, zero and negative values are outside the modeled domain rather than boundary values accepted by the log transformation. Parameters declared positive must be assigned strictly positive values at every instantiated solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DGP logarithmic semantics require strictly positive variables, parameters, and transformed atom values; zero and negative values are outside the domain.
assumptions_latex: All logarithms and exponentials are interpreted componentwise for vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinate transformation \(u=\log x\) is a bijection from \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^n\), with inverse \(x=\exp u\).

notation.meaning: Set of strictly positive real numbers.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-domain definition and log-coordinate bijection are mathematically correct and fit the container, but the DGP-specific semantic claims require a disciplined geometric programming source.

children.title: Log-Log Affine Functions
children.top_down_role: The affine function class in logarithmic coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable characterization on an open log-convex positive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\) be open and log-convex and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\) be continuously differentiable. Then \(f\) is log-log affine if and only if every logarithmic elasticity \(x_i\partial_i f(x)/f(x)\) is constant on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable positive function is log-log affine exactly when all coordinate elasticities are constant.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ is open and log-convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is log-log affine}\iff\exists a\in\mathbb R^n:\ x_i\partial_i f(x)/f(x)=a_i\ \forall x,i.

notation.meaning: Elasticity with respect to coordinate i.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Elasticity Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic closure of log-log affine functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are log-log affine and \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R\), then \(h(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m f_i(x)^{a_i}\) is log-log affine on their common positive domain. Thus the class is closed under products, quotients, arbitrary real powers, and multiplication by positive constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-log affine functions form a multiplicative class closed under real powers and quotients.
assumptions_latex: f_i(x)>0\text{ on the common domain}.
a_i\in\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \log h(e^u)=\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\log f_i(e^u)\text{ is affine}.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Affine Calculus

assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) and \(\log D=\{\log x:x\in D\}\) is convex.
\(f:D\to\mathbb{R}_{++}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is log-log affine exactly when \(F(u)=\log f(\exp u)\) is affine on \(\log D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar positive-valued functions on log-convex positive domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) have convex logarithmic image \(\log D\), and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}_{++}\). The function \(f\) is log-log affine if its logarithmic-coordinate transform \(F:\log D\to\mathbb{R}\), defined by \(F(u)=\log f(\exp u)\), is affine. Equivalently, there exist \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(F(u)=a^{\mathsf T}u+b\) for every \(u\in\log D\), or, equivalently, \(f(x)=e^b\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}\) for every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive function is log-log affine when taking logarithms of both its inputs and output produces an affine function.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Log Affine Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the exact leaf, and the notation and equivalent monomial representation are mathematically coherent. However, no citation or inspectable locator is supplied for the log-log affine definition and its equivalences.

children.title: Log-Log Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: The convex function class in logarithmic coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order criterion on open positive domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\) be twice continuously differentiable and \(F(u)=\log f(e^u)\). On an open log-convex domain \(D\), \(f\) is log-log convex if and only if \(\nabla^2F(u)\succeq0\) for every \(u\in\log D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth log-log convexity is positive semidefiniteness of the Hessian in logarithmic coordinates.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\text{ is open and log-convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is log-log convex}\iff\nabla^2[\log f(e^u)]\succeq0\quad\forall u\in\log D.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Log-Log Convexity Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordinary and Log-Log Convexity Are Incomparable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between ordinary and logarithmic-coordinate curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R_{++}\), \(f(x)=1/(1+x)\) is ordinarily convex but not log-log convex because \(\log f(e^u)=-\log(1+e^u)\) is strictly concave. Conversely, \(g(x)=\sqrt{x}\) is log-log affine, hence log-log convex, but ordinarily strictly concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary convexity neither implies nor is implied by log-log convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{ordinary convexity}\not\Rightarrow\text{log-log convexity},\qquad\text{log-log convexity}\not\Rightarrow\text{ordinary convexity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary and Log-Log Convexity Are Incomparable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental finite closure operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a common log-convex domain, positive finite sums, products, nonnegative powers, positive scalar multiples, and finite pointwise maxima of positive log-log convex functions are log-log convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sums, products, nonnegative powers, positive scaling, and finite maxima preserve log-log convexity.
assumptions_latex: f_i>0\text{ are log-log convex on a common log-convex domain}.
a\geq0,\ c>0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_i f_i,\ \prod_i f_i,\ f_1^a,\ cf_1,\ \max_i f_i\text{ are log-log convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Log Convex Closure Calculus

assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) and \(\log D\) is convex.
\(f:D\to\mathbb{R}_{++}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is log-log convex exactly when \(u\mapsto\log f(\exp u)\) is convex on \(\log D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar log-log convexity on a log-convex positive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) have convex logarithmic image and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}_{++}\). The function \(f\) is log-log convex if \(F(u)=\log f(\exp u)\) is convex on \(\log D\). Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\) such that \(x^\theta y^{1-\theta}\in D\), it satisfies \[f\!\left(x^\theta y^{1-\theta}\right)\leq f(x)^\theta f(y)^{1-\theta},\] where powers and products of vectors are interpreted componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive function is log-log convex when its output logarithm is convex as a function of the input logarithms.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Log Convex Functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the log-log convex-function leaf, and the transformed-convexity and geometric-interpolation formulations agree. No source reference or specific locator supports the definition and equivalence.

children.title: Log-Log Concave Functions
children.top_down_role: The concave function class in logarithmic coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order criterion on open positive domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\) be twice continuously differentiable and \(F(u)=\log f(e^u)\). On an open log-convex domain \(D\), \(f\) is log-log concave if and only if \(\nabla^2F(u)\preceq0\) for every \(u\in\log D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth log-log concavity is negative semidefiniteness of the Hessian in logarithmic coordinates.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\text{ is open and log-convex}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is log-log concave}\iff\nabla^2[\log f(e^u)]\preceq0\quad\forall u\in\log D.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Log-Log Concavity Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Addition Is Not a Concavity Closure Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of additive closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The functions \(f(x)=x\) and \(g(x)=x^{-1}\) are log-log affine, hence log-log concave, on \(\mathbb R_{++}\). Their sum is not log-log concave because \(u\mapsto\log(e^u+e^{-u})\) is strictly convex and nonaffine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of log-log concave functions need not be log-log concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f,g\text{ are log-log concave but }f+g\text{ is not}.
knowledge_statements.title: Addition Is Not a Concavity Closure Rule

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic closure operations intrinsic to the class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_i:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\) are log-log concave, \(a_i\geq0\), and \(c>0\), then \(c\prod_i f_i^{a_i}\) is log-log concave. The pointwise minimum of finitely many positive log-log concave functions is also log-log concave on their common log-convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative weighted geometric products and finite pointwise minima preserve log-log concavity.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ is log-convex}.
f_i>0\text{ are log-log concave}.
a_i\geq0,\ c>0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c\prod_i f_i^{a_i}\text{ and }\min_i f_i\text{ are log-log concave}.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Log Concave Closure Calculus

assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) and \(\log D\) is convex.
\(f:D\to\mathbb{R}_{++}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is log-log concave exactly when \(u\mapsto\log f(\exp u)\) is concave on \(\log D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar log-log concavity on a log-convex positive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) have convex logarithmic image and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}_{++}\). The function \(f\) is log-log concave if \(F(u)=\log f(\exp u)\) is concave on \(\log D\). Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\) such that \(x^\theta y^{1-\theta}\in D\), it satisfies \[f\!\left(x^\theta y^{1-\theta}\right)\geq f(x)^\theta f(y)^{1-\theta},\] with vector powers and products interpreted componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive function is log-log concave when its output logarithm is concave as a function of the input logarithms.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Log Concave Functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialized primal-dual certificate for a differentiable finite classical GP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a primal-feasible \(x^\star\), define each normalized term contribution by \[	heta_{ik}(x^\star)= rac{c_{ik}(x^\star)^{a_{ik}}}{f_i(x^\star)}.\] Let \((
u,\lambda,\eta)\) satisfy the feasibility and exponent-balance conditions of the classical GP dual. If \(
u_{0k}=	heta_{0k}(x^\star)\), \(
u_{ik}=\lambda_i	heta_{ik}(x^\star)\) for \(i\geq1\), and \(\lambda_i\log f_i(x^\star)=0\) for every inequality, then the primal-dual gap is zero and both points are globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized monomial contributions, exponent balance, feasibility, and complementary slackness provide a zero-gap optimality certificate for a classical GP.
assumptions_latex: All posynomial values at \(x^\star\) are positive.
The primal and dual use the conventions stated in the immutable seed and Classical Geometric-Programming Dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log f_0(x^\star)=d(\nu,\lambda,\eta)\), so the primal and dual feasible points are optimal.

notation.meaning: fractional contribution of term k to posynomial i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entropy-form dual of a finite log-transformed classical GP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical GP dual assigns nonnegative weights to monomial terms, normalizes objective weights, balances exponent vectors, and maximizes an entropy-like expression.
assumptions_latex: The finite primal has the standard form in the immutable Classical Geometric Programs seed.
Natural logarithms and the displayed minimization and equality conventions are used.
Strong duality additionally requires an appropriate convex constraint qualification, such as strict feasibility of the posynomial inequalities relative to consistent monomial equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d^\star\leq\log p^\star,\quad\text{with equality and dual attainment under the stated regularity condition}.

notation.meaning: dual weight of monomial term k in posynomial i

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Geometric-Programming Dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Source-form variants reducible to classical standard form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\) is a posynomial and \(m,m_1,m_2\) are monomials, then on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \[p(x)\leq m(x)\iff \frac{p(x)}{m(x)}\leq1,\qquad m_1(x)=m_2(x)\iff\frac{m_1(x)}{m_2(x)}=1.\] Here \(p/m\) is a posynomial and \(m_1/m_2\) is a monomial. Likewise, maximizing a monomial \(m\) is equivalent to minimizing the monomial \(1/m\). These normalizations preserve feasible points and optimizer ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monomial right-hand sides can be divided out, and monomial maximization can be inverted, yielding classical standard-form geometric programs.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
All monomial coefficients are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed constraint and objective variants reduce exactly to classical GP standard form.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Classical GP Normalizations

assumptions_latex: The decision variable satisfies \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\).
Each \(f_i\) is a posynomial and each \(g_j\) is a monomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The substitution \(u=\log x\) converts the problem into a convex optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard minimization form of a classical geometric program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A classical geometric program in standard form is \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\leq 1\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad g_j(x)=1\ (j=1,\ldots,p),\] where every \(f_i\), including \(f_0\), is a posynomial and every \(g_j\) is a monomial. Under \(u=\log x\), the objective may be replaced by \(\log f_0(\exp u)\), each inequality becomes \(\log f_i(\exp u)\leq0\), and each equality becomes \(\log g_j(\exp u)=0\); these are respectively convex inequalities and affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A classical geometric program minimizes a posynomial subject to posynomial inequalities and monomial equalities, and logarithmic coordinates convert it to a convex problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Geometric Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard-form representation and logarithmic convexification match the classical geometric-program leaf; representation is an appropriate content kind because the record presents both the canonical form and its convex-coordinate representation. The claim lacks a cited source and inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical geometric program in posynomial form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard geometric-program problem class with the strict positivity of every variable imposed implicitly by the domains of its monomials and posynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A geometric program in posynomial form is \[\begin{aligned}\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n}\quad & f_0(x)\\ \operatorname*{subject\ to}\quad & f_i(x)\le 1,\quad i=1,\ldots,m,\\ & h_j(x)=1,\quad j=1,\ldots,p,\end{aligned}\] where \(f_0,\ldots,f_m\) are posynomials and \(h_1,\ldots,h_p\) are monomials. The restriction \(x\succ0\) is implicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A classical geometric program minimizes a posynomial over strictly positive variables, subject to posynomial inequalities bounded above by one and monomial equalities to one. Strict positivity of every variable is an implicit domain restriction.
assumptions_latex: n\in\mathbb{N},\quad n\ge1
m,p\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}
f_0,\ldots,f_m\text{ are posynomials on }\mathbb{R}_{++}^n
h_1,\ldots,h_p\text{ are monomials on }\mathbb{R}_{++}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n} f_0(x)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad f_i(x)\le1\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\quad h_j(x)=1\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\quad\text{is a classical geometric program.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric-program standard form and logarithmic convexification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the geometric-program model class and gives the explicit convex log-sum-exp reformulation for the standard-posynomial case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A geometric program over \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{n}\) minimizes a generalized posynomial \(f_0(x)\) subject to generalized-posynomial inequalities \(f_i(x)\le1\) and positive-monomial equalities \(h_i(x)=1\). In the standard-posynomial case, let \(f_i(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K_i}c_{ki}x^{a^{(ki)}}\) and \(h_i(x)=g_i x^{r^{(i)}}\), with \(c_{ki},g_i>0\). Under \(y=\log x\), the problem is equivalently \(\min_y\operatorname{lse}(A_0y+b_0)\) subject to \(\operatorname{lse}(A_i y+b_i)\le0\) and \(Ry+d=0\), where the rows of \(A_i\) are \((a^{(ki)})^{\top}\), \((b_i)_k=\log c_{ki}\), the rows of \(R\) are \((r^{(i)})^{\top}\), and \(d_i=\log g_i\). The transformed problem is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric program minimizes a generalized posynomial subject to generalized-posynomial upper bounds and monomial equalities over positive variables. When the objective and inequalities are standard posynomials, taking logarithms of the variables yields an equivalent convex problem with log-sum-exp objective and inequalities and affine equalities.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{n}
f_0,\ldots,f_m\text{ are generalized posynomials}
h_1,\ldots,h_p\text{ are positive monomials}
\text{for the explicit reformulation, }f_i(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K_i}c_{ki}x^{a^{(ki)}}\text{ with }c_{ki}>0
h_i(x)=g_i x^{r^{(i)}}\text{ with }g_i>0
y=\log x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_x f_0(x)\ \text{s.t. }f_i(x)\le1,\ h_i(x)=1\quad\equiv\quad\min_y\operatorname{lse}(A_0y+b_0)\ \text{s.t. }\operatorname{lse}(A_i y+b_i)\le0,\ Ry+d=0,\ \text{which is convex}.

children.title: Generalized Geometric Programs
children.top_down_role: Closure-generated extensions of classical geometric programs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why generalized geometric programs retain monomial equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equality \(x+y=1\), with \(x,y>0\), has a posynomial rather than monomial left side. In logarithmic coordinates it becomes \(\log(e^u+e^v)=0\). Its solution set is nonconvex: the logarithms of \((1/4,3/4)\) and \((3/4,1/4)\) are feasible, while their midpoint corresponds to \((\sqrt3/4,\sqrt3/4)\), whose coordinates sum to \(\sqrt3/2<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general posynomial equality can destroy convexity after logarithmic transformation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(u,v):\log(e^u+e^v)=0\}\text{ is nonconvex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonomial Equality Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard scalar generalized-posynomial closure convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generalized posynomials are the smallest class of positive functions on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\) containing the posynomials and closed under finite sums, products, positive real powers, and pointwise maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized posynomials are generated from posynomials by sums, products, positive powers, and maxima.
assumptions_latex: All expressions are evaluated on their strictly positive domains.
The power constructor uses exponents \(a>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal G=\operatorname{cl}_{+,\times,(\cdot)^{a>0},\max}(\mathcal P).

notation.meaning: Classes of posynomials and generalized posynomials.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Generalized-Posynomial Grammar

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive logarithmic-coordinate representation for the stated grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\widehat f(u)=\log f(e^u)\), the constructors satisfy \(\widehat{fg}=\widehat f+\widehat g\), \(\widehat{f^a}=a\widehat f\) for \(a>0\), \(\widehat{\max(f,g)}=\max(\widehat f,\widehat g)\), and \(\widehat{f+g}=\operatorname{lse}(\widehat f,\widehat g)\). Hence every generalized posynomial generated by the stated grammar is log-log convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized-posynomial constructors become convexity-preserving operations in logarithmic coordinates.
assumptions_latex: f,g\text{ are positive generalized posynomials}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat f\text{ is convex for every generalized posynomial }f.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Images of Generalized-Posynomial Constructors

assumptions_latex: The decision variable satisfies \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\).
Objective and inequality expressions are generalized posynomials; equality expressions are monomials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Logarithmic coordinates transform the generalized geometric program into a convex problem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard generalized-posynomial extension of classical geometric programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized geometric program has the standard form \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\leq1\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad g_j(x)=1\ (j=1,\ldots,p),\] where each \(f_i\), including \(f_0\), is a generalized posynomial and each \(g_j\) is a monomial. Because generalized posynomials are log-log convex and monomials are log-log affine, the change of variables \(u=\log x\), together with logarithms of all positive expressions, yields convex objective and inequality functions and affine equality functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized geometric program replaces classical posynomials by closure-generated generalized posynomials while retaining monomial equalities and logarithmic convexification.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Geometric Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the generalized geometric-program leaf and uses an appropriate definition role, but the precise generalized-posynomial convention and the resulting convexification depend on the adopted closure definition. No source or locator establishes that convention.

children.title: Log-Log Convex Programs
children.top_down_role: The ambient positive-domain problem class convexified by logarithmic coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent two-sided presentation of log-log convex constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive-domain inequality \(f(x)\leq g(x)\) transforms to a convex constraint when \(f\) is log-log convex and \(g\) is log-log concave; equivalently, \(f(x)/g(x)\leq1\) has a log-log convex left side. An equality \(h(x)=k(x)\) is admissible when both sides are log-log affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid inequalities place a log-log convex expression below a log-log concave one; equality sides must be log-log affine.
assumptions_latex: f,g,h,k\text{ are strictly positive on their joint domains}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \log f(e^u)-\log g(e^u)\leq0\text{ is convex, and }\log h(e^u)-\log k(e^u)=0\text{ is affine}.
knowledge_statements.title: Admissible Constraint Orientations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the reversed inequality orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Although \(f(x,y)=x+y\) is log-log convex, its superlevel constraint need not be log-convex. The points \((0.9,0.2)\) and \((0.2,0.9)\) satisfy \(x+y\geq1\), but their componentwise geometric midpoint \((\sqrt{0.18},\sqrt{0.18})\) does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A superlevel constraint on a log-log convex function can be nonconvex in logarithmic coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(x,y)\in\mathbb R_{++}^2:x+y\geq1\}\text{ is not log-convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Reversed-Curvature Constraint Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of feasible points, values, attainment, and optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a log-log convex program, the bijection \(x=e^u\) maps its feasible set exactly onto that of the logarithmically transformed convex program. With \(F_0(u)=\log f_0(e^u)\), one has \(f_0(x)=e^{F_0(u)}\); hence objective ordering, attainment, and minimizers are preserved, and the infimal values satisfy \(p^*=e^{q^*}\) with the extended convention \(e^{-\infty}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logarithmic coordinates preserve feasibility and minimizers, and exponentiation recovers the original infimal value.
assumptions_latex: All modeled expressions are strictly positive.
Logarithm and exponential are applied componentwise to variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_x f_0(x)=\exp\!\left(\operatorname*{argmin}_u F_0(u)\right),\qquad p^*=e^{q^*}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Logarithmic-Coordinate Correspondence

assumptions_latex: All variables lie in \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\), and every function is positive on its domain.
The logarithmic transforms of the objective and inequality functions are convex, and those of equality functions are affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinate change \(u=\log x\) produces an equivalent convex program.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-domain minimization form with log-log convex inequalities and log-log affine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A log-log convex program is a positive-domain problem \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{x\in D}\ f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\leq1\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad h_j(x)=1\ (j=1,\ldots,p),\] where \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) is log-convex, the functions \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are positive and log-log convex, and the functions \(h_1,\ldots,h_p\) are positive and log-log affine. Setting \(u=\log x\) and applying the logarithm to each positive expression gives an equivalent convex program on \(\log D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A log-log convex program has positive variables, log-log convex objectives and inequalities, and log-log affine equalities; logarithmic coordinates make it convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Log-Log Convex Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-domain standard form and logarithmic-coordinate convexification fit the ambient log-log convex-program class, and definition is the correct content kind. No citation or inspectable locator supports the problem-class definition.

children.title: DGP-Certified Programs
children.top_down_role: Library-relative log-log convex programs recognized compositionally.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between mathematical log-log convexity and library-relative certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a library containing positive constants, variables, products, quotients, and real powers, but no addition atom. The function \(f(x)=1+x\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}\) is log-log convex because \(u\mapsto\log(1+e^u)\) is convex, yet this expression is not representable or certifiable in that library.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A log-log convex function can fall outside a chosen DGP library.
assumptions_latex: The library has exactly the stated constructors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is log-log convex but is not certified by the stated library.}
knowledge_statements.title: Library Incompleteness Witness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity-sensitive rule underlying sound DGP curvature propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=f(g_1(x),\ldots,g_k(x))\) be positive on a log-convex domain. If \(f\) is log-log convex, then \(h\) is log-log convex when, for every argument \(i\), either \(f\) is nondecreasing in that argument and \(g_i\) is log-log convex, \(f\) is nonincreasing and \(g_i\) is log-log concave, \(g_i\) is log-log affine, or \(f\) is independent of that argument. For a log-log concave outer function, interchange convex and concave in the inner-function requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary monotonicity-sensitive composition rule applies after transforming inputs and outputs logarithmically.
assumptions_latex: All functions and intermediate values are strictly positive on their modeled domains.
Each stated monotonicity holds on the range of the corresponding inner function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\text{ has the curvature assigned by the stated composition rule.}
knowledge_statements.title: DGP Composition Rule

assumptions_latex: A fixed atom library specifies each atom's log-log curvature, sign, monotonicity, and domain.
Every expression is formed by the library's permitted composition rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A successful compositional check certifies membership in the library-recognized subclass of log-log convex programs.

notation.meaning: Expression tree of the modeled problem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic certification relative to a declared DGP atom library and composition rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed disciplined geometric programming library, a program is DGP-certified when a bottom-up traversal of each expression tree verifies positive domains and assigns log-log curvature using the declared curvature and monotonicity of every atom and the library's composition rules. Certification requires a log-log convex objective for minimization, log-log convex left sides of normalized inequalities \(f_i(x)\leq1\), and log-log affine expressions in normalized equalities \(h_j(x)=1\). Passing this finite syntactic check certifies that the represented program is log-log convex, although failure to pass does not prove that the program lacks log-log convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DGP certificate is a library-relative compositional check proving that a modeled positive-domain problem is log-log convex.
knowledge_statements.title: DGP-Certified Programs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct content kind for this leaf, and the record properly distinguishes successful syntactic certification from mathematical necessity. Because certification is relative to a particular atom library and composition rules, a source with a precise DGP grammar and certification specification is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementation-dependent complexity of curvature certification after parsing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an expression DAG with \(N\) nodes and \(E\) argument edges, a fixed atom library, bounded-size metadata, and constant-time local rule matching per edge, a bottom-up certification pass takes \(O(N+E)\) time and \(O(N)\) metadata storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under fixed-cost metadata assumptions, DGP certification is a linear graph traversal.
assumptions_latex: The atom library and metadata representation are fixed.
Each local rule check has constant cost apart from visiting arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{cert}}=O(N+E),\qquad S_{\mathrm{metadata}}=O(N).

notation.meaning: Numbers of expression nodes and argument edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Time DGP Certification

The proposed complexity claim is deferred as implementation-dependent optional detail. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monomial and posynomial functions and their closure properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical monomial and posynomial classes on the strictly positive orthant, including the zero-scaling boundary implied by the positive-coefficient definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge 1\). A function on \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) of the form \(m(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}\), with \(c>0\) and \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}\), is a monomial. For \(K\ge 1\), a function \(p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_{ik}}\), with \(c_k>0\) and \(a_{ik}\in\mathbb{R}\), is a posynomial. Posynomials are closed under addition and multiplication, and under scaling by a positive scalar. Monomials are closed under multiplication and division. The product of a posynomial and a monomial, and the quotient of a posynomial by a monomial, are posynomials. Scaling by zero is also a closure operation only if the zero function is admitted as a posynomial by convention; it is not representable by the displayed positive-coefficient definition with \(K\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the strictly positive orthant, a monomial is a positive coefficient times a product of arbitrary real powers, and a posynomial is a nonempty finite sum of monomials with positive coefficients. Posynomials are closed under addition, multiplication, and positive scaling; monomials are closed under multiplication and division; and multiplying or dividing a posynomial by a monomial yields a posynomial. The source's claim of closure under nonnegative scaling requires a convention adjoining the zero function, since zero scaling falls outside the stated positive-coefficient definition.
assumptions_latex: n\in\mathbb{N},\quad n\ge1
K\in\mathbb{N},\quad K\ge1
x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n
c>0,\quad c_k>0
a_i,a_{ik}\in\mathbb{R}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}\text{ is a monomial and }p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_{ik}}\text{ is a posynomial, with the stated closure properties and zero-scaling boundary.}

children.title: Monomial Families
children.top_down_role: Classical monomial expressions within positive-variable modeling.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary separating monomials from nontrivial positive sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite positive sum of monomials is itself a monomial exactly when all summands have the same exponent vector, after which their coefficients combine. Consequently, \(1+x\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}\) is not a monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monomials are not closed under general addition; 1+x is the canonical counterexample.
assumptions_latex: All summand coefficients are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 1+x\text{ is not a monomial on }\mathbb R_{++}.
knowledge_statements.title: Addition Boundary for Monomials

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic closure of positive generalized monomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For monomials \(m_j(x)=c_jx^{a_j}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), \[m_1m_2=(c_1c_2)x^{a_1+a_2},\qquad \frac{m_1}{m_2}=\frac{c_1}{c_2}x^{a_1-a_2},\qquad m_1^\alpha=c_1^\alpha x^{\alpha a_1}.\] Thus monomials are closed under products, quotients, and arbitrary real powers on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive monomials are closed under multiplication, division, and arbitrary real powers.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
\(c_1,c_2>0\), \(a_1,a_2\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m_1m_2,\ m_1/m_2,\text{ and }m_1^\alpha\text{ are monomials}.
knowledge_statements.title: Monomial Algebra and Closure

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\).
\(c>0\) and \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i}\) is a monomial and is log-log affine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-coefficient generalized monomials with arbitrary real exponents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A monomial on \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) is a function of the form \[m(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_i},\] where \(c>0\) and every exponent \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}\). Its logarithmic-coordinate transform is \[\log m(\exp u)=\log c+a^{\mathsf T}u,\] so every monomial is log-log affine. Under this convention, negative and nonintegral exponents are allowed because all arguments are strictly positive; the identically zero function is not a monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monomial is a positive coefficient times arbitrary real powers of positive variables; it becomes affine after taking input and output logarithms.
knowledge_statements.title: Monomial Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generalized monomial definition, positive-domain convention, and log-log affine classification fit the monomial-family leaf. No citation or inspectable locator supports the convention allowing arbitrary real exponents and excluding the zero function.

children.title: Posynomial Families
children.top_down_role: Classical posynomial expressions within geometric programming.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common operations that do not generally preserve the posynomial class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Positive integer powers preserve posynomials, but arbitrary positive real powers do not: \((1+x)^{1/2}\) is not a posynomial. Pointwise maxima also need not be posynomials, as shown by \(\max\{1,x\}\). Both expressions are generalized posynomials. Reciprocals and division likewise fail in general; \((1+x)^{-1}\) is not log-log convex and therefore is not a generalized posynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer powers preserve posynomials, whereas noninteger powers and maxima can leave the class; reciprocals and division can even destroy log-log convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (1+x)^{1/2},\ \max\{1,x\}\notin\mathcal P,\qquad (1+x)^{-1}\notin\mathcal{GP}.
knowledge_statements.title: Noninteger-Power, Maximum, and Division Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operations preserving finite positive sums of monomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\) and \(q\) are posynomials and \(c>0\), then \(p+q\), \(pq\), and \(cp\) are posynomials. Consequently, \(p^k\) is a posynomial for every positive integer \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Posynomials are closed under finite addition, multiplication, positive scaling, and positive integer powers.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) and \(q\) are posynomials on a common positive domain.
\(c>0\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\) with \(k\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p+q,\ pq,\ cp,\text{ and }p^k\text{ are posynomials}.
knowledge_statements.title: Posynomial Closure Algebra

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\).
Each summand is a monomial with a positive coefficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite positive sum of monomials is a posynomial and is log-log convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite positive sums of generalized monomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A posynomial on \(\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) is a finite sum \[p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{a_{ik}},\qquad K\geq1,\quad c_k>0,\quad a_{ik}\in\mathbb{R}.\] In logarithmic coordinates its transform is \[\log p(\exp u)=\log\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^K \exp\!\left(a_k^{\mathsf T}u+\log c_k\right)\right),\] which is convex. Hence every posynomial is log-log convex, while a single-term posynomial is a monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A posynomial is a finite sum of positive-coefficient monomials and is log-log convex through the log-sum-exp representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Posynomial Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite positive sum definition and log-sum-exp characterization fit the posynomial-family leaf, with definition as the appropriate content kind. No source reference or specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive monomials, posynomials, and generalized posynomials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the geometric-polynomial classes on the strictly positive orthant while preserving the extract's unspecified constant-power qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{n}\), \(a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), and \(c>0\), a positive monomial is \(cx^{a}=c\prod_{j=1}^{n}x_j^{a_j}\). A posynomial is a function \(f:\mathbb{R}_{++}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}\) of the form \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{K}c_i x^{a^{(i)}}\), where \(c_i>0\) and \(a^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\). A generalized posynomial is any function obtained from posynomials through finitely many applications of addition, multiplication, pointwise maximum, and raising to a constant power.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive monomial is a positive coefficient times a product of positive variables raised to real powers. A posynomial is a finite sum of positive monomials. Generalized posynomials are constructed from posynomials using addition, multiplication, pointwise maximum, and constant powers.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^{n}
a,a^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
c,c_i>0
K\in\mathbb{N}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: cx^{a}=c\prod_{j=1}^{n}x_j^{a_j},\qquad f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{K}c_i x^{a^{(i)}};\quad\text{generalized posynomials are obtained by the stated closure operations}.

children.title: Generalized-Posynomial Families
children.top_down_role: Extended expression families built from permitted positive-domain operations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operations that do not generally preserve generalized posynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generalized posynomials are not closed under negative powers or division by generalized posynomials. For example, \(p(x)=1+x\) is a posynomial, but \(p(x)^{-1}\) has logarithmic transform \(-\log(1+e^u)\), which is strictly concave and nonaffine. Hence \((1+x)^{-1}\) is not log-log convex and therefore is not a generalized posynomial. Division remains valid in special cases such as division by a monomial because a monomial reciprocal is a monomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocals and division do not generally preserve generalized posynomials; the reciprocal of 1+x is a canonical counterexample, while monomial denominators are a special valid case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (1+x)^{-1}\notin\mathcal{GP}.
knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Power and Division Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic-coordinate representation of the finite generalized-posynomial closure grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(u)=\log f(e^u)\) and \(G(u)=\log g(e^u)\). The permitted operations satisfy \[\log((f+g)(e^u))=\operatorname{lse}(F(u),G(u)),\qquad \log((fg)(e^u))=F(u)+G(u),\] \[\log(f(e^u)^\alpha)=\alpha F(u)\quad(\alpha>0),\qquad \log(\max\{f,g\}(e^u))=\max\{F(u),G(u)\}.\] Consequently, every generalized posynomial has a convex logarithmic transform generated finitely from affine functions using log-sum-exp, addition, positive scaling, and pointwise maximum.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive functions \(f_1,\ldots,f_K\) on a common log-convex domain \(D\), define \(h(x)=\prod_{k=1}^K f_k(x)\). In particular, products of monomials are monomials, and products of posynomials are posynomials after finite distributive expansion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decision-Dependent Exponents Are Not Power Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between constant-exponent power closure and a positive decision-dependent exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x,y)=x^y\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^2\), the logarithmic-coordinate transform is \(H(u,v)=u e^v\), whose Hessian is indefinite everywhere. Power Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Log-log curvature of scalar powers and powered positive expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in\mathbb R\), the power atom \(h(x)=x^p\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}\) is log-log affine because \(\log h(e^u)=pu\). More generally, if \(f:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\) and \(F(u)=\log f(e^u)\), then \(f^p\) has logarithmic transform \(pF\). Hence \(f^p\) is log-log convex when \(p>0\) and \(f\) is log-log convex, or when \(p<0\) and \(f\) is log-log concave. The corresponding reversed-curvature statements also hold; \(p=0\) gives the constant-one function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar power is log-log affine. Raising a positive expression to a positive power preserves log-log curvature, while a negative power reverses it.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite positive sums in the log-log convex closure calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\) be log-log convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and let \(a_i>0\). Then \(h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m a_i f_i(x)\) is log-log convex. Indeed, its logarithmic-coordinate expression is \(H(u)=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m \exp(\log a_i+F_i(u))\right)\), where \(F_i(u)=\log f_i(e^u)\). Thus positive weighted sums form a log-log convex closure family. Such a sum is not generally log-log concave, even when every summand is log-log affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite positive weighted sum of positive log-log convex functions is log-log convex, but generally not log-log concave.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(m\geq1\), and \(a_i>0\).
Each \(f_i:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\) is log-log convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremum Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise maxima and minima as dual log-log closure operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive functions \(f_i:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\), define \(F_i(u)=\log f_i(e^u)\). If every \(f_i\) is log-log convex, then \(h(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\) is log-log convex because \(\log h(e^u)=\max_i F_i(u)\). Dually, if every \(f_i\) is log-log concave, then \(g(x)=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\) is log-log concave because \(\log g(e^u)=\min_i F_i(u)\). The opposite pairings have no general curvature guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise maximum preserves log-log convexity, and pointwise minimum preserves log-log concavity; the opposite pairings are not generally valid.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(m\geq1\), and all \(f_i\) are positive on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i f_i\) is log-log convex under convex inputs, while \(\min_i f_i\) is log-log concave under concave inputs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure of Log-Log Convex Positive-Matrix Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entrywise closure under basic positive matrix operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be conformably sized strictly positive matrix-valued expressions whose entries are log-log convex. Then \(A+B\), the Hadamard product \(A\circ B\), and the ordinary matrix product \(AB\) have strictly positive log-log convex entries. If \(A\) is square, every positive integer power \(A^k\) has log-log convex entries. When the relevant entries are log-log affine, Hadamard products preserve affinity, whereas sums and ordinary matrix products generally preserve only log-log convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entrywise log-log convex positive matrices are closed under addition, Hadamard products, ordinary products, and square positive integer powers; affinity survives only purely multiplicative entrywise operations.

Positive-Matrix Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive matrix-valued expressions used by spectral DGP atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive-matrix family is a mapping \(A:D\to\mathbb R_{++}^{m\times m}\), where \(D\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\), whose entries \(A_{ij}:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\) are positive scalar expressions. It is entrywise log-log convex, respectively entrywise log-log affine, when every transform \(u\mapsto\log A_{ij}(e^u)\) is convex, respectively affine. Positivity is entrywise and is distinct from positive semidefiniteness; neither symmetry nor a Loewner-order condition is part of this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-matrix family has strictly positive scalar entries, each carrying its own log-log curvature metadata; entrywise positivity does not mean positive semidefiniteness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity, Homogeneity, and Powers of Spectral Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic order and scaling laws on nonnegative matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For square nonnegative matrices \(0\le A\le B\) entrywise, \(c\ge0\), and \(k\in\mathbb N\), \[\rho(A)\le\rho(B),\qquad \rho(cA)=c\rho(A),\qquad \rho(A^k)=\rho(A)^k.\] Thus spectral radius is entrywise monotone and positively homogeneous on the nonnegative cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On nonnegative matrices, spectral radius is entrywise monotone, positively homogeneous, and compatible with integer powers.

Spectral-Radius Families

Then the spectral-radius function \(x\mapsto\rho(A(x))\) is log-log convex on \(D\); equivalently, \(u\mapsto\log\rho(A(e^u))\) is convex on \(\{u:e^u\in D\}\). In particular, if every entry is a generalized posynomial or another positive log-log convex expression, applying the spectral radius produces a valid log-log convex expression. This claim concerns entrywise-positive matrices and the ordinary eigenvalue spectral radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The spectral radius of an entrywise-positive matrix whose entries are log-log convex functions is itself log-log convex.

children.title: Perron-Frobenius Families

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic consequence of the strong Perron-Frobenius theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R_{++}^{m\times m}\), and normalize positive Perron vectors \(v,w\) by \(w^{\mathsf T}v=1\). Then \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\rho(A)^{-k}A^k=vw^{\mathsf T}.\] Consequently, for every nonzero \(z\in\mathbb R_+^m\), normalized power iterates converge in direction to \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized powers of a strictly positive matrix converge to the rank-one Perron projection, and nonnegative power iterates converge to the Perron direction.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R_{++}^{m\times m}\).
\(Av=\rho(A)v\), \(w^{\mathsf T}A=\rho(A)w^{\mathsf T}\), and \(w^{\mathsf T}v=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho(A)^{-k}A^k\to vw^{\mathsf T}.
knowledge_statements.title: Perron Projection Limit

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Perron-Frobenius Theorem for Positive Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong spectral conclusions for a strictly entrywise-positive square matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A\in\mathbb R_{++}^{m\times m}\), then \(\rho(A)>0\) is an algebraically simple eigenvalue. There exist right and left eigenvectors \(v,w\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\) satisfying \(Av=\rho(A)v\) and \(w^{\mathsf T}A=\rho(A)w^{\mathsf T}\), each unique up to positive scaling. Every other eigenvalue \(\lambda\) satisfies \(|\lambda|<\rho(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly positive matrix has positive left and right Perron eigenvectors, an algebraically simple Perron root, and strict dominance over all other eigenvalues.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R_{++}^{m\times m}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho(A)\text{ is algebraically simple and }|\lambda|<\rho(A)\text{ for every other eigenvalue}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Perron-Frobenius Theorem for Positive Matrices

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R_{++}^{m\times m}\), and \(t\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed variational equalities hold, and \(\rho(A)\leq t\iff\exists v\in\mathbb R_{++}^m:Av\leq tv\).

notation.meaning: real scalar used in the spectral-radius upper-bound certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collatz-Wielandt representations for a strictly positive matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(A\in\mathbb R_{++}^{m\times m}\), the Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue equals the spectral radius and admits the Collatz-Wielandt representations
\[\rho(A)=\inf_{v\in\mathbb R_{++}^m}\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\frac{(Av)_i}{v_i}=\sup_{v\in\mathbb R_{++}^m}\min_{1\leq i\leq m}\frac{(Av)_i}{v_i}.\]
Moreover, there is \(v_\star\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\), unique up to positive scaling, satisfying \(Av_\star=\rho(A)v_\star\). Consequently, for every \(t\in\mathbb R\), \(\rho(A)\leq t\) holds exactly when some \(v\in\mathbb R_{++}^m\) satisfies \(Av\leq tv\) componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly positive matrix, the spectral radius has Collatz-Wielandt min-max formulas and a positive eigenvector; for every real scalar t, a positive vector inequality certifies an upper bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Irreducibility Does Not Imply Perron Spectral Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical imprimitive boundary counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) is nonnegative and irreducible but not primitive. Its eigenvalues are \(1\) and \(-1\), so \(\rho(A)=1\) is not strictly larger in modulus than every other eigenvalue. Its normalized powers also alternate rather than converge.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-theoretic regimes separating nonnegative boundary matrices from strictly positive matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times m}\), \(A\) is irreducible exactly when its directed graph is strongly connected. It is primitive exactly when \(A^k>0\) entrywise for some integer \(k\ge1\). Every strictly positive matrix is primitive, and every primitive matrix is irreducible, but neither converse holds.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times m}\).

Matrix-Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which logarithmic matrix atoms or strict Perron conclusions fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The DGP positive-matrix domain requires \(A_{ij}(x)>0\) for every entry used in logarithmic coordinates. If an entry is zero, \(\log A_{ij}(x)\) is not finite; if an entry is negative, its real logarithm is undefined. Thus, for example, \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) lies outside the strict positive-matrix domain, even though \(\rho(A)=1\). More generally, allowing reducible nonnegative matrices invalidates the strict conclusion that the Perron eigenvector is unique up to scale and entrywise positive, so such matrices require extended-value or sparsity-aware rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero or negative entries leave the ordinary logarithmic domain. Reducible nonnegative matrices can also lose the strictly positive, unique Perron eigenvector used by basic DGP rules.
assumptions_latex: Matrix logarithmic coordinates are interpreted as finite real entrywise logarithms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict entrywise positivity is necessary for the stated basic DGP matrix domain and its strict Perron metadata.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R_{++}^m\to\mathbb R_{++}\), let \(g_i:D\to\mathbb R_{++}\), and set \(f(x)=h(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\).
