knowledge_statements.title: Spectral-to-Semidefinite Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite representation of the spectral norm epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), \[\|X\|_2\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{bmatrix}tI_m&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&tI_n\end{bmatrix}\succeq0.\] Feasibility of the block inequality forces \(t\ge0\). For \(t>0\), taking a Schur complement yields \(t^2I_n-X^{\mathsf T}X\succeq0\), which is equivalent to every singular value of \(X\) being at most \(t\); the equivalence extends to \(t=0\) by direct evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix spectral-norm bound is equivalent to one symmetric block positive-semidefinite constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\)
\(t\in\mathbb{R}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|X\|_2\le t\iff \begin{bmatrix}tI_m&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&tI_n\end{bmatrix}\succeq0\)

children.title: Matrix-Structure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where missing symmetry or definiteness metadata blocks recognition.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Structure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry requirements for eigenvalue and semidefinite-order rewrites.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equivalence \(\lambda_{\max}(X)\le t\iff tI-X\succeq0\) requires \(X\) to be symmetric, or Hermitian over \(\mathbb{C}\). For a nonsymmetric real matrix, \(tI-X\) is not an element of the symmetric semidefinite cone, and its eigenvalues may be nonreal. A norm bound must instead use singular values, for example \[\|X\|_2\le t\iff\begin{bmatrix}tI&X\\X^{\mathsf T}&tI\end{bmatrix}\succeq0.\] Thus symmetry cannot be omitted from eigenvalue-to-LMI rewrites.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eigenvalue LMIs require symmetric or Hermitian matrices; nonsymmetric matrices generally require singular-value block LMIs instead.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=X^{\mathsf T}\) is required for \(\lambda_{\max}(X)\le t\iff tI-X\succeq0\)

children.title: Sign Declarations

knowledge_statements.title: Sign Declarations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound sign metadata for expressions in disciplined convex modeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sign declaration for an expression \(e:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is a certified range assertion of one of the forms \(e(x)\ge0\), \(e(x)\le0\), or \(e(x)=0\) for every \(x\in D\). The corresponding metadata values are nonnegative, nonpositive, and zero; unknown means that none has been certified. A declaration is sound only if the asserted inequality holds throughout the modeled domain, not merely at a candidate solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sign metadata certifies that an expression is nonnegative, nonpositive, or zero everywhere on its modeled domain; otherwise its sign remains unknown.
assumptions_latex: \(e:D\to\mathbb{R}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sign}(e)\) records a domain-wide certified range assertion

children.title: Positivity Declarations
children.top_down_role: Strictly positive annotations needed by positive-domain constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Positivity Declarations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict and nonstrict positivity metadata and their domain consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an expression \(e:D\to\mathbb{R}\), a nonnegative declaration certifies \(e(x)\ge0\) for every \(x\in D\), whereas a strictly positive declaration certifies \(e(x)>0\) for every \(x\in D\). These declarations are not interchangeable: \(\log(e)\), reciprocal atoms restricted to the positive branch, and positive-denominator fractional rewrites require \(e>0\) on their effective domains, while \(\sqrt{e}\) permits \(e=0\). A modeling system may encode strict positivity through an atom's open effective domain rather than through a closed conic constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegativity permits zero, whereas strict positivity excludes it; logarithms, positive-branch reciprocals, and positive-denominator rewrites require the stronger domain assertion.
assumptions_latex: \(e:D\to\mathbb{R}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e>0\) implies \(e\ge0\), but \(e\ge0\) alone does not certify an atom or rewrite whose effective domain requires \(e>0\)

children.title: Monotonicity Refinement
children.top_down_role: Improved composition analysis enabled by stronger sign metadata.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of a positive-region monotonicity tag without certified range containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex outer function \(f(t)=t^2\) is nondecreasing only on \([0,\infty)\). The inner function \(g(x)=x^2-1\) is convex but takes negative values. Consequently \(f(g(x))=(x^2-1)^2\) is not convex on \(\mathbb R\), since its second derivative is \(12x^2-4\), which is negative near zero. Thus the nondecreasing tag cannot be used without certifying \(g(x)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squaring a convex inner expression need not preserve convexity when the inner expression leaves the nonnegative region on which squaring is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(\mathbb R)\nsubseteq[0,\infty)\quad\text{and}\quad f\circ g\text{ is not convex on }\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Outside the Monotonicity Region

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Argument-wise monotonicity and curvature propagation after certified region containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) have certified curvature, and let \(R\subseteq D\) contain every attainable tuple \(g(x)=(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\). Argument \(i\) is nondecreasing on \(R\) when \(u_i\le v_i\) and \(u_{-i}=v_{-i}\) imply \(f(u)\le f(v)\), and nonincreasing when the inequality reverses. If \(f\) is convex, \(f\circ g\) is DCP-certified convex when each \(g_i\) is affine, or \(f\) is nondecreasing in argument \(i\) on \(R\) and \(g_i\) is convex, or \(f\) is nonincreasing there and \(g_i\) is concave. For concave \(f\), interchange convex with concave in these inner requirements. A restricted tag may be used only after metadata certifies \(g(x)\in R\) throughout the modeled domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted monotonicity can drive the standard DCP composition rule only after all attainable argument tuples are certified to remain in the supporting region.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has certified convex or concave curvature.
\(g(x)\in R\subseteq D\) throughout the modeled domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated argument-wise curvature and monotonicity conditions certify the curvature of \(f\circ g\).

notation.meaning: all coordinates of u except coordinate i
region supporting the refined monotonicity tags

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Domain DCP Monotonicity Refinement
Monotonicity Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Argument-wise monotonicity metadata used by a DCP composition checker.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an atom \(f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) have known curvature and let \(R_i\subseteq D\) contain every attainable argument tuple. Its metadata may refine the monotonicity of argument \(i\) to nondecreasing on \(R_i\) when \(u_i\le v_i\) and \(u_{-i}=v_{-i}\) imply \(f(u)\le f(v)\); nonincreasing is defined by the reversed inequality. A composition \(f(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\) may use this refined tag only after the inferred domains and signs of all \(g_j\) establish membership in the declared region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A checker may use restricted-domain monotonicity only after inferred argument metadata proves that every attainable argument tuple lies in the region where that monotonicity holds.
assumptions_latex: \(f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) has certified curvature.
\((g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\in R_i\) throughout the modeled domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The argument-wise monotonicity tag is valid for the stated composition on its modeled domain.

notation.meaning: all coordinates of u except coordinate i
region supporting the refined monotonicity tag

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restricted-domain monotonicity principle fits the leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no source supports the DCP-specific conditions under which refined metadata may be used.

children.title: Declared-Sign Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between declared signs and admissible values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary distinction between sign assertions and domain-restricting declarations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e:D\to\mathbb R\), let \(S_{\mathrm{dec}}\subseteq\{-,0,+\}\) be a declared sign set, and let \(\Sigma(e(D))\) be the actual signs attained by \(e\) on \(D\). If the declaration is an assertion about the existing domain, it is sound exactly when \(\Sigma(e(D))\subseteq S_{\mathrm{dec}}\). Mere nonempty overlap with an inferred sign overapproximation is insufficient. If instead the declaration is an enforced domain restriction, it produces \(D_{\mathrm{new}}=\{x\in D:\operatorname{sgn}(e(x))\in S_{\mathrm{dec}}\}\), and it is feasible exactly when \(D_{\mathrm{new}}\ne\varnothing\). A checker must not interchange these two semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sign assertion must contain every actually attained sign. A domain-restricting declaration instead intersects the domain and is consistent when that restricted domain is nonempty; overlap with a coarse inferred sign set proves neither fact.
assumptions_latex: \(e:D\to\mathbb R\).
\(S_{\mathrm{dec}}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Assertion soundness}\iff\Sigma(e(D))\subseteq S_{\mathrm{dec}};\qquad \text{restriction feasibility}\iff D_{\mathrm{new}}\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: set of signs actually attained by e over D
domain remaining after an enforced sign restriction

knowledge_statements.title: Declared-Sign Consistency by Declaration Semantics

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Overlap Does Not Validate a Sign Assertion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to consistency based only on overlap with coarse inferred signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e(x)=x\) on \(D=[-1,1]\). Its actual and coarse inferred sign sets may both be \(\{-,0,+\}\). The declaration \(e\ge0\) corresponds to \(S_{\mathrm{dec}}=\{0,+\}\), whose intersection with the inferred set is nonempty, yet the assertion is false on every \(x<0\). If interpreted as a restriction, the same declaration instead changes the domain to \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For e(x)=x on [-1,1], a nonnegative declaration overlaps the possible signs but is false as an assertion; only as a domain restriction does it yield [0,1].
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{\mathrm{inf}}\cap S_{\mathrm{dec}}\ne\varnothing\not\Rightarrow e(x)\ge0\text{ for all }x\in D.
knowledge_statements.title: Overlap Does Not Validate a Sign Assertion
Declared-Sign Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency predicate for user-declared and structurally inferred scalar signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a scalar expression's possible signs by a nonempty set \(S_{\mathrm{inf}}\subseteq\{-,0,+\}\), inferred from its construction and domain, and represent its declared sign by \(S_{\mathrm{dec}}\subseteq\{-,0,+\}\). The declaration is consistent precisely when \(S_{\mathrm{inf}}\cap S_{\mathrm{dec}}\ne\varnothing\). After accepting it, the checker may refine the sign set to \(S_{\mathrm{new}}=S_{\mathrm{inf}}\cap S_{\mathrm{dec}}\). An empty intersection is a metadata contradiction and cannot certify any composition depending on that declaration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sign declaration is consistent exactly when it overlaps the expression's inferred possible signs; acceptance replaces the inferred set by their intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(S_{\mathrm{inf}}\ne\varnothing\) and \(S_{\mathrm{dec}}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistency holds if and only if \(S_{\mathrm{inf}}\cap S_{\mathrm{dec}}\ne\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intersection test is valid only if declared signs are enforced admissible-sign restrictions. A source is needed to establish those declaration semantics; mere overlap with an inferred overapproximation would not by itself validate an assertion.

children.title: Symmetry Declarations
children.top_down_role: Annotations identifying symmetric or Hermitian matrix structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Declarations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-variable symmetry as a structural domain declaration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real matrix expression \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), a symmetry declaration restricts its domain to the linear subspace \(\mathbb S^n=\{Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}:Y=Y^{\mathsf T}\}\). Equivalently, the declaration imposes \(X_{ij}=X_{ji}\) for every \(i,j\). The declaration supplies structural metadata and does not, by itself, imply positive or negative semidefiniteness, entrywise sign, or diagonal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declaring a square real matrix symmetric restricts it to matrices equal to their transpose, without asserting definiteness or entrywise signs.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), equivalently \(X=X^{\mathsf T}\).

source_refs.locator: 2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complex analogue of a real symmetry declaration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\), a Hermitian declaration restricts \(X\) to \(\mathbb H^n=\{Y:Y=Y^*\}\). Equivalently, \(X_{ij}=\overline{X_{ji}}\) for every \(i,j\), so every diagonal entry is real. For real matrices this reduces to \(X=X^{\mathsf T}\). Hermitian structure alone implies neither definiteness nor entrywise sign restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complex matrix is Hermitian exactly when it equals its conjugate transpose; real symmetry is the real specialization.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\in\mathbb H^n\iff X=X^*\iff X_{ij}=\overline{X_{ji}}\text{ for all }i,j.
knowledge_statements.title: Hermitian Symmetry Declaration

children.title: Definiteness Declarations
children.top_down_role: Annotations identifying positive or negative semidefinite matrix structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Definiteness Declarations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loewner-order declarations for real symmetric matrix expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), the declarations positive semidefinite, positive definite, negative semidefinite, and negative definite mean, respectively, \(z^{\mathsf T}Xz\ge0\), \(z^{\mathsf T}Xz>0\), \(z^{\mathsf T}Xz\le0\), and \(z^{\mathsf T}Xz<0\) for every nonzero \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). They are denoted \(X\succeq0\), \(X\succ0\), \(X\preceq0\), and \(X\prec0\). Each definiteness declaration includes symmetry and restricts the matrix domain accordingly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Definiteness declarations constrain every quadratic form of a symmetric matrix to have the declared weak or strict sign.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The declared Loewner inequality holds exactly when the corresponding quadratic-form inequality holds for every nonzero \(z\in\mathbb R^n\).

children.title: Spectral Analysis Refinement
children.top_down_role: Improved spectral recognition enabled by matrix metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Analysis Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation of symmetric-matrix spectral bounds into modeling metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) and let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\) satisfy \(\alpha\le\beta\) and \(\alpha I\preceq X\preceq\beta I\). Then \(\alpha\le\lambda_i(X)\le\beta\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Consequently, \(\alpha\ge0\) certifies \(X\succeq0\), \(\alpha>0\) certifies \(X\succ0\), \(\beta\le0\) certifies \(X\preceq0\), and \(\beta<0\) certifies \(X\prec0\). A modeling checker may propagate only conclusions justified by certified spectral bounds; an unknown bound yields no corresponding definiteness refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified lower and upper eigenvalue bounds provide the stated sufficient refinements of matrix definiteness metadata; absent a certified bound, the associated refinement is unavailable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^n\).
\(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\), \(\alpha\le\beta\), and \(\alpha I\preceq X\preceq\beta I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(\alpha\le\lambda_i(X)\le\beta\), and the stated endpoint conditions provide sufficient definiteness certificates.

children.title: Semidefinite Domain Refinement
children.top_down_role: Narrowing of admissible matrix domains through definiteness metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Domain Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of affine symmetric matrices to semidefinite cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=F_0+\sum_{k=1}^p x_kF_k\), where \(F_k\in\mathbb S^n\). Refining the domain of \(F(x)\) to the positive semidefinite cone is the constraint \(F(x)\in\mathbb S_+^n\), equivalently \(F(x)\succeq0\), or \(z^{\mathsf T}F(x)z\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). The feasible parameter set \(\{x\in\mathbb R^p:F(x)\succeq0\}\) is convex. Negative-semidefinite refinement is obtained by applying the same condition to \(-F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine symmetric matrix is restricted to the semidefinite cone by a Loewner inequality, producing a convex feasible set of parameters.
assumptions_latex: \(F_k\in\mathbb S^n\) for \(k=0,\ldots,p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)\in\mathbb S_+^n\iff F(x)\succeq0\iff z^{\mathsf T}F(x)z\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), and the feasible set is convex.

notation.meaning: cone of real positive-semidefinite n-by-n matrices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict positive- and negative-definite affine-matrix domains and their distinction from fixed-margin closed LMIs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb S^n\) be affine. The sets \(\{x:F(x)\succ0\}\) and \(\{x:F(x)\prec0\}\) are convex and open. Moreover, \(F(x)\succ0\iff\lambda_{\min}(F(x))>0\iff(\exists\varepsilon>0)\ F(x)\succeq\varepsilon I\), with the analogous statement for negative definiteness. For any fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), \(F(x)\succeq\varepsilon I\) is a closed semidefinite constraint sufficient for, but generally not equivalent to, \(F(x)\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict definiteness gives an open convex affine-matrix domain. A fixed positive eigenvalue margin is a stronger closed LMI and is not an exact replacement in general.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb S^n\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x)\succ0\iff\lambda_{\min}(F(x))>0\iff(\exists\varepsilon>0)\,F(x)\succeq\varepsilon I.

notation.meaning: identity matrix of the appropriate order

children.title: Matrix-Attribute Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility among matrix values, symmetry metadata, and definiteness metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Attribute Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint satisfiability of declared matrix structure and definiteness attributes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A_1,\ldots,\mathcal A_r\subseteq\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be the sets represented by declared matrix attributes. The declarations are consistent exactly when \(\bigcap_{j=1}^r\mathcal A_j\ne\varnothing\). For example, a positive-definite declaration requires \(m=n\), symmetry, and strictly positive eigenvalues; it is inconsistent with a negative-semidefinite declaration because no symmetric matrix satisfies both \(X\succ0\) and \(X\preceq0\). Accepted declarations refine the admissible domain to their intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix attributes are jointly consistent exactly when at least one matrix satisfies all declarations; accepted attributes restrict the domain to that intersection.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\mathcal A_j\) denotes the matrix set defined by one declaration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistency holds if and only if \(\bigcap_{j=1}^r\mathcal A_j\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: matrix set allowed by declaration j

source_refs.locator: 2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility, forced equality, implication, and redundancy among weak and strict definiteness declarations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), the simultaneous declarations \(X\succeq0\) and \(X\preceq0\) are consistent exactly when \(X=0\). The pairs \(X\succ0\) with \(X\preceq0\), and \(X\prec0\) with \(X\succeq0\), are inconsistent. Moreover, \(X\succ0\Rightarrow X\succeq0\) and \(X\prec0\Rightarrow X\preceq0\), so adding the corresponding same-sign weak declaration is redundant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposite weak definiteness declarations force the zero matrix; a strict declaration conflicts with the opposite weak declaration and subsumes its same-sign weak declaration.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\succeq0\land X\preceq0\iff X=0\), \(X\succ0\Rightarrow X\succeq0\), and \(X\prec0\Rightarrow X\preceq0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Definiteness Compatibility Consequences

children.title: Domain-Specific Atom Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection of atom branches whose global classifications match the intended domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when metadata do not certify that all attainable arguments remain in the selected branch's valid region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If some attainable argument \(u\in g(C)\) lies outside the region on which the selected branch agrees with the intended function, the branch substitution is not equivalent: it may exclude that point through an implicit domain restriction or assign it different extended-value semantics. Pointwise agreement on only a sampled or nominal subset of \(g(C)\) is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branch is invalid when any attainable argument escapes its agreement domain; checking only nominal or sampled arguments does not certify equivalence.
assumptions_latex: The intended model admits an argument \(u\in g(C)\) outside the branch's agreement region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(C)\nsubseteq\{u:f_j(u)=f(u)\}\Rightarrow f_j\circ g\) is not an equivalent substitution on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Domain Escape

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection of a certified atom branch whose extended-value semantics agree with the intended function on every attainable argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be the modeled domain, let \(g(C)\) be the attainable argument set, and let \(f_j:D_j\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a certified atom branch. Selecting branch \(j\) preserves the intended function only if its extended-value semantics agree with that function on every point of \(g(C)\); for a real-valued intended function this requires \(g(C)\subseteq D_j\). The branch is admissible for disciplined-convex certification only when its declared curvature and argument-wise monotonicity also validate the composition with \(g\). Agreement of two branches on \(g(C)\) makes them interchangeable for this model, even if they differ elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an atom branch only when it agrees with the intended function on every attainable argument and its global metadata validates the composition; branches agreeing on the attainable range are model-equivalent there.
assumptions_latex: \(g(C)\) is contained in the region where the selected branch has the intended extended-value semantics.
The selected branch's certified composition rule applies to \(g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected branch represents the intended function on \(C\) and is admissible for disciplined-convex certification.

notation.meaning: effective domain of certified atom branch j

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Correct Atom-Branch Selection
Domain-Specific Atom Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Choosing a globally certified atom branch whose domain contains all attainable arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a mathematical function has certified atom branches \(f_j:D_j\to\mathbb R\), each with fixed curvature and argument-wise monotonicity metadata. For an argument expression \(g(x)\) on modeled domain \(C\), branch \(j\) is admissible only if \(g(C)\subseteq D_j\) and its metadata makes the composition \(f_j\circ g\) satisfy the DCP composition rule. If several branches agree pointwise on \(g(C)\), selecting any admissible branch preserves the modeled function; selecting a branch whose domain does not contain \(g(C)\) is invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an atom branch only when every attainable argument lies in its certified domain and its global curvature and monotonicity tags validate the composition.
assumptions_latex: \(g(C)\subseteq D_j\).
The selected branch's certified composition rule applies on \(D_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The branch represents the intended function on \(C\) and is admissible for DCP certification.

notation.meaning: certified domain of atom branch j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The branch-selection principle fits the node, but its library-specific notions of certified branches, global metadata, and DCP admissibility have no cited support.

children.title: Extension-Based Reformulation
children.top_down_role: Routes for preserving reusable structure when ordinary source rewrites are insufficient.

children.title: Trusted Custom-Atom Route
children.top_down_role: Library extension for recurring functions with established convex semantics.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates metadata unsoundness from graph-implementation inexactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Incorrect curvature or monotonicity metadata can cause a disciplined-composition checker to accept a nonconvex composition. An inexact graph implementation instead changes the projected feasible set even when the metadata are correct. Passing metadata checks therefore does not compensate for an inexact graph, and graph exactness does not compensate for false metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: False metadata can make certification unsound, while an inexact graph can change the modeled problem; both obligations must hold independently.
assumptions_latex: A custom atom is used through both semantic metadata and a graph canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{sound registration}\Rightarrow\text{sound metadata}\land\text{exact graph implementation}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unsound Custom-Atom Registration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Framework-independent soundness requirements for encapsulating a recurring function as a trusted disciplined-convex atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be registered as a custom atom. Sound use requires its declared effective domain, curvature, sign, and argument-wise monotonicity to be valid, and its canonicalization to project exactly to the appropriate epigraph when \(f\) is convex or hypograph when \(f\) is concave. Compositions containing the atom must then satisfy the same disciplined-composition rules as compositions of built-in atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A custom atom is sound only when its semantic metadata are valid, its graph implementation is exact, and ordinary disciplined-composition rules still govern every use.
assumptions_latex: The atom's declared metadata are valid on its effective domain.
The projected canonicalization equals the declared epigraph or hypograph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The registered atom preserves both disciplined-convex certification and the represented function when used according to its declared composition rules.

notation.meaning: declared effective domain of the custom atom

knowledge_statements.title: Sound Custom-Atom Contract
Trusted Custom-Atom Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension of a DCP library by a pre-certified atom implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A custom atom \(f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is trusted only when its domain, curvature, sign, argument-wise monotonicity, and graph implementation are declared and independently validated. For a convex atom, the implementation must represent \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(u,t):u\in D,\ f(u)\le t\}\) by certified affine and conic constraints; for a concave atom it must analogously represent the hypograph. Once registered, a composition using \(f\) is accepted only through the same DCP argument rules applied to built-in atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A custom atom becomes trusted only after its semantics and graph representation are validated, after which ordinary DCP composition rules still govern its use.
assumptions_latex: The declared graph representation is exact on \(D\).
The atom metadata has been independently validated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uses of \(f\) may be certified by its registered metadata and exact graph implementation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Custom-atom trust and canonicalization protocols are implementation-sensitive. No source establishes that all required metadata, validation, and exact graph conditions have the stated form.

children.title: Explicit Graph-Modeling Route
children.top_down_role: Source-level use of established epigraph, hypograph, or cone representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Graph-Modeling Route
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replacement of an unsupported atom by an exact epigraph, hypograph, or cone model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be convex and suppose a convex set \(G\subseteq D\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^q\) satisfies \((u,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) if and only if there exists \(y\in\mathbb R^q\) with \((u,t,y)\in G\). In any minimization model where \(t\) upper-bounds \(f(u)\), the unsupported relation \(f(u)\le t\) may be replaced by \((u,t,y)\in G\) with auxiliary variable \(y\). A concave hypograph relation is treated analogously with the inequality reversed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace an unsupported function inequality by an exact convex graph representation with auxiliary variables; projection must reproduce the original epigraph or hypograph.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(D\).
The projection of \(G\) onto \((u,t)\) equals \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(u)\le t\iff\exists y\in\mathbb R^q:(u,t,y)\in G\).

source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry
source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251

source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry
source_witnesses.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes an equivalent explicit graph model from an outer relaxation or inner restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{(u,t):\exists y\; (u,t,y)\in G\}\). Replacing \(f(u)\le t\) by \((u,t,y)\in G\) is exact precisely when \(P=\operatorname{epi}f\), including the effective-domain restrictions of \(f\). If \(P\supsetneq\operatorname{epi}f\), the substitution is an outer relaxation; if \(P\subsetneq\operatorname{epi}f\), it is an inner restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted graph substitution is equivalent only when its projection is exactly the intended epigraph, including its domain; a strict superset relaxes the model and a strict subset restricts it.
assumptions_latex: \(G\subseteq\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^q\)
\(P=\operatorname{proj}_{u,t}G\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{epi}f\) is necessary and sufficient for exact epigraph substitution.

notation.meaning: projection of the lifted graph set onto the original argument and level coordinates

children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating mathematical convexity, grammatical recognition, representability, and numerical solution.

children.title: DCP Incompleteness
children.top_down_role: The boundary between convex models and models recognized by a fixed grammar and atom library.

children.title: Convex but Non-DCP Expressions
children.top_down_role: Convex expressions rejected because their written composition is not grammatical.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DCP Recognition Is Sufficient but Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between semantic convexity and recognition of a written expression by a fixed sound DCP grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{DCP}}\) be the written expressions certified convex by a fixed sound DCP grammar, and let \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{cvx}}\) be the written expressions denoting convex extended-real-valued functions. Then \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{DCP}}\subseteq\mathcal E_{\mathrm{cvx}}\), and the inclusion can be strict. Consequently, rejection by that grammar does not imply nonconvexity of the denoted function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sound DCP grammar certifies only convex expressions, but it need not recognize every written expression that denotes a convex function.
assumptions_latex: The grammar is fixed and sound for its registered atoms, domains, and composition rules.
Classification applies to written expression trees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{DCP}}\subseteq\mathcal E_{\mathrm{cvx}}\), possibly strictly.

notation.meaning: Written expressions certified convex by the fixed grammar

knowledge_statements.title: DCP Recognition Is Sufficient but Not Necessary
Convex but Non-DCP Expressions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation between mathematical convexity and acceptance of a written DCP expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The scalar function \(h(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}\) is convex on \(\mathbb R\), since \(h''(x)=(1+x^2)^{-3/2}>0\). Nevertheless, the written composition \(\sqrt{1+x^2}\) is rejected by the standard DCP composition rule: the square-root atom is concave and nondecreasing, while its argument \(1+x^2\) is convex rather than concave. The equivalent expression \(\lVert(1,x)\rVert_2\) uses a convex norm atom applied to an affine argument and is DCP-certifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex function square root of one plus x squared fails DCP in that syntax, although its equivalent Euclidean-norm representation is accepted.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R\).
Standard DCP curvature and monotonicity rules are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is convex, but \(\sqrt{1+x^2}\) is non-DCP while \(\lVert(1,x)\rVert_2\) is DCP-certifiable.

notation.meaning: the function defined by the displayed square-root expression

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example is mathematically standard and the counterexample kind fits, but the syntax-dependent DCP acceptance claims lack a source. The second-derivative justification is also proof text and should be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

children.title: Atom-Library Incompleteness
children.top_down_role: Recognition failures caused by unavailable trusted atoms or representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite toy library demonstrating library-relative incompleteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalar library generated from affine functions by finite pointwise maxima and affine composition produces only convex polyhedral functions. The convex function \(x\mapsto x^2\) is not polyhedral, so neither it nor its epigraph is expressible in that library. Adding a square atom or an exact nonpolyhedral graph representation removes this failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A library restricted to polyhedral convex expressions cannot recognize a convex quadratic.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many affine pieces may occur
No square atom or nonpolyhedral graph representation is available
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^2\notin\mathcal E(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{aff,max}})\quad\text{although }x\mapsto x^2\text{ is convex}.

notation.meaning: Library generated by affine functions and finite maxima.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Max Library Misses a Quadratic

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp exclusion hypothesis for library-relative nonexpressibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Absence of a primitive atom named \(f\) does not establish that \(f\) is outside a trusted library: other atoms may compose to it, or an exact graph lift may represent it. Nonexpressibility requires excluding every construction admitted by the fixed grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing primitive name proves no incompleteness if existing atoms can compose or lift to the same function.
assumptions_latex: Expressibility includes every construction licensed by the fixed grammar
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
f
otin\mathcal L_{\mathrm{primitive}}
ot\Rightarrow f
otin\mathcal E(\mathcal L).
knowledge_statements.title: Primitive Absence Alone Is Insufficient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition behavior when trusted atoms, graph representations, and rules are added.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathcal L_2\) retains every atom, exact graph representation, metadata declaration, and rule of \(\mathcal L_1\), then \(\mathcal E(\mathcal L_1)\subseteq\mathcal E(\mathcal L_2)\). Such extension can enlarge recognition but does not change the mathematical curvature of represented functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conservative trusted-library extension preserves old derivations and can only enlarge the recognized class.
assumptions_latex: The extension retains all old declarations and rules
All certification rules remain sound
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal L_1\subseteq\mathcal L_2\Longrightarrow\mathcal E(\mathcal L_1)\subseteq\mathcal E(\mathcal L_2).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Under Trusted-Library Extension
Atom-Library Incompleteness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition boundary imposed by the finite trusted atom and graph library.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L\) be a trusted DCP library and let \(\mathcal E(\mathcal L)\) be the expressions generated from its atoms by its certified composition rules. If a convex function \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) has neither an atom in \(\mathcal L\) nor an exact graph representation expressible using \(\mathcal L\), then the direct expression \(f(x)\) lies outside \(\mathcal E(\mathcal L)\) and cannot be certified by that library. This failure concerns recognition relative to \(\mathcal L\), not the mathematical convexity of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function can remain uncertifiable when the trusted library contains neither the function nor an expressible exact graph representation of it.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\).
No certified atom or exact graph representation for \(f\) is expressible in \(\mathcal L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\notin\mathcal E(\mathcal L)\), so library-relative DCP certification fails despite convexity.

notation.meaning: expressions certifiable from the library's rules

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The library-relative failure boundary needs a source and a sharper hypothesis: absence of a primitive atom or named graph representation does not exclude an equivalent expression composed from existing atoms unless the definition of expressibility explicitly covers all such constructions.

children.title: Conservative Local Inference
children.top_down_role: Unresolved metadata produced by deliberately local compositional analysis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable witness for a successful local DCP judgment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A successful local certification is a finite derivation tree whose leaves carry trusted declarations and whose internal nodes cite applicable composition rules with certified child metadata. Bottom-up checking certifies the root. Failure to construct such a tree is inconclusive about actual convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid local-rule derivation certifies acceptance; absence of one is not a nonconvexity certificate.
assumptions_latex: Leaf declarations and rules are trusted and sound
The expression tree is finite
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{valid derivation for }E\Longrightarrow\operatorname{DCP}(E),\qquad\text{no derivation}\not\Longrightarrow f_E\text{ nonconvex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Derivation Tree Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity of bottom-up inference on an expression tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an expression tree with \(N\) nodes, if each atom has bounded arity and its metadata transfer rule is checked in \(O(1)\) time, one postorder traversal computes all local metadata and checks a derivation in \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) stored annotations, or \(O(h)\) traversal stack space for tree height \(h\) when annotations need not be retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under bounded-cost atom rules, local DCP inference is linear in expression-tree size.
assumptions_latex: The expression is represented as a tree with \(N\) nodes
Atom arity and transfer-rule cost are uniformly bounded
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(N)=O(N),\qquad S(N)=O(N)\text{ annotations, with traversal stack }O(h).
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Pass Local-Inference Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of more precise sign, domain, or curvature metadata in a monotone analyzer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order abstract metadata by precision, with \(m_1\preceq m_2\) meaning that \(m_1\) is at least as precise. If each transfer rule \(F\) is monotone, soundly refining every child cannot make the inferred parent less precise. Refinement may resolve an inconclusive composition but cannot license a rule whose hypotheses remain false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a monotone analyzer, sound metadata refinement can improve or preserve a conclusion but cannot justify unsupported reasoning.
assumptions_latex: Transfer rules are monotone in the precision order
Every refinement remains sound
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m_i'\preceq m_i\ \forall i\Longrightarrow F(m_1',\ldots,m_k')\preceq F(m_1,\ldots,m_k).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Under Sound Metadata Refinement

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal representation of deliberately local metadata propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local analyzer maps each expression subtree to abstract curvature, sign, monotonicity, and domain metadata. Each atom transfer rule consumes only its declaration and immediate-child metadata. When distinct concrete possibilities share an abstract state, their least sound abstraction may be \(\mathrm{unknown}\); loss of relational information therefore produces conservative conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local DCP analysis soundly abstracts expression behavior, and merged possibilities can yield unknown metadata.
assumptions_latex: The metadata domain has sound concretization semantics
Transfer rules are sound and use only immediate-child metadata
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma(\widehat m(E))\supseteq\{m(f_E)\},\quad\text{and abstraction joins may strictly enlarge }\gamma(\widehat m(E)).

notation.meaning: Abstract metadata inferred for expression E.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Analysis as Abstract Interpretation

assumptions_latex: The expression tree uses a fixed atom library with declared curvature, sign, monotonicity, and domain metadata.
Certification applies only local composition rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure to infer convexity does not imply nonconvexity of the represented function.

notation.meaning: Function represented by expression tree E

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: DCP composition analysis is deliberately sufficient rather than complete
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates local syntactic certification from global convexity of the represented function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be an expression tree representing \(f_E:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). A conservative local inference system assigns curvature using only atom metadata and the certified properties of immediate children. Its soundness requirement is \(\operatorname{DCP}(E)\Rightarrow f_E\) is convex on \(D\). Completeness is not required: there may exist an \(E\) for which \(f_E\) is convex on \(D\), while some local composition rule is inconclusive and hence \(\operatorname{DCP}(E)\) is false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local DCP analysis may reject a convex expression because its rules are sufficient for convexity, not necessary.
knowledge_statements.title: Conservative Local Inference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary statement is mathematically standard and fits the container, but it has no inspectable citation supporting the sound-but-incomplete characterization of local DCP inference.

children.title: Representation-Sensitive Acceptance
children.top_down_role: Equivalent mathematical models receiving different certification outcomes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Certification Is Not Invariant Under Expression Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-sensitive certification by a fixed syntactic grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_1\equiv E_2\) mean that two expressions have the same domain and denote the same function there, and let \(C_G(E)\in\{0,1\}\) denote certification by a fixed grammar \(G\). In general, \(E_1\equiv E_2\) does not imply \(C_G(E_1)=C_G(E_2)\), because certification is determined from expression trees and registered rules rather than all semantic identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mathematically equivalent expressions need not receive the same result from a fixed syntactic certification system.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is fixed, sound, and potentially incomplete.
Equivalence includes equality of domains and represented functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_1\equiv E_2\not\Rightarrow C_G(E_1)=C_G(E_2)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Certification Is Not Invariant Under Expression Equivalence

assumptions_latex: Both expressions are interpreted over \(x\in\mathbb R\).
The grammar recognizes affine vector construction and the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent expressions can receive different DCP certification outcomes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical DCP example of representation-dependent certification
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a standard scalar example of equivalent expressions with unequal syntactic certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb R\), \[E_1(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}=\lVert(1,x)\rVert_2=E_2(x).\] Thus both expressions represent the same convex function. A DCP grammar may reject \(E_1\) because the outer square root is concave and increasing while its argument is convex, yet accept \(E_2\) because the Euclidean norm is convex and is applied to an affine vector. Hence DCP acceptance is a property of the expression tree and available atom rules, not solely of the represented function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same convex function may be rejected as a square-root composition but accepted when written as a norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Acceptance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and appropriately representation-sensitive, but no source is cited for the grammar-dependent acceptance claims.

children.title: Semantic Modeling Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by inconsistency between symbolic declarations and intended mathematics.

children.title: Hidden or Inconsistent Domains
children.top_down_role: Conflicts involving atom-implied restrictions and declared attributes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete inconsistency between a declared variable domain and an atom-implied domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\) is declared nonpositive and the model contains \(\log x\), then \(D_0=(-\infty,0]\) while \(\operatorname{dom}\log=(0,\infty)\), so \[D_0\cap\operatorname{dom}\log=\varnothing.\] With the logarithm's domain enforced, the model is infeasible. Omitting that domain restriction instead produces a different encoded model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonpositive variable used as the argument of a logarithm has no domain-feasible value; dropping the logarithm's positivity requirement changes the model.
assumptions_latex: x\in(-\infty,0]
\operatorname{dom}\log=(0,\infty)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (-\infty,0]\cap(0,\infty)=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Empty Pulled-Back Atom Domain
Hidden or Inconsistent Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers feasibility conflicts between declared attributes and effective domains of composed atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_0\) be the declared domain of the decision variable \(x\). For each atom occurrence \(\phi_i(a_i(x))\), let \(\operatorname{dom}\phi_i\) be the atom's effective domain and \(a_i\) its argument map. Semantic consistency requires \[\left\{x\in D_0: a_i(x)\in\operatorname{dom}\phi_i\text{ for every }i=1,\ldots,m\right\}\ne\varnothing.\] For example, \(\log(g(x))\) requires \(g(x)>0\), while \(-\log\det X\) requires \(X\succ0\). If declared attributes make these restrictions inconsistent, the modeled feasible set is empty; if an implementation omits an atom-implied restriction, the encoded problem does not represent the intended extended-valued model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declared attributes and the preimages of all atom effective domains must have a common feasible point, with each restriction applied to its atom's actual argument.
assumptions_latex: Each atom \(\phi_i\) is interpreted as an extended-valued function with an effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}\phi_i\).
Declared variable and parameter attributes are treated as semantic constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in D_0:a_i(x)\in\operatorname{dom}\phi_i\ \forall i\}\ne\varnothing\) is required for semantic consistency.

notation.meaning: Argument map for atom occurrence i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: extended-value atom semantics induce implicit domain constraints through argument-map preimages

children.title: Strict-Inequality Modeling
children.top_down_role: Topological and representational difficulties associated with strict constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal example showing that replacing a strict inequality by a non-strict one can change attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\inf_x x\) subject to \(-x<0\), the feasible set is \((0,\infty)\), the infimum is \(0\), and no minimizer exists. Replacing the constraint by \(-x\le0\) gives \([0,\infty)\), where \(x=0\) attains the same value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing x>0 to x≥0 preserves the infimum of minimizing x but creates a boundary optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x>0}x=\min_{x\ge0}x=0,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x>0}x=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Creates an Optimizer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equality of Strict and Closed Infima Under Density
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when closing a strict feasible set preserves value but may alter attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_{<}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(F_{\le}=\overline{F_{<}}\), and let \(f:F_{\le}\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. Then \[\inf_{x\in F_{<}}f(x)=\inf_{x\in F_{\le}}f(x).\] A minimizer of the closed problem may nevertheless lie in \(F_{\le}\setminus F_{<}\), so attainment need not be preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous objective has the same infimum on a set and its closure, although the closure may create a boundary minimizer.
assumptions_latex: F_{\le}=\overline{F_{<}}.
f\text{ is real-valued and continuous on }F_{\le}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{F_{<}}f=\inf_{F_{\le}}f,\quad\text{while attainment need not agree}.

notation.meaning: Closure of the strict feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Equality of Strict and Closed Infima Under Density

assumptions_latex: Optimization is over real variables.
The available conic representation uses closed non-strict inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing a strict inequality by its closed counterpart can change attainment, while a fixed positive margin changes the feasible set.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: strict feasible sets are generally open and are not exactly represented by closed cone inequalities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes strict feasibility, closure, and fixed-margin approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a continuous function \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), the constraint \(g(x)<0\) defines the generally open set \(F_{<}\). Replacing it by \(g(x)\le0\) yields the closure candidate and may introduce boundary points or an optimizer absent from \(F_{<}\). Replacing it by \(g(x)\le-\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon>0\), gives a closed inner approximation \(F_\varepsilon\subset F_{<}\) but changes the problem. Therefore strict inequalities require a problem-specific margin, normalization, or limiting interpretation; they cannot generally be encoded exactly by merely changing \(<\) to \(\le\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict constraints are generally open; closure may change attainment, while a positive margin defines a different, smaller feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Inequality Modeling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction among a strict feasible set, its closed relaxation, and a fixed-margin inner approximation is precise and fits the failure-boundary container, but it lacks an inspectable citation.

children.title: Invalid Parameter Attributes
children.top_down_role: Parameter values inconsistent with declared domains or matrix structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates checking a parameter assignment from modifying it to satisfy declared attributes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the set specified by a parameter's declared attributes and let \(p\notin S\). Replacing \(p\) by \(\widehat p\in S\), including by projection or clipping, produces the instance parameterized by \(\widehat p\); it does not establish that the supplied value satisfies \(p\in S\). Such repair is semantics-preserving only when the model explicitly defines the replacement map as part of its parameter semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting or clipping an invalid parameter normally changes the parameterized instance and is not validation of the supplied value.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is the intersection of the declared attribute sets}.
p\notin S.
\widehat p\in S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\mapsto\widehat p\text{ is a model modification unless that map is explicitly part of the model}.
knowledge_statements.title: Validation Is Not Parameter Repair

assumptions_latex: A parameter declaration specifies a domain or structural set \(S\).
A numerical value \(p\) is assigned before solving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assignment is valid exactly when \(p\in S\), including every declared numerical and structural property.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats signs, symmetry, definiteness, integrality, and shape as semantic parameter obligations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameter assignment is semantically valid if and only if \(p\in S\), where \(S\) is the intersection of all declared attribute sets. Thus a nonnegative parameter requires \(p\ge0\); a symmetric matrix parameter requires \(p=p^{\mathsf T}\); and a positive-semidefinite parameter requires a symmetric \(p\) satisfying \(z^{\mathsf T}pz\ge0\) for every conforming \(z\). An assignment violating any declared property is invalid even if dimensions match. Because parameter attributes may determine curvature, monotonicity, or canonicalization, silently accepting \(p\notin S\) invalidates the model's certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter value must satisfy every declared sign, shape, integrality, symmetry, and definiteness attribute before canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Parameter Attributes

children.title: Array Semantics Failure Family

children.title: Shape Compatibility Failures
children.top_down_role: Dimension mismatches among expressions, variables, parameters, or constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typing boundary between defined array semantics and disciplined curvature analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the operand-shape tuple of \(\phi(A_1,\ldots,A_k)\) lies outside the operator's declared signature after applying only permitted explicit broadcasting rules, the application denotes no expression in the modeling language. Curvature, sign, monotonicity, feasibility, and canonicalization metadata are therefore unavailable for that application; a DCP rule cannot certify a shape-invalid operator application.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator application must first have defined array semantics; curvature analysis cannot certify incompatible operand shapes.
assumptions_latex: Operator signatures are part of the expression type system.
Metadata analysis is defined only for well-formed expression nodes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{sh}(A_1),\ldots,\operatorname{sh}(A_k))\notin\Sigma_\phi\Rightarrow\phi(A_1,\ldots,A_k)\) is not a certifiable expression.
knowledge_statements.title: Shape Validity Precedes Curvature Certification

assumptions_latex: Every array expression has an ordered shape tuple.
An operator has a specified scalar, elementwise, matrix, or reduction signature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An operator application is defined only when operand shapes satisfy its signature or an explicitly specified broadcasting rule.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: array operators are defined on explicit shape signatures
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates mathematical operator domains from implementation-specific implicit broadcasting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi\) be an array operator with shape signature \(\Sigma_\phi\). The expression \(\phi(A_1,\ldots,A_k)\) is shape-compatible precisely when \((\operatorname{sh}(A_1),\ldots,\operatorname{sh}(A_k))\in\Sigma_\phi\), after applying only broadcasting transformations explicitly defined by the modeling language. For example, matrix multiplication of \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(B\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\) requires \(n=p\) and returns shape \((m,q)\). If the tuple is outside \(\Sigma_\phi\), the expression has no defined array semantics and must be rejected before curvature analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Array operands must satisfy the operator's exact shape signature after only explicitly defined broadcasting transformations.
knowledge_statements.title: Shape Compatibility Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The shape-signature condition is coherent and fits the leaf, but its language-dependent broadcasting and rejection requirements need a specific source.

children.title: Broadcasting Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Unclear or unintended array expansion across operands.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for removing ambiguity without prescribing a particular language convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For operand space \(V\) and target array space \(W\), a broadcast convention specifies a fixed expansion map \(B:V\to W\), typically by replicating entries along declared axes. The expression \(A+B(b)\) has determined broadcast semantics when the language or model selects a particular map \(B\). If two admissible maps \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) remain possible and produce different expanded values for some \(b\), the notation does not determine a unique function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Broadcasting is determined by a declared fixed expansion map; ambiguity remains when plausible maps can produce different expanded arrays.
assumptions_latex: Broadcasting uses fixed, data-independent entry replication.
The target output shape is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists b\in V:\ B_1(b)\ne B_2(b)\) for two unresolved admissible maps implies ambiguous broadcast semantics.

notation.meaning: Operand and target array value spaces

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Broadcast-Map Criterion

assumptions_latex: Operands have ordered shape tuples.
Broadcasting aligns dimensions according to a declared convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a unique declared expansion map, broadcasted expressions do not determine a unique mathematical function.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinct axis-alignment conventions can expand the same low-rank operand differently
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies nonuniqueness caused by unstated leading-axis versus trailing-axis alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider elementwise addition of \(A\in\mathbb R^{1\times n\times1}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\). Under trailing-axis alignment, \(b\) is interpreted with shape \((1,1,n)\), producing an array of shape \((1,n,n)\). Under alignment with the middle axis, it is interpreted with shape \((1,n,1)\), producing shape \((1,n,1)\). These expansions generally yield different arrays. Therefore a broadcasted operation is mathematically unambiguous only when the language fixes an alignment convention or the model supplies an explicit reshape identifying the intended axes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Implicit broadcasting is ambiguous when multiple axis expansions are plausible and produce different arrays or output shapes.
knowledge_statements.title: Broadcasting Ambiguity

children.title: Axis Alignment Errors
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by incompatible axis meanings or ordering.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic for whether exchanging semantically labeled axes preserves an array operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_\pi\) permute input axes and let \(P_{\pi'}\) be the corresponding declared output-axis permutation. Treating the permuted axes as interchangeable for an operation \(F\) is valid only when \(F(P_\pi X)=P_{\pi'}F(X)\) on the modeled domain. Equal axis lengths or equal resulting shapes do not establish this identity; if it fails, the interchange changes the modeled function while dimension checks may still pass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal-length axes are safely interchangeable for an operation only when the operation respects the corresponding labeled-axis permutation.
assumptions_latex: Input and output axes have declared semantic labels.
\(P_\pi\) and \(P_{\pi'}\) are fixed axis permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(P_\pi X)\ne P_{\pi'}F(X)\) implies that the proposed axis interchange is semantically invalid.
knowledge_statements.title: Permutation-Equivariance Test for Interchangeable Axes

assumptions_latex: A reduction or concatenation specifies an axis index.
Array axes are ordered and have fixed lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Choosing the wrong axis generally defines a different function, even when the resulting expression remains shape-valid.

notation.meaning: Matrix with row and column axes

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reductions over distinct ordered axes have different codomains and coordinate formulas
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers semantically wrong but potentially well-typed reductions and concatenations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), define row and column sums by \((R_1(X))_i=\sum_{j=1}^n X_{ij}\) and \((R_0(X))_j=\sum_{i=1}^m X_{ij}\). Then \(R_1(X)\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(R_0(X)\in\mathbb R^n\), and they encode different aggregations. If \(m=n\), both outputs even have the same shape, so shape checking alone cannot detect their interchange. Consequently, axis labels or indices are part of the mathematical model; an incorrect axis can yield a valid expression representing the wrong objective or constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wrong reduction axis can produce a well-typed expression with the wrong mathematical meaning, especially for square arrays.
knowledge_statements.title: Axis Alignment Errors

children.title: Bilinear Models
children.top_down_role: Models whose nonconvex structure arises from products of decision-dependent quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines continuous bilinear decision models and states their basic DCP failure mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bilinear model is an optimization model whose objective or constraints contain \(b(x,y)=x^{\mathsf T}By\), where \(x\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) are decision vectors and \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is fixed. The map is affine in either decision block when the other is fixed. If \(B\ne0\), it is neither jointly convex nor jointly concave on any nonempty open convex domain in \(\mathbb R^{m+n}\). Consequently, an unrestricted bilinear decision term lies outside the convex DCP grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear model contains a product between two decision blocks; separate affinity does not imply joint convexity or concavity.
assumptions_latex: The decision vectors are \(x\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(y\in\mathbb R^n\).
The fixed matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bilinear form \(x^{\mathsf T}By\) is neither jointly convex nor jointly concave on any nonempty open convex domain in \(\mathbb R^{m+n}\).

notation.meaning: Bilinear form in two decision blocks

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Outer-Product Lift of a Bilinear Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted representation isolating bilinearity in product identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(W=xy^{\mathsf T}\), \[x^{\mathsf T}By=\langle B,W\rangle.\] Thus a bilinear expression is affine in \(W\), while exactness requires the nonconvex graph identities \(W_{ij}=x_i y_j\). Dropping those identities or replacing them by convex envelopes produces a relaxation rather than an equivalent formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An outer-product lift makes a bilinear expression affine, but exactness remains in the nonconvex product identities.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^m\), \(y\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{\mathsf T}By=\langle B,xy^{\mathsf T}\rangle.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer-Product Lift of a Bilinear Form

knowledge_statements.statement_title: McCormick Convex Hull on a Rectangle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex hull of one bounded scalar bilinear graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and \(w=xy\), with finite bounds. The convex hull of the graph is defined by \[\begin{aligned}w&\geq \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\\w&\geq u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y,\\w&\leq u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\\w&\leq \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y.\end{aligned}\] Applied termwise to several products sharing variables, these inequalities generally give only a relaxation of the joint graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four McCormick inequalities give the exact convex hull of one scalar bilinear graph over a bounded rectangle.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x\leq x\leq u_x\) and \(\ell_y\leq y\leq u_y\) with finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed inequalities describe }\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,xy):x\in[\ell_x,u_x],y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\}.
knowledge_statements.title: McCormick Convex Hull on a Rectangle

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact alternating minimization can produce nonincreasing objective values in a blockwise feasible model, but its detailed convergence theory depends on the surrounding objective, constraints, and block-update policy.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial model has an objective and constraint functions of the form \[p(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in A}c_\alpha x^\alpha,\] where \(A\subset\mathbb N^n\) is finite, \(c_\alpha\in\mathbb R\), and \(x^\alpha=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha_i}\). Such a model belongs to convex DCP only when every objective and inequality has the required certified curvature and every equality is affine; otherwise it is a generally nonconvex polynomial optimization problem.

children.title: Indefinite-Quadratic Models
children.top_down_role: Quadratic models lacking the curvature required for continuous DCP certification.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite-Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines real quadratic models whose symmetric quadratic coefficient has mixed-sign spectrum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indefinite-quadratic model contains an objective or constraint function \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\), where \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(d\in\mathbb R\), with \(Q\) having at least one positive and at least one negative eigenvalue. Such a function is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^n\), so its unrestricted use as an objective or inequality lies outside the convex DCP grammar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite-quadratic model contains a quadratic whose symmetric coefficient matrix has both positive and negative eigenvalues, giving mixed curvature.
assumptions_latex: The decision variable is \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
The fixed matrix \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) has at least one positive and at least one negative eigenvalue.
The coefficients satisfy \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(d\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(q\) is neither convex nor concave on \(\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: Quadratic function with an indefinite quadratic coefficient

source_refs.locator: 2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Convex Analysis on Symmetric Matrices p. 13

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp unconstrained behavior of an indefinite quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Q\) has a negative eigenvalue, then \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\bigr)=-\infty.\] When \(Q\) is indefinite, every stationary point that exists is a saddle rather than a local minimum or maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unconstrained indefinite quadratic is unbounded below, and any stationary point is a saddle.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) has at least one positive and one negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}q(x)=-\infty,\qquad \nabla q(\bar x)=0\Rightarrow \bar x\text{ is a saddle}.
knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Indefinite Quadratic Unboundedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical curvature decomposition of an indefinite quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), write \(Q=Q_+-Q_-\), where \(Q_+,Q_-\succeq0\) are its positive and negative spectral parts. Then \[q(x)=\bigl(x^{\mathsf T}Q_+x+c^{\mathsf T}x+d\bigr)-x^{\mathsf T}Q_-x\] is a difference of two convex quadratic functions. This exact decomposition exposes but does not remove the original nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every indefinite quadratic has an exact spectral difference-of-convex decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q=g-h\text{ for convex quadratics }g,h.

notation.meaning: Positive-semidefinite positive and negative spectral parts of Q.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Difference-of-Convex Decomposition

children.title: Nonaffine-Equality Models
children.top_down_role: Equality-constrained nonlinear models outside the affine disciplined regime.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp semantic exception to the DCP rejection of nonaffine equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(h:D\to\mathbb R\) be convex and nonnegative. If \(\min_Dh=0\), then \[\{x\in D:h(x)=0\}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}h(x)\] is convex. Hence a rejected nonaffine equality can nevertheless define a convex set; for example, \(x^2=0\) defines \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative convex function's zero set is its convex minimizer set, so DCP rejection does not imply semantic nonconvexity.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is convex.
\(h\) is convex and nonnegative on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x\in D:h(x)=0\}\text{ is convex}.

notation.meaning: Set of minimizers of h over D.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Nonaffine Zero Sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary DCP equality syntax and its semantic nonconvexity risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Standard DCP accepts an equality only when its two sides are affine. Convexity of a nonaffine expression \(h\) does not make \(\{x:h(x)=0\}\) convex: for \(h(x)=x^2-1\), the zero set is \(\{-1,1\}\). Thus a nonaffine equality is outside ordinary DCP and may require elimination, an exact reformulation, relaxation, or a nonconvex framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DCP permits affine equalities; even a convex nonaffine function can have a nonconvex zero set.
assumptions_latex: The equality is imposed on a convex domain.
Ordinary DCP equality rules are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\text{ nonaffine}\Rightarrow h(x)=0\text{ is not DCP-admissible, and its feasible set need not be convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonaffine Equality DCP Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation and its ordinary-DCP obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For real-valued \(h\), \[h(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h(x)\leq0\ \text{and}\ -h(x)\leq0.\] On a convex domain both displayed inequalities are convex constraints only when \(h\) is both convex and concave, hence affine. Splitting a nonaffine equality into opposite inequalities therefore does not restore ordinary DCP admissibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality is two opposite inequalities, but both are convex constraints only for an affine function.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is real-valued on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h=0\text{ is representable by the two ordinary-DCP inequalities }h\leq0,-h\leq0\text{ only when }h\text{ is affine}.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Inequality Equality Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact substitution when an equality explicitly determines a variable block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an equality uniquely determines \(y\) as \(y=\phi(x)\), consistently replacing every occurrence of \(y\) by \(\phi(x)\) yields an equivalent reduced model. Feasible points correspond by \(x\mapsto(x,\phi(x))\). The elimination is exact, but a nonaffine \(\phi\) need not preserve convexity of the resulting compositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph-form nonlinear equality can be eliminated exactly, although the reduced model need not be convex.
assumptions_latex: The equality uniquely determines \(y\) as \(y=\phi(x)\).
Every occurrence and restriction involving \(y\) is substituted consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Original and reduced feasible points correspond bijectively, but reduced convexity requires a separate composition check}.

notation.meaning: Equality determining the eliminated variable block.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Nonlinear Equality Elimination

assumptions_latex: The equality constraint is \(h(x)=0\) on a convex domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
The DCP equality rule requires both sides to be affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonaffine equality is outside DCP and can define a nonconvex feasible set even when \(h\) is convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convexity is preserved by affine equalities but not by general convex-function level sets
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains why convexity of an equality expression does not make its zero-level set convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), an equality \(h(x)=0\) is admissible in standard DCP only when \(h\) is affine, equivalently when it can be written as equality of affine expressions. Convexity of \(h\) alone is insufficient because a zero-level set need not be convex. For example, with \(D=\mathbb R\) and \(h(x)=x^2-1\), the feasible set is \(F=\{-1,1\}\), which is nonconvex. A nonaffine equality therefore requires reformulation, elimination, relaxation, or a nonconvex modeling framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DCP permits affine equalities; a nonaffine equality can have a nonconvex zero-level set even when its function is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonaffine-Equality Models

children.title: Mixed-Integer Convex Models
children.top_down_role: Models retaining disciplined expressions while adding discrete restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Convex Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional mixed-integer convex formulation defined through its continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and consider \[\min_x f_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x)\leq 0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\quad Ax=b,\quad x_j\in\mathbb{Z}\ (j\in I).\] This is a mixed-integer convex model when every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), including \(f_0\), is convex and the model obtained by replacing \(x_j\in\mathbb{Z}\) with \(x_j\in\mathbb{R}\) is a convex optimization problem. The integrality restrictions generally make the original feasible set nonconvex.
