knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures explicit graph-implementation expansion of nested atom occurrences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the input expression representation contain \(N\) nodes and \(m\) atom occurrences selected for expansion. If occurrence \(i\) produces \(s_i\) auxiliary expression, variable, and constraint records, then an explicit recursive expansion visits the original representation and all generated records. Its time and additional storage are therefore \(\Theta\!\left(N+\sum_{i=1}^{m}s_i\right)\), provided record construction is constant-time and coefficients are referenced rather than copied. Nested atoms affect cost through the total recursively generated size, not merely through the depth of the original syntax tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit atom expansion costs time and storage proportional to the original graph plus the total size of all recursively generated graph implementations.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Expansion Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits Graph Expansion Costs. The time bound is coherent under explicit materialization, but the storage claim alternates between total representation storage, which includes N, and additional generated storage, which ordinarily includes only the generated records. A source and a precise storage convention are needed before the bound can be relied upon.

children.title: Canonical Data Assembly Costs
children.top_down_role: Construction of sparse solver matrices, vectors, and cone layouts.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Materialization lower bound for canonical matrices, vectors, and cone descriptors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be the number of scalar and descriptor cells explicitly materialized in the canonical output. Any unit-cost algorithm that writes the complete output requires \(\Omega(L)\) time. Under the deferred seed's dense-vector and sparse-matrix convention, \(L=r+n+z+b\), so its \(O(r+n+z+b)\) bound is asymptotically tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete canonical-data materialization requires time linear in the explicit output size.
assumptions_latex: Every counted output cell is explicitly materialized.
Each scalar or descriptor write has unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{assembly}}=\Omega(L)=\Omega(r+n+z+b)

notation.meaning: Number of explicitly materialized output cells.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Output Assembly Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extra finalization work for unordered or duplicate coordinate emissions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(z_e\) emitted coordinate-value triples are unordered or duplicated while the target format requires ordered unique coordinates, output-linear finalization is not automatic. Comparison sorting has worst-case \(\Theta(z_e\log z_e)\) time, after which duplicate aggregation costs \(O(z_e)\); the final stored count may be smaller than \(z_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unordered or duplicate sparse emissions can require sorting and aggregation beyond output-linear assembly.
assumptions_latex: The target format requires ordered, duplicate-free coordinates.
Ordering uses a comparison-based method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{finalize}}=\Theta(z_e\log z_e)\ \text{in the comparison-sorting worst case}

notation.meaning: Number of emitted coordinate-value triples before aggregation.

review_flags: not a lower bound for bounded-key or order-preserving assembly
knowledge_statements.title: Unordered Sparse-Finalization Boundary

assumptions_latex: The canonical form contains \(r\) scalar rows, \(n\) scalar variables, and \(z\) stored matrix coefficients.
Sparse matrix entries and cone-block descriptors are emitted once and then finalized by linear-time sparse-format construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Canonical data assembly takes \(O(r+n+z+b)\) time and \(O(r+n+z+b)\) output storage.

notation.meaning: Number of stored nonzero matrix coefficients.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers sparse solver-data construction after graph expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose canonicalization has fixed the row, variable, and cone-block order. Constructing the sparse constraint matrix requires emitting \(z\) stored coefficients; constructing objective and right-hand-side vectors requires initializing or writing \(n+r\) scalar positions; and constructing the cone layout requires \(O(b)\) descriptors. Under linear-time sparse-format finalization, total assembly time and output storage are \(O(r+n+z+b)\). This bound excludes expression analysis, graph expansion, solver preprocessing, and any sorting or duplicate aggregation not already included in the finalization assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once ordering is fixed, sparse matrices, vectors, and cone layouts can be assembled in time and storage linear in their explicit output size.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Data Assembly Costs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits Canonical Data Assembly Costs, and the output-linear bound is properly conditional on fixed ordering and linear-time sparse finalization. The implementation assumptions and exclusion of sorting or duplicate aggregation need an inspectable sparse-assembly source.

children.title: Incremental Compilation Cost Calculus
children.top_down_role: Parameter updates, cached compilation, and inverse mapping overhead.

children.title: Parameter-Update Recompilation
children.top_down_role: Front-end work triggered when parameter changes invalidate reusable compiled artifacts.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental evaluation restricted to canonical entries depending on changed parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d(p)=Rp+d_0\), let \(\Delta\) index parameter coordinates changed from \(p\) to \(p'\), and let \(W=\{i:\exists j\in\Delta,\ R_{ij}\ne0\}\). With cached sparse column adjacency, update \(d_i\) only for \(i\in W\) using \(d_i(p')=d_i(p)+\sum_{j\in\Delta}R_{ij}(p'_j-p_j)\). The cost is \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(R_{:,\Delta})+|W|)\), including affected-entry writes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cached dependency information permits updating only canonical data affected by changed parameter coordinates.
assumptions_latex: The parameter-to-data map is affine and its sparse column adjacency is cached.
Dimensions, parameter domains, sparsity, and structural compilation choices remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{incremental}}=O\!\left(\operatorname{nnz}(R_{:,\Delta})+|W|\right)
knowledge_statements.title: Dependency-Restricted Parameter Update

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive lower bound for incremental parameter updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a parameter change alters \(w\) explicitly stored canonical entries and the downstream interface requires each altered entry to be rewritten, then the update requires \(\Omega(w)\) writes. The bound concerns changed output size and does not bound the coefficient-processing work needed to discover or compute those changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rewriting w changed canonical entries requires at least w writes.
assumptions_latex: Exactly w materialized canonical entries change.
The downstream interface requires explicit rewriting of each changed entry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{update}}=\Omega(w)

notation.meaning: Number of changed materialized canonical entries.

review_flags: coefficient-processing cost may exceed the write lower bound
knowledge_statements.title: Changed-Data Write Lower Bound

assumptions_latex: The problem structure and parameter locations are unchanged between solves.
Each canonical scalar datum is an affine function of a parameter vector \(p\), represented by a cached linear map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Updating canonical data costs \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(R))\) arithmetic, plus the cost of writing changed output entries, without repeating structural canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies when parameters change but expression and cone structure remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the vectorized canonical data satisfy \(d(p)=Rp+d_0\), where \(R\) and \(d_0\) were produced and cached during an initial compilation. For a new parameter value \(p'\), recompilation consists of validating parameter dimensions and domains, evaluating \(d(p')=Rp'+d_0\), and writing the affected matrix, vector, and offset entries. Sparse evaluation requires \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(R))\) arithmetic in the worst case. No expression analysis or graph expansion is required unless a parameter change alters dimensions, domains, sparsity structure, or control-dependent model structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When structure is fixed and data depend affinely on parameters, recompilation reduces to evaluating a cached sparse parameter-to-data map.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Update Recompilation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits Parameter-Update Recompilation. The cached affine-map formulation is plausible, but its O(nnz(R)) arithmetic claim depends on how d0, zero rows, validation, and output writes are represented. An authoritative parametric-compilation source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Cached Compilation Reuse
children.top_down_role: Cost behavior when prior analysis or canonical data can be reused.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementation-independent correctness condition for reuse over an admitted parameter set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a cached compilation with numerical data map \(d_C(p)\), and let \(\operatorname{Can}(M(p))\) denote fresh canonicalization. The cache is reusable on \(P\) exactly when, for every \(p\in P\), its canonical data are equivalent to fresh canonicalization under declared coordinate and cone identifications and its inverse maps reconstruct the same advertised source outputs. A matching cache key is only a certificate intended to establish this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cached artifacts are reusable exactly when their data and recovery semantics agree with fresh canonicalization for every admitted parameter value.
assumptions_latex: Canonical-data equivalence accounts for declared coordinate and cone-block identifications.
Advertised source outputs include every requested primal, dual, and status result.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ reusable on }P\iff\forall p\in P,\ d_C(p)\simeq\operatorname{Can}(M(p))\ \text{and recovery semantics agree}

notation.meaning: Canonical data produced by the cache.

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Cache-Reuse Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Changes requiring renewed structural validation before reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A change capable of altering expression topology, dimensions, atom implementation, variable or constraint ordering, cone types or sizes, sparsity pattern, target-interface requirements, or inverse-recovery semantics invalidates unqualified reuse. Reuse remains sound only if the cache contract verifies that the change preserves the Semantic Cache-Reuse Criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changes that may affect canonical structure or recovery invalidate a cache hit unless the cache contract proves semantic invariance.
assumptions_latex: The changed field is not already certified irrelevant by the cache contract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta\text{ may alter canonical or recovery semantics}\Longrightarrow\text{reuse requires renewed validation}
knowledge_statements.title: Structural Cache Invalidation

assumptions_latex: The expression graph, dimensions, atom implementations, target solver interface, and structural parameter metadata match a cached compilation key.
Only numerical parameter values may differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cache hit permits reuse of the canonical sparsity, cone layout, reduction chain, and recovery maps; only parameter-dependent numerical data need updating.

notation.meaning: Cached compilation artifact indexed by the key.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines reusable artifacts and the structural validity test for a compilation cache hit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute a structural key \(\kappa\) from the expression graph, dimensions, atom versions, target interface, and parameter metadata. If \(C[\kappa]\) exists and its validity checks pass, reuse its variable ordering, constraint ordering, sparse pattern, cone layout, reduction chain, and inverse maps. Substitute current parameter values into the cached data map, invoke the solver, and recover user-level results through the cached inverse maps. If the key is absent or any structural check fails, perform full compilation and replace or add \(C[\kappa]\). The output is either updated canonical data or a newly compiled artifact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid structural cache hit reuses canonical layouts and recovery maps, updating only numerical data before solving.
knowledge_statements.title: Cached Compilation Reuse

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Cached Compilation Reuse, and the record identifies the cache test, reusable artifacts, miss path, and output. The proposed structural key and reusable reduction artifacts are implementation-specific and have no cited source or inspectable validity contract.

children.title: Inverse-Mapping Recovery Overhead
children.top_down_role: Work required to transport solver results back to source-model objects.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Materialization lower bound for requested source-level outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If recovery must explicitly materialize \(u\) requested source-level scalar outputs, every recovery algorithm requires \(\Omega(u)\) output writes. Consequently, a valid reverse reduction chain with total application cost \(O(u)\) is asymptotically optimal with respect to output size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicitly returning u source-level values requires at least linear time.
assumptions_latex: All u requested scalar outputs must be explicitly materialized.
Each scalar write has unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{recovery}}=\Omega(u)

notation.meaning: Number of requested source-level scalar outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Recovered-Output Lower Bound

assumptions_latex: Canonicalization records a finite reduction chain \(T_1,\ldots,T_k\) and corresponding inverse maps \(I_k,\ldots,I_1\).
Applying \(I_j\) to its stored solver result costs \(c_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recovery costs \(O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_j\right)\) time, in addition to storage for the retained inverse-map metadata and recovered user variables.

notation.meaning: Cost of applying inverse map j.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures post-solve reconstruction through the recorded reduction chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from the solver result \(y_k\), recover intermediate results in reverse reduction order by \(y_{j-1}=I_j(y_j)\) for \(j=k,k-1,\ldots,1\). If applying \(I_j\) costs \(c_j\), complete recovery costs \(O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_j\right)\) time. The retained metadata must identify eliminated variables, auxiliary-variable projections, dual-variable correspondences, scaling transformations, and status translations needed by the inverse maps. Recovery overhead is separate from solver time and may be output-linear when every recovered primal or dual entry must be materialized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: User-level solutions are reconstructed by applying recorded inverse reductions in reverse order, with cost equal to the sum of their application costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Mapping Recovery Overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits Inverse-Mapping Recovery Overhead, and the reverse composition and summed application-cost bound are internally consistent. The claimed retained metadata and output-linear behavior require a source describing the intended reduction and inversion framework.

children.title: Solver Capability Contracts
children.top_down_role: Capabilities used to choose compatible canonical targets and recovery interfaces.

children.title: Solver Cone Capability Interface
children.top_down_role: Available cone families and specialized constraint interfaces.

children.title: Specialized Constraint Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Solver-facing support for structured constraint classes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Input Admission Does Not Imply Dual-Output Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates a specialized handler's input capability from optional output and recovery capabilities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Acceptance of a canonical constraint by a specialized input handler \(H_{\mathcal S}\) establishes only that the constraint can be represented through that handler. Availability of primal recovery, source dual values, certificates, or sensitivity data requires separately declared output maps and solver capabilities. When a requested output has no declared recovery map, the interface must report that output as unavailable rather than infer it from input support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support for submitting a specialized constraint does not by itself guarantee dual values, certificates, sensitivities, or other recovered outputs.
assumptions_latex: \(H_{\mathcal S}\) accepts the canonical constraint under its declared input contract.
Output transport is governed by separately declared recovery maps and solver capabilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(H_{\mathcal S})\) determines input eligibility but does not imply availability of any particular inverse-mapped output.

notation.meaning: A specialized input handler for constraint class S.
The canonical constraints admitted by the handler.

knowledge_statements.title: Input Admission Does Not Imply Dual-Output Support

assumptions_latex: A canonical constraint belongs to a recognized specialized class \(\mathcal S\).
The solver advertises an interface \(H_{\mathcal S}\) with stated dimensional, domain, and data-format requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Direct dispatch through \(H_{\mathcal S}\) is valid exactly when the constraint satisfies the interface contract; otherwise another supported representation is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes direct dispatch to solver-specific structured-constraint handlers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A specialized constraint interface is a partial handler \(H_{\mathcal S}\) whose domain consists of canonical constraints in a declared class \(\mathcal S\), such as semidefinite, exponential, power-cone, indicator, or structured quadratic constraints. A constraint may be dispatched directly only if its type, dimensions, coefficient domains, symmetry conventions, supported senses, and required solver options satisfy the handler's contract. The handler must map accepted data to a solver constraint and provide status and primal-dual recovery maps. Rejection by \(H_{\mathcal S}\) concerns interface support, not the mathematical convexity of the original constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A specialized constraint is dispatched directly only when its type, dimensions, data conventions, options, and recovery behavior satisfy the solver handler's contract.
knowledge_statements.title: Specialized Constraint Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Specialized Constraint Interfaces. The partial-handler formulation is reasonable, but the listed specialized classes mix cone-native and solver-specific constraint categories, and the asserted primal-dual recovery obligations are interface-dependent. A concrete solver or modeling-interface contract is needed.

children.title: Supported Cone Families
children.top_down_role: Cone categories accepted directly by a solver interface.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cone Support Is Necessary but Full Dispatch Is Contract-Wide
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes blockwise cone-family support from complete solver-dispatch eligibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a canonical conic target require blocks \(K_1,\ldots,K_b\), and let \(\mathfrak K_S\) contain the dimensioned cone blocks accepted by solver \(S\). Blockwise membership \(K_i\in\mathfrak K_S\) for every \(i\) is necessary for direct conic dispatch. It is sufficient only when the canonical data also satisfy every non-cone requirement of the target contract, including supported scalar domains, matrix formats, objective form, and integrality restrictions, if any.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support for every cone block is necessary for direct conic dispatch, but complete dispatch also requires all non-cone parts of the solver contract to be satisfied.
assumptions_latex: The canonical target requires cone blocks \(K_1,\ldots,K_b\).
\(\mathfrak K_S\) records the solver's dimensioned cone-block capabilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(\forall i,\ K_i\in\mathfrak K_S\bigr)\) is necessary for direct conic dispatch and becomes sufficient only together with satisfaction of the remaining target-contract predicates.

notation.meaning: The i-th cone block required by the canonical target.
The selected solver's dimensioned cone capability set.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Support Is Necessary but Full Dispatch Is Contract-Wide

assumptions_latex: The canonical program uses cone blocks \(K_1,\ldots,K_b\).
The selected solver declares a capability set \(\mathfrak K_S\) including supported dimensions and conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Direct conic dispatch is available if and only if \(K_i\in\mathfrak K_S\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,b\}\).

notation.meaning: Cone blocks required by the canonical program.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats cone support as a dimensioned solver capability contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For solver \(S\), let \(\mathfrak K_S\) be the declared set of cone families together with admissible dimensions, products, scaling conventions, and primal-dual orientations. A canonical conic program with product cone \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_b\) is directly supported precisely when every block \(K_i\) matches an entry of \(\mathfrak K_S\) under those conventions. Typical capability entries may include the nonnegative orthant, second-order cones, positive-semidefinite cones, exponential cones, and power cones, but membership is solver-specific and cannot be inferred solely from mathematical closedness or convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic model is directly supported only when every dimensioned cone block belongs to the selected solver's declared capability set.
knowledge_statements.title: Supported Cone Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Supported Cone Families. Cone-block membership is necessary for direct conic support, but the stated if-and-only-if conclusion may omit coefficient-domain, data-format, integrality, and other target-contract requirements unless all such requirements are explicitly included in the capability set. A sourced capability definition is needed to settle the exact condition.

children.title: Unsupported Cone Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cone requirements that exceed a solver contract or require another target.

assumptions_latex: A certified model canonicalizes to cone blocks \(K_1,\ldots,K_b\).
At least one required block lies outside the selected solver's capability set \(\mathfrak K_S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of direct dispatch follows from \(\{K_1,\ldots,K_b\}\nsubseteq\mathfrak K_S\), unless an exact supported reformulation is applied.

notation.meaning: Cone blocks required by the model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates unsupported solver representations from invalid convex models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unsupported-cone boundary is crossed when some required canonical block \(K_j\) does not belong to the selected solver's dimensioned capability set \(\mathfrak K_S\). Direct dispatch must then fail before solving. The model may proceed only if the front end has an exact reformulation replacing every unsupported block by constraints over supported cones while preserving feasible projections and objective values. If no such registered reformulation exists, the correct outcome is an unsupported-representation status, not a claim of nonconvexity, infeasibility, or unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unsupported required cone prevents direct dispatch unless an exact registered reformulation replaces it using cones the solver accepts.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Cone Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits Unsupported Cone Boundaries, and the record correctly separates representational failure from nonconvexity or infeasibility. The direct-dispatch rule and the required equivalence properties of an exact reformulation need an authoritative modeling-system or solver-interface source.

children.title: Quadratic-Conic Target Interface
children.top_down_role: Direct quadratic interfaces and alternative cone reductions.

children.title: Direct Quadratic Targets
children.top_down_role: Solver interfaces that preserve supported quadratic objectives or constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eligibility of convex quadratic inequalities for a target expressly supporting quadratic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_j(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}P_jx+r_j^{\mathsf T}x+s_j\), with \(P_j=P_j^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\), for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). Each inequality \(q_j(x)\leq0\) is eligible for direct quadratic-constraint dispatch exactly when its sense, dimension, coefficient domain, Hessian convention, and data representation satisfy the selected target contract. Positive-semidefinite curvature establishes convexity but does not by itself establish interface eligibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic inequality can be dispatched directly only when its positive-semidefinite quadratic data also satisfy every requirement of the selected quadratic-constraint interface.
assumptions_latex: \(P_j=P_j^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\) for every \(j\).
The target contract declares its supported quadratic-constraint forms and data conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_j(x)\leq0\) is directly dispatchable for every \(j\) if and only if every \(q_j\) satisfies the declared quadratic-constraint contract.

notation.meaning: The j-th convex quadratic constraint function.
The positive-semidefinite quadratic coefficient of q_j.

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Convex Quadratic-Constraint Eligibility

assumptions_latex: The target accepts convex quadratic objectives and affine constraints directly.
The objective is \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Px+r^{\mathsf T}x+s\) with symmetric \(P\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model may be emitted as a direct convex quadratic program without an epigraph cone reduction of \(q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers direct emission of a convex quadratic objective to a quadratic-capable target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Px+r^{\mathsf T}x+s\) subject to affine equalities and inequalities, where \(P=P^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\). If the selected target contract accepts the Hessian convention, coefficient domains, constraint senses, and required sparsity format, canonicalization may emit \((P,r,s)\) and the affine constraint data directly as a convex quadratic program. No auxiliary epigraph variable or second-order-cone representation of the quadratic objective is required. Direct eligibility depends on both mathematical convexity and the target's advertised quadratic interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic objective with affine constraints can be sent directly to a compatible quadratic solver without conic epigraph expansion.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Quadratic Targets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits Direct Quadratic Targets. For symmetric positive-semidefinite P and affine constraints, the direct convex-quadratic representation is mathematically appropriate when the target contract accepts it. No cited source documents the target interface, Hessian convention, or direct-emission behavior.

children.title: Conic Target Reductions
children.top_down_role: Representations that translate quadratic structure into supported cone forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Target Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order-cone epigraph reduction of a convex quadratic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) satisfy \(P\succeq0\), let \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and choose \(R\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) such that \(P=R^{\mathsf T}R\). The problem \[\min_{x\in C}\;\frac12x^{\mathsf T}Px+q^{\mathsf T}x\] and the conic problem \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n,\,t\in\mathbb R}\;t+q^{\mathsf T}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\in C,\quad (t,1,Rx)\in\mathcal Q_r\] have the same optimal value, and the projection of the conic problem's optimal-solution set onto \(x\) equals the optimal-solution set of the quadratic problem, where \[\mathcal Q_r=\{(u,v,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^r:2uv\geq\lVert z\rVert_2^2,\ u\geq0,\ v\geq0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic objective can be replaced by a linear epigraph objective and one rotated second-order-cone constraint without changing its optimal value or optimal decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(P\succeq0\).
\(q\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
\(C\) is representable by the target conic interface.
\(R\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) satisfies \(P=R^{\mathsf T}R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}(\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Px+q^{\mathsf T}x)\) equals the projection onto \(x\) of the conic problem's solution set, and the two problems have the same optimal value.

notation.meaning: Rotated second-order cone in two scalar coordinates and one r-dimensional vector coordinate.
A matrix factor satisfying P = R^T R.

children.title: Target-Selection Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural, numerical, or compatibility consequences of choosing a quadratic or conic target.

knowledge_statements.title: Target-Selection Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capability-preserving choice between direct quadratic and conic solver targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a canonical convex problem \(P\), let \(T_q(P)\) be a direct quadratic target and \(T_c(P)\) an equivalent conic target. A valid selector may choose \[T(P)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{T\in\{T_q,T_c\}}\Phi(T)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\mathcal K(T)\subseteq\mathcal K_S\ \text{and}\ \varepsilon(T)\leq\bar\varepsilon,\] where \(\mathcal K(T)\) is the set of required primitive cones or quadratic features, \(\mathcal K_S\) is the solver capability set, and \(\Phi\) measures predicted computational cost. Equivalence alone does not determine the preferred target: auxiliary-variable growth, sparsity preservation, numerical scaling, and available solver features may change \(\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose among equivalent targets only after checking solver support and accuracy; target size, sparsity, scaling, and native quadratic support determine the computational tradeoff.
assumptions_latex: \(T_q(P)\) and \(T_c(P)\) preserve the feasible solutions and objective value of \(P\).
\(\Phi\) and \(\varepsilon\) are fixed selection metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(P)\) is capability-compatible and minimizes the declared predicted-cost criterion among admissible targets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the tradeoff leaf, but the selector, cost model, error measure, capability set, solver S, and tolerance are interface-dependent and lack cited definitions. The displayed minimization also alternates between target constructors and instantiated targets, so authoritative modeling-system support is needed before fixing the formal version.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Capability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transfer of disciplined continuous expressions to discrete solver interfaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capability test after canonicalization of continuous expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose canonicalization produces affine constraints over cone blocks \(K_1,\ldots,K_q\) and marks coordinate set \(J\) as integral. A solver target is admissible only if its contract supports every \(K_i\), every required variable type and bound, and integrality on \(J\) jointly with those cone blocks. Separate cone-support and integer-support flags are insufficient when their combination is unsupported.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A target must support all generated cones, integral coordinates, bounds, and their joint combination.
assumptions_latex: Canonicalization records all cone blocks, variable types, bounds, and integral coordinates.
Capabilities are interpreted from an explicit solver contract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{admissible}\Longrightarrow\bigl(\forall i,\ K_i\text{ supported}\bigr)\land\bigl(J\text{ supported jointly with }K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\bigr)

notation.meaning: Canonical coordinates constrained to integral values.

review_flags: solver contracts may support only selected mixed-integer cone combinations
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Target Admissibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Continuous Slices Do Not Imply Joint Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal separation between fixed-integer convexity and joint mixed-integer convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R\times\{0,1\}:x=z\}\). Each fixed-\(z\) continuous slice is a singleton and hence convex, but \((0,0),(1,1)\in S\) while \((1/2,1/2)\notin S\). Thus convexity of every continuous slice does not make the mixed-integer feasible set convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every fixed-integer continuous slice can be convex while the joint mixed-integer set remains nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: x=z.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall z\in\{0,1\},\ S_z\text{ is convex},\qquad S\text{ is not convex}

notation.meaning: Continuous feasible slice at fixed z.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Continuous Slices Do Not Imply Joint Convexity
Mixed-Integer Capability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between disciplined continuous canonicalization and mixed-integer solver support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a disciplined convex model with continuous variables \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), discrete variables \(z\in\mathbb Z^m\), and constraints that are convex in \(x\) for every fixed \(z\). Disciplined convex verification can certify and canonicalize the continuous expressions, but it does not make the joint feasible set convex when \(m>0\). A solver interface can accept the resulting model only if its capability contract supports every generated cone together with the declared integrality pattern. Otherwise compilation must terminate as unsupported; relaxing \(z\in\mathbb Z^m\) to \(z\in\mathbb R^m\) changes the problem and is not a semantics-preserving fallback.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex expression rules transfer to mixed-integer models, but integrality remains nonconvex and requires explicit mixed-integer support for every generated cone.
assumptions_latex: For each fixed \(z\), the continuous subproblem satisfies the modeling system's disciplined convex rules.
At least one component of \(z\) is constrained to a discrete set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Continuous canonicalizability does not imply solver admissibility; admissibility additionally requires mixed-integer support for the target primitives.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits. However, convexity in continuous variables for each fixed integer assignment is not by itself a disciplined-convex certification criterion, and mixed-integer canonicalization policies vary by modeling system. A specific interface source must establish the intended boundary and hypotheses.

children.title: Solver Output Transport Interface
children.top_down_role: Solver outputs available for transport through inverse reductions.

children.title: Solution Status Outputs
children.top_down_role: Termination or problem-status information returned through the modeling interface.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separation of Termination and Returned-Object Quality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent classifications for why computation stopped and what returned objects establish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sound solver-output record separates a termination classification \(t\) from classifications \(q_j\) of returned objects. The former describes why computation stopped; each latter classification records whether a returned point, multiplier, or certificate satisfies declared exact or tolerance-qualified predicates. Thus a resource limit may coexist with an approximate feasible incumbent, while a termination label alone does not validate an unverified returned array.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Termination and the mathematical quality of returned objects are independent status dimensions.
assumptions_latex: Each returned-object classification is tied to declared mathematical or residual predicates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{status}(o)=(t,(q_j)_j),\text{ with }t\text{ and }q_j\text{ interpreted independently}.

notation.meaning: Validity or quality classification of returned object j.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation of Termination and Returned-Object Quality
Solution Status Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized status semantics for solver results transported to a modeling interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A normalized solution-status output is a pair \((s,\delta)\), where \(s\) belongs to \(\{\mathrm{optimal},\mathrm{infeasible},\mathrm{unbounded},\mathrm{limit},\mathrm{error},\mathrm{unknown}\}\) and \(\delta\) retains solver-specific details. The interface may report \(\mathrm{optimal}\) only when returned primal and, when required, dual residuals and the duality gap meet its declared tolerances. It may report \(\mathrm{infeasible}\) or \(\mathrm{unbounded}\) only when the solver supplies the corresponding accepted termination claim or certificate. Reaching an iteration or time limit must remain distinguishable from a mathematical conclusion, even if an incumbent point is returned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A modeling interface normalizes solver termination while preserving details and must distinguish certified mathematical conclusions from limits, errors, and unknown outcomes.
assumptions_latex: The interface declares residual, gap, and certificate acceptance policies.
The raw solver termination record is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized status \(s\) does not assert a stronger conclusion than the raw termination evidence supports.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is appropriate, but the proposed status set and the conditions for emitting each status are interface-specific. No solver-interface specification or locator supports this normalization contract.

children.title: Dual Outputs
children.top_down_role: Dual information recoverable for source-model constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonuniqueness and Partial Availability of Dual Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dual-output interface returns admissible multiplier representatives rather than an intrinsically unique source quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex source problem, the set \(\mathcal D^*\) of source multipliers satisfying the applicable optimality conditions may contain more than one element, for example under redundant or degenerate constraints. A correctly transported solver multiplier need only be an admissible member of \(\mathcal D^*\). If an inverse reduction declares no source map for a target multiplier, that component has no source dual-output semantics and must be reported as unavailable rather than assigned arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Source dual values may be nonunique, and target multipliers lacking a declared inverse map must be reported as unavailable rather than fabricated.
assumptions_latex: The source problem admits at least one multiplier satisfying the applicable source optimality conditions.
Dual transport follows declared inverse-reduction maps and sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat d\in\mathcal D^*\) is a valid transported dual output even when \(\mathcal D^*\) is not a singleton, while unmapped target components yield no source dual value.

notation.meaning: The set of admissible optimal source-model multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness and Partial Availability of Dual Outputs
Dual Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transport of target-problem multipliers to source-constraint dual values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the convex problem \[\min_x f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\leq0,\quad h(x)=0,\] a dual output consists of multipliers \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\nu\) associated with the source constraints. If the solver returns target multipliers \(y\), the modeling interface applies the adjoints and sign conventions of its canonicalization maps to obtain \((\lambda,\nu)\). For a primal-dual solution, the transported values must satisfy dual feasibility and complementary slackness \(\lambda_i g_i(x)=0\). Multipliers introduced solely for auxiliary target constraints are internal and are not source dual outputs unless an explicit inverse mapping assigns them source semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver multipliers become source-model dual values only after inverse mapping, sign normalization, and removal or aggregation of auxiliary-constraint multipliers.
assumptions_latex: Strong duality holds and a primal-dual solution is returned.
Canonicalization records the correspondence between source and target constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transported \((\lambda,\nu)\) satisfy the source problem's multiplier conventions, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leaf and representation kind match, but the generic convex program does not state that f and the g_i are convex and h is affine. The asserted adjoint, sign, and aggregation transport also depends on a particular canonicalization framework and requires a cited inverse-dual mapping contract.

children.title: Certificate Outputs
children.top_down_role: Solver-provided evidence associated with infeasibility, unboundedness, or related statuses.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable conic certificates for infeasibility and unboundedness claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For conic feasibility \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), an infeasibility certificate is \(y\) satisfying \[A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.\] These relations contradict feasibility and are directly checkable. For the primal conic program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), a recession certificate of unboundedness is \(d\in K\) satisfying \[Ad=0,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}d<0,\] together with a known feasible point. A modeling interface must inverse-map the certificate and report its residuals; a status string without the displayed checks is not itself a mathematical certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are certificates only when mapped vectors satisfy independently checkable cone, linear, and strict-sign conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
Certificate signs follow the displayed primal convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vector satisfying the corresponding displayed relations certifies infeasibility or, with primal feasibility, unboundedness.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind and displayed conic alternatives are mathematically standard under the stated sign convention, but no authoritative conic-alternatives locator or output-transport specification is supplied.

children.title: Sensitivity Outputs
children.top_down_role: Derivative or perturbation information exposed through supported interfaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between multiplier-derived subgradients and a unique parameter gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose constraint perturbations have the form \(u=B\theta\), and every optimal multiplier \(\lambda\in\Lambda^*\) yields the parameter-space subgradient \(-B^{\mathsf T}\lambda\in\partial(v\circ B)(0)\). Nonunique multipliers need not determine a unique sensitivity. If \(v\circ B\) is differentiable at zero, then \(-B^{\mathsf T}\lambda=\nabla(v\circ B)(0)\) for every \(\lambda\in\Lambda^*\), equivalently \(B^{\mathsf T}(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)=0\) for all optimal multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonunique multipliers may give different sensitivities, but differentiability forces their parameter-space pullbacks to agree.
assumptions_latex: Strong duality and multiplier attainment hold at the reference problem.
The perturbation map and multiplier sign convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{-B^{\mathsf T}\lambda:\lambda\in\Lambda^*\}\subseteq\partial(v\circ B)(0),\quad v\circ B\text{ differentiable}\Longrightarrow B^{\mathsf T}(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)=0.

notation.meaning: Map from source parameters to constraint perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness and Sensitivity Ambiguity
Sensitivity Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local optimal-value sensitivity represented by transported optimal multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(u)\) be the optimal value of \[\min_x f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g(x)\leq u,\quad h(x)=0,\] and suppose strong duality holds at \(u=0\) with an optimal inequality multiplier \(\lambda^*\geq0\). Then \(-\lambda^*\in\partial v(0)\), equivalently \[v(u)\geq v(0)-{\lambda^*}^{\mathsf T}u\] for perturbations in the value function's domain. If \(v\) is differentiable at zero, then \(\nabla v(0)=-\lambda^*\). A transported sensitivity output is valid only after accounting for canonicalization scaling, parameter signs, and source-to-target parameter maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strong duality, a correctly transported optimal multiplier gives a subgradient of the value function; differentiability turns it into the local gradient.
assumptions_latex: The perturbed problems define a proper convex value function near \(u=0\).
Strong duality holds at \(u=0\) and \(\lambda^*\) is dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\lambda^*\in\partial v(0)\), with \(\nabla v(0)=-\lambda^*\) when \(v\) is differentiable at zero.

notation.meaning: Optimal inequality multiplier at zero perturbation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sensitivity property is consistent with the displayed right-hand-side convention and fits the leaf. It still requires an authoritative perturbation-analysis locator, and the canonicalization-scaling transport claim needs framework-specific support.

children.title: Inverse-Reduction Output Transport
children.top_down_role: Preservation or loss of solver outputs while mapping results to source-model objects.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic obstruction to deterministic inverse-output transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E(u)\) denote all reduced output and retained metadata available to an inverse map, and let \(T(u)\) be a desired source-level output. If \(E(u_1)=E(u_2)\) but \(T(u_1)\ne T(u_2)\), then no deterministic map \(I\) can satisfy \(I(E(u))=T(u)\) for every admissible \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source output cannot be recovered when identical retained information corresponds to different source values.
assumptions_latex: The inverse map may use only the reduced output and metadata retained by the reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(u_1)=E(u_2)\land T(u_1)\ne T(u_2)\Longrightarrow\nexists I\;\forall u,\ I(E(u))=T(u).

notation.meaning: Reduced output together with retained inverse metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Irrecoverable-Output Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fieldwise composition through a fixed chain of reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P_0\xrightarrow{R_1}\cdots\xrightarrow{R_k}P_k\), let \(I_i:\mathcal O_i\to\mathcal O_{i-1}\) be defined for a supported output field. The source-level inverse is \(I_{1:k}=I_1\circ\cdots\circ I_k\). It is exact for that field if every \(I_i\) is exact on the corresponding intermediate field. Information discarded at any stage cannot be restored by later composition without additional retained metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse maps compose in reverse pipeline order; fieldwise exactness survives composition, but discarded information does not.
assumptions_latex: Each inverse map is defined on the preceding map's output.
Exactness is assessed separately for each output field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\forall i,\ I_i\text{ is fieldwise exact})\Longrightarrow I_{1:k}\text{ is fieldwise exact}.

notation.meaning: Output space at reduction level i.

knowledge_statements.title: Compositionality of Inverse Output Maps
Inverse-Reduction Output Transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse traversal that restores source-level primal, dual, status, and certificate semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a reduction pipeline be \(P_0\xrightarrow{R_1}P_1\xrightarrow{R_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{R_k}P_k\), and let each reduction store an inverse map \(I_i\) for supported output fields. Given a solver result \(o_k\), initialize \(o\leftarrow o_k\) and apply \[o\leftarrow I_i(o)\qquad\text{for }i=k,k-1,\ldots,1.\] Each \(I_i\) reconstructs eliminated primal variables, maps duals by the recorded affine adjoint and sign convention, aggregates auxiliary multipliers, and translates statuses or certificates only when its validity conditions hold. Stop with an explicit unavailable field if an inverse map lacks required data; output \(o_0=o\) in source-model coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transport solver outputs by applying stored inverse reductions in reverse order, reconstructing source variables and mapping other fields only when their validity conditions hold.
assumptions_latex: Every forward reduction records the metadata required by its supported inverse map.
\(o_k\) conforms to the terminal solver-result schema.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns \(o_0\) expressed in the coordinates and semantics of \(P_0\), with unsupported fields marked unavailable.

notation.meaning: Forward reduction from one problem representation to the next.
Output record at representation level i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct role, and reverse traversal is plausible, but the supported fields, inverse maps, status translations, dual adjoints, and failure behavior constitute a framework-specific contract without a cited backend source.

children.title: Canonicalization Backend Families
children.top_down_role: Implementation variants for symbolic model construction, rewriting, and solver-data generation.

children.title: Embedded Domain-Specific-Language Front Ends
children.top_down_role: Operator-overloading and expression-building interfaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decision-Dependent Host Control Flow Is Not Symbolic Modeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between expression construction and immediate host-language execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be an unassigned symbolic decision variable. A host-language conditional controlled by \(x>0\) requires an immediate Boolean value during model construction, but that truth value depends on the eventual decision. Ordinary host control flow therefore cannot represent the branch. A valid model needs an explicitly supported symbolic piecewise construction or a formulation with discrete decisions; coercing the comparison to a host Boolean rejects or changes the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A comparison involving an unassigned decision variable cannot drive ordinary host-language control flow during symbolic graph construction.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is an unassigned symbolic decision variable}.
The host conditional requires an immediate Boolean value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{bool}(x>0)\text{ is unavailable at model-construction time}.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Dependent Host Control Flow Is Not Symbolic Modeling
Embedded Domain-Specific-Language Front Ends
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Host-language construction of typed symbolic optimization expression graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An embedded optimization domain-specific-language front end is a host-language interface whose overloaded operators and constructors map user expressions to a directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\). Each node \(v\in V\) stores an atom, shape, sign information, curvature class, and children; variables and parameters are distinguished leaves. Constructing \(G\) is symbolic: overloaded arithmetic records an expression rather than evaluating it numerically. A model is accepted under disciplined convex programming exactly when the root objective and every constraint satisfy the front end's declared composition rules, after which \(G\) is passed to a canonicalization backend.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedded DSL uses host-language syntax to build a typed symbolic expression graph, checks disciplined composition rules, and submits accepted graphs for canonicalization.
assumptions_latex: The host language supports operator overloading or equivalent expression constructors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted models have symbolic graphs whose curvature and domain annotations satisfy the declared disciplined rules.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the topic, but not every embedded optimization DSL stores all listed annotations at every graph node or uses exactly this acceptance pipeline. A concrete embedded-language source is needed to delimit the definition and substantiate the implementation claims.

children.title: Canonicalization Transformation Backends
children.top_down_role: Composable transformation architectures for canonicalization.

children.title: Composable Reduction Pipelines
children.top_down_role: Backend organizations built from sequenced model transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Composable Reduction Pipelines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential canonicalization by reductions with explicit applicability and inverse-output maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A composable reduction pipeline is an ordered tuple \((R_1,\ldots,R_k)\). Given a source problem \(P_0\), for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), verify the applicability predicate \(A_i(P_{i-1})\), compute \[(P_i,m_i)=R_i(P_{i-1}),\] and store metadata \(m_i\) defining the supported inverse output map. If any predicate fails, terminate without invoking later reductions. Otherwise solve \(P_k\), then apply the inverse maps in order \(k,k-1,\ldots,1\). The pipeline is semantics-preserving when each reduction preserves the declared solution relation and the composed inverse maps return every supported output field to source-model coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction pipeline checks each stage, transforms sequentially, stores inverse metadata, solves the terminal problem, and reverses the stages to restore source outputs.
assumptions_latex: Each \(R_i\) declares an applicability predicate and a preserved solution relation.
Required inverse metadata is retained until output transport completes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful execution produces a terminal problem and a composed inverse map preserving the pipeline's declared source-level semantics.

notation.meaning: Applicability predicate for the i-th reduction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind matches the pipeline leaf, but applicability predicates, preserved solution relations, metadata, and inverse-map guarantees are backend-architecture contracts. No source establishes this particular pipeline semantics.

children.title: Expression Rewriting Engines
children.top_down_role: Canonicalization architectures centered on symbolic rewrite systems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Termination and Local Confluence Give Unique Normal Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard condition for rewrite-order independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\to\) be a terminating rewrite relation on expression graphs. If it is locally confluent, so every one-step fork \(G\to G_1\) and \(G\to G_2\) is joinable, then Newman's lemma implies that \(\to\) is confluent. Consequently each graph has a unique irreducible normal form up to the engine's declared graph equivalence. Termination alone guarantees existence of a normal form but not uniqueness or rule-order independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminating, locally confluent rewrite system has unique normal forms; termination alone does not prevent rule-order-dependent outputs.
assumptions_latex: \to\text{ is terminating}.
\to\text{ is locally confluent}.
Graph identity is taken modulo the engine's declared equivalence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \to\text{ is confluent, and normal forms are unique up to declared equivalence}.
knowledge_statements.title: Termination and Local Confluence Give Unique Normal Forms
Expression Rewriting Engines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rule-directed normalization of symbolic expressions with preserved value and domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an expression directed acyclic graph and let each rewrite rule be a partial map \(r:L\to R\) equipped with a guard \(C_r\). Traverse \(G\) in topological order; whenever a subgraph matches \(L\) and \(C_r\) holds for its shapes, signs, domains, and curvature annotations, replace it by \(R\), update annotations, and reuse structurally identical nodes. Continue according to a fixed terminating strategy until no rule applies. Every admitted rule must satisfy \[\operatorname{dom}L=\operatorname{dom}R,\qquad L(x)=R(x)\quad\text{for all }x\in\operatorname{dom}L,\] or explicitly declare a weaker equisatisfiable reformulation relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rewriting engine applies guarded graph rules to a fixed point while preserving expression values and domains, or an explicitly declared reformulation relation.
assumptions_latex: The rewrite strategy is terminating.
Rule guards are decidable from stored expression annotations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output graph is irreducible under the selected rules and preserves each rule's declared semantics.

notation.meaning: A guarded rewrite from a left pattern to a replacement.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the leaf and its mathematical conditions are coherent under the stated termination assumption. The fixed-point strategy, structural sharing, annotations, and permitted equisatisfiable rewrites nevertheless require a specific rewriting-engine source.

children.title: Backend Composition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compatibility limits governing how reductions or rewriters can be combined.

knowledge_statements.title: Backend Composition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility contract required when adjoining canonicalization backend stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let backend stage \(B_i\) expose a contract \((\mathcal I_i,\mathcal O_i,S_i,M_i)\), consisting of accepted input representations, produced output representations, preserved semantics, and inverse-map metadata. Stages \(B_i\) and \(B_{i+1}\) are composable exactly when \[\mathcal O_i\subseteq\mathcal I_{i+1},\qquad S_{i+1}\circ S_i\text{ is defined},\qquad M_i\cup M_{i+1}\text{ suffices for reverse output transport}.\] Shape, cone, parameter, variable-identity, and sign conventions must agree at the boundary. If any condition fails, an explicit adapter with its own semantic and inverse-map contract is required; implicit coercion is not a valid composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backend stages compose only when their representations, semantics, conventions, and inverse metadata agree; otherwise a contract-bearing adapter is required.
assumptions_latex: Each backend stage publishes its input, output, semantic, and inverse-metadata contract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed compatibility predicate is necessary for direct composition of adjacent backend stages.

notation.meaning: Accepted input and produced output representation classes.
Preserved semantic relation and inverse metadata.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the appropriate kind, but the claimed exact characterization is framework-dependent and not fully typed: S_i is described as a semantic relation yet composed as a map, and metadata sufficiency is not defined. The conclusion states only necessity while the statement asserts an equivalence. A sourced backend contract is required to determine the correct formulation.

children.title: Compiled Data-Generation Backends
children.top_down_role: Lower-level implementations optimized for sparse assembly and repeated use.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive runtime for general stored entry maps, with a sparse-affine specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a compiled backend emit \(q\) stored entries \(d_j(\theta)\), and let evaluating entry map \(d_j\) cost \(T_j\). Evaluation followed by scattering into preallocated arrays costs \[O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{q}T_j+q\right),\] excluding compilation and solver time. In the affine representation \(d(\theta)=D\theta+d_0\) with sparse \(D\), the corresponding bound is \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(D)+q)\), with storage \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(D)+q)\) apart from parameter storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime is the cost of evaluating the stored entry maps plus linear output assembly; a sparse affine map costs time and storage proportional to its nonzeros and emitted entries.
assumptions_latex: Scatter destinations are preallocated.
For the specialization, D\text{ is stored sparsely}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{runtime}}=O\!\left(\sum_jT_j+q\right),\quad T_{\mathrm{affine}}=O(\operatorname{nnz}(D)+q).

notation.meaning: Cost of evaluating stored entry map j
Number of stored nonzeros in the affine operator

knowledge_statements.title: Compiled Entry-Evaluation Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compiled repeated data generation when canonical entries depend affinely on parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the vector \(d(\theta)\) of stored numerical entries of \(A(\theta),b(\theta),c(\theta)\) depends affinely on \(\theta\in\mathbb R^p\). Then fixed \(D\) and \(d_0\) exist such that \[d(\theta)=D\theta+d_0.\] With fixed scatter maps, evaluating this operator produces the canonical arrays, and the entry-map derivative is the constant operator \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine canonical data can be compiled as a fixed sparse operator plus an offset and fixed scatter maps.
assumptions_latex: The canonical cone, dimensions, and stored-entry layout are fixed.
Every stored canonical-data entry is affine in \theta.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d(\theta)=D\theta+d_0,\qquad \nabla d(\theta)=D.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Parameter-to-Data Operator
Compiled Data-Generation Backends
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric canonical-form data generation after disciplined-convex certification and symbolic canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a certified parametric model, compile its canonicalization map into a routine as follows. Fix a cone product \(K\), a parameter vector \(\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), and sparse templates for the cone program \[\operatorname{minimize}_{x}\;c(\theta)^{\mathsf T}x\quad\operatorname{subject\ to}\quad A(\theta)x+b(\theta)\in K.\] Precompute the sparsity patterns and parameter-to-entry maps for \(A(\theta)\), \(b(\theta)\), and \(c(\theta)\). For each supplied \(\theta\), evaluate only the stored entry maps, assemble the numerical arrays in the fixed sparse layout, and return those arrays with \(K\) and the primal-variable recovery map. Reject inputs outside \(\Theta\) or violating declared dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compile fixed sparsity and parameter-entry maps once; for each parameter value, evaluate and assemble numerical cone-program data, then return it with cone metadata and a solution-recovery map.
assumptions_latex: The model has passed the applicable disciplined-convex certification rules.
Canonicalization fixes the cone product, dimensions, sparse layouts, and recovery map before parameter evaluation.
Every parameter-to-entry map is evaluable on the declared domain \(\Theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted \(\theta\in\Theta\) produces numerical data \((A(\theta),b(\theta),c(\theta),K)\) for the canonical cone program without rebuilding its symbolic graph or sparsity structure.

notation.meaning: Numerical parameter vector supplied at runtime.
Fixed product cone of the canonical problem.

review_flags: implementation-specific mathematical interface requires an authoritative backend specification
no supplied source locator supports compiled sparse data generation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and compiled sparse-data-generation scope fit the terminal container, and the notation is internally coherent. However, no citation supports the specific interface guarantees, including fixed canonical layouts, stored parameter-to-entry maps, recovery-map output, domain rejection, and avoidance of symbolic rebuilding. An authoritative compiled-backend or parametric canonicalization specification with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Model Interchange Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Portable representations for certified models and canonical problem data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic and dimensional validation before semantic decoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A serialized affine-conic record for \(Ax+b\in K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\), with \(A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\), is dimensionally well formed only if \(b\in\mathbb R^r\), the objective coefficient has dimension \(n\), \(\sum_{j=1}^q\dim K_j=r\), and every mapping or reconstruction reference names a declared object of the required type and dimension. These checks certify record consistency, not equivalence to a source model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dimensions, cone blocks, and references must agree, but syntactic validity alone does not certify semantic equivalence.
assumptions_latex: The schema declares dimensions, cone blocks, identifiers, and reference types.
Every encoded cone family has a defined finite-dimensional representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{j=1}^q\dim K_j=r\quad\text{and all typed references are valid}
review_flags: well-formedness is necessary but not sufficient for semantic fidelity
knowledge_statements.title: Interchange Record Well-Formedness Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Format-independent definition of a portable canonical-model interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A model-interchange interface consists of an encoder \(E\), a decoder \(D\), a declared class \(\mathcal M\) of supported models, and a declared semantic equivalence \(\simeq\). It is lossless on \(\mathcal M\) exactly when \(D(E(M))\simeq M\) for every \(M\in\mathcal M\). The equivalence must cover every advertised observable, including feasible-set projection, objective values, variable types, and requested result recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lossless interchange interface must preserve every advertised model and recovery semantic under decode-after-encode.
assumptions_latex: E(M) is defined for every M\in\mathcal M.
\simeq specifies all source-level observables promised by the interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall M\in\mathcal M,\quad D(E(M))\simeq M
knowledge_statements.title: Interchange Interface Semantics

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of lossless translation when the schema omits an observable feature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If some \(M\in\mathcal M\) has an advertised semantic feature that the interchange schema cannot represent and that feature affects \(\simeq\), then no encoder into that schema can be lossless on all of \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schema cannot provide universal lossless translation when it cannot encode an observable semantic feature.

knowledge_statements.title: Unrepresentable-Semantics Boundary
Model Interchange Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A portable, lossless representation of certified canonical cone programs and reconstruction metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A model-interchange record for a certified cone program is a tuple \[\mathcal I=(A,b,c,K,\mathcal V,\mathcal P,\mathcal R),\] representing \[\operatorname{minimize}_{x}\;c^{\mathsf T}x\quad\operatorname{subject\ to}\quad Ax+b\in K.\] Here \(A,b,c\) carry explicit dimensions and numeric types; \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\) carries an ordered list of cone types and dimensions; \(\mathcal V\) maps source variables to canonical coordinates; \(\mathcal P\) records parameter-to-data dependencies when parameters remain; and \(\mathcal R\) reconstructs source-level primal and dual results. Two compliant implementations must decode the same record into the same feasible set and objective value, up to declared coordinate permutations and exact representational equivalences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interchange tuple stores canonical cone data, ordered cone metadata, variable and parameter mappings, and recovery information, preserving feasible points and objective values across compliant implementations.
assumptions_latex: The source model has a valid certified canonical cone representation.
All coordinate permutations, cone orderings, dimensions, and numeric encodings are explicitly declared.
The recovery metadata is defined on every canonical solution exported by the interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decoding \(\mathcal I\) preserves the canonical feasible set and objective, while \(\mathcal R\) maps exported canonical solutions back to the declared source-level quantities.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the terminal container, and the tuple is mathematically intelligible. However, the proposed fields and the cross-implementation preservation guarantee define substantive interchange-format invariants without any cited specification. A precise authoritative source is needed to establish the required metadata, dual-result reconstruction semantics, permitted equivalences, and lossless decoding claim.
